<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) has emerged as a promising minimally invasive biomarker in solid tumors. In primary brain tumors, however, the blood-brain barrier and tumor-specific biological characteristics may limit the detectability and interpretation of plasma-derived biomarkers. Quantitative cfDNA levels and fragment length patterns in plasma from patients with CNS tumors remain insufficiently characterized. This study aimed to investigate cfDNA concentrations and fragment length distributions in plasma from patients with benign and malignant brain tumors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Between April 2022 and March 2024, plasma samples were prospectively collected from patients with intracranial tumors and healthy controls. cfDNA was isolated from preoperative EDTA plasma using the QIAamp Circulating Nucleic Acid Kit (Qiagen). Concentrations were determined using the Qubit dsDNA HS assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and were calculated as ng per ml plasma. Fragment length distributions were analyzed using the Bioanalyzer High Sensitivity DNA Assay (Agilent Technologies).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study included 25 controls, 71 patients with meningioma, and 51 patients with glioblastoma. Plasma cfDNA concentrations differed significantly between groups, showing a stepwise increase from controls (11.44 ng/ml) to meningiomas (18.24 ng/ml) and glioblastomas (21.55 ng/ml) (Kruskal-Wallis test, p = 0.0003). cfDNA fragment lengths both in meningioma and glioblastoma patients showed significantly shorter mononucleosomal cfDNA fragments compared with controls (p &lt; 0.05).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Plasma cfDNA concentrations differ significantly between controls and patients with benign and malignant CNS tumors. Furthermore, fragment length analysis with the Agilent Bioanalyzer showed shortening of cfDNA fragments in meningioma and glioblastoma patients. Our findings support the potential of plasma cfDNA as a biomarker in CNS tumors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: MO04.5.A Plasma cell-free DNA concentrations and fragment length alterations in meningioma and glioblastoma patients

items.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Human umbilical cord platelet-rich plasma (hUC-PRP) has emerged as a promising regenerative therapy for endometrial disorders due to a high content of growth factors and bioactive molecules; however, the cellular mechanisms underlying the regenerative effects of hUC-PRP on the human endometrium remain poorly understood. This study investigated the molecular effects of hUC-PRP on human endometrial organoids (hEOs), with a particular emphasis on the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and the modulatory role of progesterone.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>hEOs derived from healthy donors were cultured under conditions that maintained an undifferentiated state before being treated with progesterone/15% hUC-PRP. hUC-PRP samples were characterized by SomaScan proteomics. Cell viability, immunocytochemistry, EMT-related gene expression, and RT-qPCR analyses were performed to evaluate cellular responses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      hUC-PRP supplementation preserved cell viability while inducing morphological and molecular alterations consistent with EMT in undifferentiated hEOs. hUC-PRP-treated hEOs exhibited loss of epithelial features, acquisition of mesenchymal-like morphology, and significantly upregulated expression of EMT-associated genes (including
                      <jats:italic>COL1A2</jats:italic>
                      ,
                      <jats:italic>FN1</jats:italic>
                      , and
                      <jats:italic>MAP1B</jats:italic>
                      ). Proteomic profiling revealed that hUC-PRP samples contained numerous proteins apparently involved in wound healing processes, and EMT. In contrast, progesterone-treated hEOs largely maintained their epithelial phenotype and functional marker expression (Progesterone-associated endometrial protein; PAEP), while hUC-PRP failed to induce significant EMT-associated transcriptional changes, indicating that progesterone attenuated the EMT-promoting effects of hUC-PRP.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>hUC-PRP supplementation promoted a physiological EMT-like program associated with endometrial regeneration in undifferentiated hEOs, whereas progesterone preserved epithelial identity and mitigated this response. These findings provide mechanistic insight into the regenerative effects of hUC-PRP and establish hEOs as a valuable platform for studying endometrial remodeling and developing regenerative therapies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Human umbilical cord platelet-rich plasma modulates endometrial epithelial cell plasticity: implications for regenerative therapies

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Current standard therapy regimens of high-grade glioma (HGG) often neglect immunomodulatory vulnerabilities, contributing to dismal survival rates. Furthermore, the highly immunosuppressive and heterogeneous tumor microenvironment (TME) remains a barrier to effective treatment and tumor-neuron-immune cell interactions additionally drive tumor progression. Medical gas plasma has emerged as a promising therapeutic modality capable of generating a plethora of short- and intermediate reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (ROS/RNS) that induce selective tumor toxicity and stress signatures linked to immunogenic cell death (ICD). While its anti-tumor activity has been demonstrated in several cancer entities in vivo, the efficacy of gas plasma targeting HGG remains insufficiently investigated.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Primary HGG cell models (IDH-wildtype) were established from patient-derived tumor specimens and exposed to cold atmospheric pressure gas plasma (kINPen MED) under defined conditions. Treatment responses were analyzed by multiplate viability assays, dynamic longitudinal high-content imaging, cell death characterization, measurement of ICD surface marker and cytokine profiles via multicolor flow cytometry, immunofluorescence staining with confocal microscopy and western blot analysis of selected signaling targets.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Gas plasma treatment of primary HGG cells induced significant and complex intracellular oxidation, resulting in a pronounced reduction of metabolic activity, growth inhibition and morphological changes associated with regulated cell death processes, even with short exposure times of few seconds, across all tested primary cell models with distinct mutational backgrounds. Responses varied between the individual cell lines reflecting inter-tumoral heterogeneity and non-malignant control cells were partially less affected. Notably, oxidation significantly increased the exposure of key ICD-surface markers, including the highly pro-immunogenic “eat-me-signal” calreticulin (CRT) on viable survivor cells. In parallel, the secretome was altered upon treatment with pro-inflammatory and danger/stress-related tendencies, indicating broad immunological processes mediated by gas plasma.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Primary HGG cultures can be primed into a pro-immunogenic phenotype using gas plasma oxidation. The findings highlight the potential of this approach as an intraoperative adjuvant therapy to eradicate residual tumor cells at the resection margins while priming the TME for immunotherapy. By expanding the studies onto more advanced models with investigations on specific tumor-immune cell interactions, the potential adjuvant application in neuro-oncology for targeting HGG will be further evaluated.</jats:p>
                    <jats:p>The project is funded by the Mehdorn Family Foundation and the Margaretha Hehberger Cancer Research Fund.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: EP18.23 Induction of immunogenic stress patterns and cell death signatures in patient-derived high-grade glioma cultures through medical gas plasma-mediated oxidation

items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease driven by persistent synovial inflammation. The cGAS-STING innate immune pathway has recently emerged as a critical mediator of inflammatory responses, yet its involvement in RA synovial tissue and modulation by traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) remain unexplored. We hypothesized that paeoniflorin, the core bioactive component of Guizhi-Shaoyao-Zhimu Decoction (GSZD)-a classical TCM formula for RA-exerts anti-inflammatory effects through the cGAS-STING pathway. Using a multi-scale computational strategy, we integrated database- and literature-based compilation of GSZD bioactive components, single-cell RNA-seq analysis of 198,535 RA synovial cells (from 4 patients), revealing 9 distinct cell types, cell–cell communication profiling, network pharmacology, molecular docking, and 100-ns molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with MM-PBSA binding free energy analysis. Pathway activity scoring revealed significantly elevated cGAS-STING signaling in fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLS) compared to other cell types (p = 2.75 × 10
                    <jats:sup>−12</jats:sup>
                    ), with concurrent upregulation of downstream inflammatory mediators including
                    <jats:italic>TNF</jats:italic>
                    ,
                    <jats:italic>TBK1</jats:italic>
                    , and
                    <jats:italic>NFKB1</jats:italic>
                    (all p &lt; 10
                    <jats:sup>-6</jats:sup>
                    ). Network pharmacology identified 37 intersection targets; machine learning identified 20 core targets with
                    <jats:italic>STING1</jats:italic>
                    ranked as a top hub gene. Molecular docking predicted that paeoniflorin binds within the STING ligand-binding region (−8.975 kcal/mol), with affinity comparable to reference STING ligands (ADU-S100 −11.47 kcal/mol; cGAMP −9.59 kcal/mol), and redocking validation confirmed protocol reliability (RMSD = 0.61 Å). One-hundred-nanosecond MD simulations indicated complex stability through RMSD plateau, radius of gyration analysis, and hydrogen-bond occupancy. MM-PBSA analysis yielded a predicted binding free energy of −24.77 ± 3.36 kcal/mol (SD). These computational findings provide the first evidence linking paeoniflorin to the cGAS-STING pathway in RA and propose a computationally predicted mechanism that establishes a foundation for essential future experimental validation.
                  </jats:p>
title: Paeoniflorin targets the cGAS-STING signaling pathway in rheumatoid arthritis: an integrated multi-scale computational study combining single-cell transcriptomics, molecular dynamics simulation, and network pharmacology

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Simulation-based healthcare practice is increasingly recognized as a critical component of healthcare training, yet its infrastructure and implementation vary across regions. We surveyed 246 publicly identifiable simulation centers in the German-speaking European region (Germany, Austria, Switzerland), of which 105 responded, providing a cross-sectional snapshot of responding centers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a cross-sectional survey using an adapted 19-item questionnaire covering demographics, coordinator qualifications, course-level credentials, educational scope, curricula, infrastructure, and technology. Eligible centers were identified through web searches, professional directories, and networks. Data were collected online (November 2024 – May 2025) and analysed using descriptive statistics, with geospatial mapping.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Of 246 publicly identifiable centers contacted, 105 responded (43% response rate). Among identified and responding simulation centers, geographic clustering was observed in urban corridors in Germany and around major cities in Austria and Switzerland, with few or no responding centers reported in regions such as Saarland and Rhineland-Palatinate, parts of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and northern Brandenburg. Among identified and responding centers, Austria and the German-speaking parts of Switzerland showed an apparent geographic concentration, with few responding centers outside major cities such as Vienna, Graz, Zürich, and St. Gallen. Accreditation is heterogeneous: most identified and responding centers do not have formal center-level accreditation, whereas instructor-level certification and qualification is more common, often via InPASS. Patient safety was the dominant mission among identified and responding centers and the uptake of immersive technologies was low, with virtual reality reported by about 22% and augmented reality by about 14% among those centers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among identified and participating centers, the survey showed geographic clustering of those centers, a low prevalence of formal center-level accreditation, and selective uptake of advanced digital tools. Future studies should further investigate regional differences in simulation provision and the potential role of harmonized accreditation and certification, shared and remote solutions, and new technologies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Simulation-based healthcare practice in German-speaking Europe: a cross-sectional survey of publicly identifiable simulation centers

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Accurate prediction of fuel octane numbers, including Research Octane Number (RON) and Motor Octane Number (MON), is a critical technical requirement for reliable quantitative evaluation of fuel knocking propensity in combustion systems. Direct construction of predictive models for these properties from chemistry-derived kinetic features is hindered by the extreme high dimensionality of the raw simulation-generated input space, which leads to unstable training, redundant noise interference, and poor generalization for conventional machine learning architectures. Herein, we present a robust, kinetics-informed modeling framework that maps combustion simulation features to RON and MON values entirely in a compressed principal component space. The input to the model consists of features extracted from homogeneous, constant-volume kinetic simulations of each fuel, namely the initial pressure and temperature, the maximum mole fractions of the individual species and the times at which these maxima are attained, and the first- and second-stage ignition delay times. The workflow first applies Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to reduce the dimensionality of three distinct raw input feature sets, with nominal dimensions of 341, 2764, and 1355 for the Primary Reference Fuel (PRF), 15-alkane, and 346 multi-component blend datasets, respectively. The PCA-transformed low-dimensional features are then used to train two representative supervised learning architectures: Artificial Neural Network (ANN) and Kernel Support Vector Regression (KSVR). A systematic accuracy-versus-complexity comparison further demonstrates that the optimal selection between ANN and KSVR should be guided by explicit project priorities that balance achievable prediction accuracy, model parsimony, and computational training cost.</jats:p>
title: Chemical Kinetic Insights into Octane Numbers Using a Principal Component-Based Machine Learning Approach

items.abstract:
<jats:p>Introduction</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>In 2024, the Association for Simulated Practice in Healthcare celebrated its 15th anniversary. In recognition of this significant milestone, the Association for Simulated Practice in Healthcare engaged with the simulation community in the United Kingdom and the Republic of Ireland to determine how simulation activities, technology-enhanced learning and immersive environments were being utilized within healthcare education and practice in health and social care settings.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Methods</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>This research study employed a Grounded Theory approach. Ethical approval was granted by Edinburgh Napier University Centre for Higher Education Research. This research study included an online survey and focus groups. The survey collected responses from September 2024 to November 2024, with focus groups being delivered in January to February 2025. The survey incorporated questions which were used as part of the first National Simulation Development Project conducted in 2014. This allowed for comparisons to be made with the data reported in 2014 and subsequently 10 years later in 2024. Respondents to the survey were invited to join focus groups where the authors presented concepts and themes which were derived from the data. These themes were discussed and validated as part of this process.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Results</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>In total, 107 surveys were submitted (52% response rate compared with 2014). Of those who completed the survey, 16 individuals attended a focus group (Higher Education Institutions, England [n = 6]; National Health Service, England [n = 8] [secondary care (n = 6); primary care (n = 2)]; Health and Social Care, Northern Ireland [n = 1]; commercial company [n = 1]).</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Discussion</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>This study highlights both progress and persistent challenges in relation to simulation across the United Kingdom and Ireland over the past decade. Whilst adoption has broadened and faculty development has improved, simulation remains under prioritized at organizational levels, with limited funding, inconsistent strategic support and underrepresentation of patient voices. Simulation needs to be conceptualized not only as a pedagogical approach but as a critical healthcare improvement intervention which is embedded within organizational strategy and workforce planning. To ensure sustainability and impact, there is a clear need for multi-sector engagement, robust evaluation frameworks and strategic investment in simulation infrastructure and workforce development.</jats:p>
title: Evolving practice: a grounded theory exploration of the simulation community in the United Kingdom and the Republic of Ireland

items.abstract: <jats:p>We investigate the free-particle linearization of n-dimensional Newtonian systems within the framework of the Eisenhart–Duval lift. For a family of constrained Hamiltonian systems with kinetic term quadratic in the momenta, the Eisenhart–Duval lift allow us to express the dynamics as geodesic equations of a higher-dimensional Riemannian geometry, while the constraint equation keeps the system invariant under conformal transformations. Consequently, when the extended geometry is conformally flat, there exists a coordinate transformation in which the geodesic equations reduce to those of the free particle. We apply this criterion, namely, the vanishing of the Cotton tensor in three dimensions and of the Weyl tensor in higher dimensions for the extended geometry, in order to determine the potential functions Vqk for which the n-dimensional system, n≥2, is free-particle linearizable. The analysis is performed for three different lifting approaches, the Riemannian lift, which introduces one additional degree of freedom, the Lorentzian lift, which introduces two additional degrees of freedom, and for a recently proposed lift with three additional degrees of freedom. A theorem is presented where it gives the linearized n-dimensional Newtonian systems via the Eisenhart–Duval lift. Finally, we discuss the existence of hidden nonlocal symmetries for the original system, which can be seen as local symmetries for the extended geometry.</jats:p>
title: Free-Particle Linearization of n-Dimensional Hamiltonian Systems via the Eisenhart–Duval Lift Approach

items.abstract: <jats:p>Prolonged scanning with a scanning tunneling microscope can induce surface etching characterized by the nucleation, growth, and coalescence of vacancy islands. Motivated by observations on 2H-TaS2, we develop a coarse-grained kinetic Monte Carlo model that couples deterministic tip motion to stochastic vacancy creation, edge removal, and the diffusion, escape, and reattachment of detached material. Starting from an intact surface, the model generates vacancy islands whose subsequent evolution reflects competition between removal and redeposition. Four of the 30 trajectories at an attachment rate of 2 s−1 satisfy a predefined isolated-island duration criterion and exhibit approximately linear perimeter and quadratic area growth over finite intervals. These fits are compatible with the experimental growth forms without establishing universal scaling. Increasing the tip-induced barrier reduction increases net etching, whereas faster reattachment suppresses vacancy production and changes the fraction of etched area contained in the largest island. A two-parameter morphology map distinguishes these effects and shows that greater vacancy coverage need not imply greater connectivity. Direct event tracking identifies coalescence driven by continued edge removal without lateral vacancy hopping or explicit island translation. The event count includes reconnections after reattachment-induced fragmentation. Six kinetic sensitivity tests and a limited triangular-lattice comparison show that vacancy growth persists, while coverage and connectivity depend quantitatively on the rates and lattice representation. The results identify competition between localized material removal and redeposition as a possible mechanism for scanning-induced vacancy-island evolution, with 2H-TaS2 providing experimental motivation rather than a quantitative calibration.</jats:p>
title: Scanning tunneling microscope-induced vacancy-island growth and coalescence: A kinetic Monte Carlo study motivated by 2H-TaS2

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Strain-path modification during rolling provides an effective route of tailoring microstructure, crystallographic texture, and local stress evolution. In this study, the influence of strain-path changes during plane strain compression of copper was investigated using full-field crystal plasticity simulations within the fast Fourier transform-based framework implemented in the Düsseldorf Advanced Material Simulation Kit. A synthetic microstructure reconstructed from electron backscatter diffraction data was subjected to three deformation routes: unidirectional rolling (UDR), two-step cross rolling, and multi-step cross rolling. The simulated texture evolution showed a good agreement with experimentally reported trends, reproducing the transition from a Copper-type texture under UDR to a Brass-type texture during cross rolling. Strain-path changes redistributed resolved shear stresses among the available slip systems, resulting in distinct deformation induced microstructural evolution, enhanced stress heterogeneity, and increased grain-boundary stress concentrations compared with UDR. Analysis of slip activity, equivalent shear rate, and the micromechanical Taylor factor revealed the mechanisms governing strain accommodation and local stress partitioning during rolling. Finally, a Bayesian-optimized extreme gradient boosting model was developed to establish the relationship between crystallographic orientation and the local von Mises stress predicted by crystal plasticity simulations, enabling quantitative evaluation of orientation-dependent stress evolution. The combined computational framework provides mechanistic insights into the influence of strain-path changes on the evolution of microstructure, crystallographic texture, and local stress during rolling.</jats:p>
title: A full-field crystal plasticity simulation of microstructure and texture evolution in copper during strain path change in plane strain compression

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In beam transport applications, especially in large
  experimental facilities, delivering the required beam to the target
  interaction point is usually one of the most critical tasks. Until
  recently, before the advent of automation and artificial
  intelligence, beam transport along the beamline was performed almost
  entirely manually, relying mainly on diagnostics, operator
  experience, and, in some cases, simulation-based approaches. Due to
  the inefficient and time-consuming nature of this procedure,
  innovative solutions based on Artificial Intelligence algorithms are
  currently being investigated.

  In this work, we present an optimization approach for automatic
  beamline tuning based on the combination of a Genetic Algorithm (GA)
  and a Neural Network (NN) surrogate model. The GA is first used as a
  global optimizer to explore the control-parameter space and identify
  suitable regions of operation. The solutions generated during this
  phase are then used to train a Neural Network surrogate that
  approximates the beam transport model locally and to efficiently
  refine the control parameters.

  The method is applied to beam transport simulations along a
  realistic beamline and acts by fine-tuning control variables that
  manage magnetic and electrostatic elements such as dipoles,
  quadrupoles, and steerers. A robustness analysis is performed by
  varying the initial beam size, centroid position, and angular
  divergence.

  The results demonstrate that the Genetic Algorithm provides reliable
  global exploration and the Neural Network refinement significantly
  improves convergence speed and computational efficiency. Compared to
  traditional manual beam tuning procedures, which rely on iterative
  operator intervention and can be time-consuming, the proposed hybrid
  strategy substantially reduces the time required to achieve optimal
  beam transport. It enables efficient and robust beamline autotuning,
  reducing the number of expensive model evaluations while maintaining
  high precision, and represents a promising approach for real-time
  and automated accelerator operation.</jats:p>
title: Autotuning of particle accelerator beamlines using hybrid genetic algorithm and Neural Network optimization

items.abstract: <jats:p>This study aimed to evaluate the physicochemical characteristics, reactive species, storage stability, and antimicrobial activity of plasma-activated water (PAW) generated using gas- and liquid-phase plasma reactors. Plasma was generated using argon, nitrogen, or oxygen as working gases and titanium or silver electrodes. The treatment time was 7 min at 30 kV. The pH, conductivity, temperature, and concentrations of H2O2, NO3−, and NO2− were determined immediately after treatment and after 7 days of storage at 4 °C. Antimicrobial activity was evaluated against Listeria monocytogenes, Salmonella enterica, and Candida utilis after 3 and 24 h of contact. Plasma treatment increased the concentrations of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species. Antimicrobial efficacy was microorganism-dependent and was generally highest for PAW generated in the liquid-phase reactor using a silver electrode. Reductions of up to 5.40 log CFU/mL for S. enterica and 6.68 log CFU/mL for C. utilis were achieved. Storage generally reduced antimicrobial efficacy. PAW demonstrated significant antimicrobial potential, with reactor configuration and electrode material being important determinants of its efficacy. Complementary biological assays indicated no detectable cytotoxicity in the MTT assay, while selected PAW samples exhibited membrane-related and pro-oxidative effects.</jats:p>
title: Influence of Plasma Reactor Configuration on the Physicochemical Properties, Stability, and Biological Activity of Plasma-Activated Water

<jats:p>
                    At muon colliders, muon decays naturally produce intense electrons and positrons with unique features, namely high energies, high repetition rates, and small intrinsic uncertainties, that are unavailable at existing accelerator facilities. We quantitatively study the feasibility of extracting such particles in two representative future muon collider designs, IMCC and
                    <a:math xmlns:a="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <a:mi>μ</a:mi>
                      <a:mi>TRISTAN</a:mi>
                    </a:math>
                    . Using Monte Carlo simulations with the corresponding design parameters, we study the spatial, angular, and energy distributions of decay electrons and positrons in the curved sections of the collider ring. We find that typical deflections of 0.1–10 mrad can be achieved even for high-energy electrons carrying large energy fractions (
                    <c:math xmlns:c="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <c:mrow>
                        <c:mo>≃</c:mo>
                        <c:mn>0.6</c:mn>
                        <c:mi>–</c:mi>
                        <c:mn>1.0</c:mn>
                      </c:mrow>
                    </c:math>
                    ) of the muon beam energy, with the ring bending magnets (or magnets providing an equivalent field) effectively serving as a “preseptum magnet” that partially deflects the beam before the main septum magnet, suggesting that the extraction scheme could be practically feasible. Exploiting the distinct beam properties of IMCC and
                    <e:math xmlns:e="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <e:mi>μ</e:mi>
                      <e:mi>TRISTAN</e:mi>
                    </e:math>
                    , we propose complementary search strategies—missing energy and momentum searches for dark matter at
                    <g:math xmlns:g="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <g:mi>μ</g:mi>
                      <g:mi>TRISTAN</g:mi>
                    </g:math>
                    and visible-decay searches for axionlike particles and light scalars at IMCC—which probe parameter space beyond the reach of current and other proposed experiments.
                  </jats:p>
title: Muon collider experiments as electron and positron beam sources: Case studies of new light-particle searches

items.abstract: <jats:p>A beat-modulated magnetic field unlocks the clinical potential of magnetic particle imaging by driving tracer nanoparticles through an unconventional excitation regime. The magnetization is theoretically computed from the relaxation-to-equilibrium dynamics of fluid-suspended magnetic nanoparticles whose core and hydrodynamic diameters entail finite magnetic-relaxation times and hence hysteretic behavior. Analysis of the low-frequency modulation of the magnetization yields a simple, real-valued system function, a quantity central to image reconstruction. This function is markedly simpler and higher-valued than its counterpart obtained under a constant-amplitude field, enabling a substantial gain in sensitivity with clear practical and clinical impact. Moreover, the model predicts that beat modulation opens periodic time windows in which the nanoparticles’ initial magnetic susceptibility can be directly measured, enabling real-time monitoring of key target parameters such as temperature and viscosity.</jats:p>
title: Beat-modulated magnetic excitation for improved magnetic particle imaging: A theoretical study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Stereo- and enantioselective living coordination cyclopolymerization of 2-methyl-1,5-hexadiene (2-MHD) using a set of cyclopentadienyl, amidinate (CPAM) group 4 metal pre-initiators, in combination with a borate co-initiator, has been reported to produce different stereochemical microstructures of poly(methylene-1,3-(1-methyl)cyclopentane) (PMMCP). Living chain transfer cyclopolymerization of 2-MHD has also been achieved in the presence of excess equivalents of ZnEt2 to provide low molar mass, end-group-functionalized PMMCP of narrow dispersity upon a reactive quench with iodine. Successful use of 2-MHD as a monomer and prior observation of selective polymerizability of 1,5-hexadiene over 1-hexene using the sterically encumbered homochiral pre-initiator (SC, SZr)-4 are rationalized by a kinetic ratchet mechanism accessible to α,ω-nonconjugated dienes but not α-olefins. These results serve to extend the mechanistic picture of coordination cyclopolymerization of α,ω-nonconjugated dienes and provide a foundation for the design of "next-generation" polyolefins.</jats:p>
title: Stereo- and Enantioselective Living Coordination Chain Transfer Cyclopolymerization of 2-Methyl-1,5-Hexadiene: A Kinetic Ratchet Mechanism for the Polymerizability of α,ω-Dienes over α-Olefins

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The clinical translation of mesenchymal stromal cell (MSC) therapy for knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is limited by the absence of a noninvasive method to quantify aspects of intra-articular cell fate through longitudinal tracking of cell-associated tracer kinetics after administration. Here, we report the first-in-human application of quantitative magnetic particle imaging (MPI) for in vivo tracking of intra-articular MSCs. Clinical-grade human umbilical cord-derived MSCs were labeled with ferumoxytol and monitored using open-geometry MPI platforms that enabled both volumetric imaging and bedside regional mapping. In vitro studies showed a strong linear correlation between MPI signal and labeled cell number, supporting quantitative analysis. In a patient with KOA, serial imaging over 10 days demonstrated rapid redistribution of cell-associated signal from the injection site into distinct joint compartments, followed by progressive decline consistent with dynamic post-injection clearance. In an osteoarthritis mouse model, longitudinal MPI kinetics were corroborated by histological detection of the iron label within joint tissues and were associated with reduced cartilage degeneration. Together, these findings establish open-geometry MPI as a clinically practical platform for quantitative cell tracking after local administration. This approach provides a measurable delivery-exposure framework for evaluating cell retention, regional redistribution, and signal persistence, and may help guide dose selection, administration strategies, and treatment optimization for regenerative therapies in osteoarthritis.</jats:p>
title: First-in-human quantitative magnetic particle imaging maps in vivo intra-articular mesenchymal stromal cell kinetics in knee osteoarthritis

items.abstract: <jats:p>Neonatal hypoxic–ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) is a major cause of neonatal mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental disability. Although neuronal energy failure, excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, and cell death remain central to HIE pathogenesis, increasing evidence indicates that HIE is not a neuron-autonomous disorder. Instead, it represents a temporally evolving disturbance of intercellular communication involving neurons, microglia, infiltrating macrophages, astrocytes, oligodendrocyte-lineage cells, endothelial cells, and extracellular vesicles. Early hypoxic–ischemic injury triggers danger-signal release, blood–brain barrier disruption, microglial activation, and peripheral immune-cell recruitment, thereby amplifying neuroinflammation. During the subacute phase, microglial phagocytosis may exert dual effects: timely efferocytosis can promote debris clearance and inflammation resolution, whereas maladaptive phagoptosis may exacerbate neuronal loss. Astrocytes further shape injury and repair through inflammatory reactivity, metabolic support, thyroid hormone shuttling, and potential regenerative reprogramming. Oligodendrocyte-lineage injury, ferroptosis, and impaired myelination link early inflammation to long-term white-matter dysfunction and cognitive impairment. Extracellular vesicles provide an additional non-contact communication route that may modulate apoptosis, inflammasome activation, immune responses, and neural repair. This review summarizes recent advances in cell–cell crosstalk after neonatal HIE and proposes that future therapies should target pathological communication while preserving repair-supportive cellular interactions.</jats:p>
title: Cell–cell crosstalk in neonatal hypoxic–ischemic encephalopathy: from neuroinflammation to repair

items.abstract:
<jats:p>Objetivo: Determinar la correlación entre el Índice Aterogénico del Plasma (IAP) y el Péptido Natriurético tipo B (BNP) en pacientes con Insuficiencia Cardíaca Crónica Agudizada.


Material y métodos: Estudio transversal, correlacional, analítico. A través de un muestreo no probabilístico, fueron evaluados pacientes con insuficiencia cardíaca crónica agudizada, con medición al ingreso de BNP, perfil de lípidos y a quienes fue realizado un ecocardiograma transtorácico durante su hospitalización.


Resultados: Fueron estudiados 30 pacientes con insuficiencia cardíaca agudizada. La mediana de los niveles de BNP al ingreso fue de 764.5 pg/mL, la mediana del IAP fue de 0.51. La media de la fracción de eyección del ventrículo izquierdo (FEVI) obtenida fue de 38%, todos los pacientes presentaron algún grado de disfunción diastólica: el 50% grado 1, el 33.3% grado 2 y sólo el 16.6% grado 3. El coeficiente de correlación de Spearman para el BNP e IAP fue de -0,02213, con un valor de p=0.5.


Conclusiones: El IAP juega un papel como un factor de riesgo cardiovascular, pero no como parte de la evaluación de los pacientes con Insuficiencia Cardíaca Crónica Agudizada. No existe correlación entre el IAP y BNP.</jats:p>
title: Correlación entre el índice aterogénico del plasma y el péptido natriurético tipo B en pacientes con insuficiencia cardíaca cronica agudizada

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Malignant brain tumors are highly lethal, with a median survival of approximately 18 months. Although RNA interference (RNAi) is a promising therapeutic strategy, its clinical application is limited by unstable and complex delivery systems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We developed a self-assembling virus-like particle (VLP) platform based on a four-way junction (4WJ) nucleic acid scaffold and a modular automated production system for efficient siRNA encapsulation. The therapeutic potential of VLPs was evaluated in vitro and in vivo, focusing on cytotoxicity and enhancement of sonodynamic therapy (SDT). MEK-targeting siRNA was identified through screening of the MAPK/ERK pathway and incorporated into the 4WJ scaffold to construct 4WJ@VLP.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>MEK siRNA-loaded VLPs effectively suppressed the MEK pathway and increased PpIX accumulation in tumor cells. This significantly enhanced SDT-induced cytotoxicity in vitro and tumor suppression in vivo.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The 4WJ-based VLP platform provides an efficient siRNA delivery system and enhances SDT efficacy, representing a promising combinational therapeutic strategy for malignant brain tumors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: EP18.27 Development of a Novel 4WJ-Based Virus-Like Particle for siRNA Delivery to Enhance Sonodynamic Therapy in Brain Tumors

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Clear cell renal cell carcinoma exhibits profound metabolic reprogramming. Yet, the mechanisms by which metabolic crosstalk within the tumor microenvironment drives natural killer cell dysfunction and immune evasion remain unclear.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We integrated bulk transcriptomic datasets, single-cell RNA sequencing, clinical tissue validation, and
                      <jats:italic>in vitro</jats:italic>
                      functional experiments to investigate the link between fatty acid and polyamine metabolism and natural killer cell dysfunction in clear cell renal cell carcinoma.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We identified a 6-gene prognostic signature associated with overall survival, with CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein beta (CEBPB) emerging as a key component. Single-cell analysis revealed a distinct S100B
                      <jats:sup>+</jats:sup>
                      natural killer cell population characterized by hypoxia- and metabolic stress-associated transcriptional signatures, higher CEBPB regulon activity, and lower scores for interferon response gene sets. Immunohistochemistry confirmed higher CEBPB expression in high-grade tumors, while multiplex immunofluorescence showed more S100B
                      <jats:sup>+</jats:sup>
                      CD56
                      <jats:sup>+</jats:sup>
                      lymphocytes per field in high-grade tumors. In tumor cells, CEBPB knockdown reduced expression of ornithine decarboxylase 1 and fatty acid synthase. In 786-O/NK-92 co-culture, CEBPB knockdown in tumor cells was associated with increased supernatant lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) activity, reduced S100B and PD-1 expression in NK-92 cells, and a higher proportion of CD107a
                      <jats:sup>+</jats:sup>
                      IFN-γ
                      <jats:sup>+</jats:sup>
                      cells. Putrescine or oleic acid partially reversed these changes, with combined supplementation producing the most complete reversal.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      These findings suggest a connection between CEBPB-associated metabolic processes and S100B
                      <jats:sup>+</jats:sup>
                      natural killer cell phenotypes in clear cell renal cell carcinoma. This tumor–immune metabolic relationship may support strategies to restore natural killer cell activity and improve immunotherapy.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: CEBPB links metabolic alterations to S100B-associated natural killer cell dysfunction in clear cell renal cell carcinoma

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Patients with intracranial meningiomas exhibit an increased risk of venous thromboembolic events (VTE), particularly pulmonary embolisms (PE), with reported incidences of 6-8% and mortality of 10-14%. Postoperative PE represents a potentially life-threatening complication and may delay recovery or adjuvant treatment. Early detection of both symptomatic and subclinical PE is therefore clinically relevant, especially as direct oral anticoagulants have not been shown to increase postoperative hemorrhage risk in this setting. This study evaluated postoperative D-dimer levels as a pragmatic tool for PE risk stratification following meningioma surgery.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>All patients undergoing meningioma resection between 2019 and 2025 with D-dimer measurement on postoperative day 3 were retrospectively analyzed. Cut-off values were adopted from Inoue et al. Patients with D-dimer levels &gt;8.2 mg/L underwent CT angiography and lower extremity venous ultrasound. Values between 5.5-8.2 mg/L were reassessed on the following day; further diagnostics were performed only in cases of rising levels. PE-positive and PE-negative groups were compared using the Mann-Whitney U and Welch t-tests. Sensitivity and specificity were calculated for different cut-offs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Twenty-nine patients were included. PE was detected in 20.7%, with 66% presenting with dyspnea or tachycardia. No deep vein thrombosis was identified. Median D-dimer levels were significantly higher in PE-positive patients (15.79 mg/L, CI 11.47-19.22) compared to PE-negative patients (2.43 mg/L, CI 1.58-3.4) (p &lt; 0.01). WHO grading showed no association (p = 1). A cut-off of 5 mg/L achieved 100% sensitivity and 83% specificity, while 8 mg/L achieved 83% sensitivity and 100% specificity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Postoperative D-dimer assessment after meningioma resection appears suitable for PE detection and allows clinically meaningful risk stratification. Larger studies are required to validate these findings. Structured postoperative D-dimer screening may support implementation of standardized diagnostic algorithms.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: EP13.24 Association of postoperative D-dimer plasma levels with pulmonary embolism after meningioma surgery

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is characterized by spatially heterogeneous degeneration, with the medial and lateral compartments frequently experiencing different mechanical and pathological conditions. However, the cellular states and molecular programs underlying compartment-specific remodeling of the subchondral bone microenvironment remain incompletely understood.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed on medial and lateral subchondral bone samples obtained from patients with knee OA to characterize cellular composition, transcriptional states, functional pathways, and exploratory pseudotime-associated transcriptional patterns. Compartment-associated differences in cell abundance and gene-expression programs were systematically evaluated. Selected differentially expressed proteins were further examined by immunohistochemistry.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Twelve major cell types were identified, with marked differences in their relative distributions between compartments. The medial compartment showed higher proportions of chondrocytes, dendritic cells, endothelial cells, memory B cells, and CD8
                      <jats:sup>+</jats:sup>
                      T cells, whereas osteoblasts and mesenchymal stromal cells showed higher proportions in the lateral compartment. Exploratory pseudotime analysis revealed differences in the distribution of medial and lateral cells across computationally inferred transcriptional states. Medial cells showed enrichment of immune-associated, extracellular-matrix-remodeling, and bone-remodeling signatures, whereas several metabolic programs were relatively less represented. Further subclustering demonstrated substantial transcriptional and functional heterogeneity among chondrocytes, osteoblasts, endothelial cells, fibroblasts, and mesenchymal stromal cells. Immunohistochemical analysis supported the transcriptomic findings, showing lower IGFBP3 and higher SPARC staining in medial than in lateral subchondral bone and cartilage.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study establishes a single-cell landscape of medial and lateral subchondral bone in knee OA and identifies compartment-specific differences in cellular composition, cell-state transitions, and molecular programs. The medial compartment displayed stronger immune- and remodeling-associated transcriptional signatures, providing a cellular framework for understanding spatially heterogeneous osteochondral remodeling in OA and prioritizing candidate pathways for future functional validation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Single-cell transcriptomics analysis of medial–lateral compartment heterogeneity in osteoarthritic knee subchondral bone

<jats:p>
                    A fast parton moving through the quark-gluon plasma trails a wake of color fields, usually characterized through its screening cloud and the associated energy loss. Its behavior in a plasma carrying a chiral imbalance, set by a chiral chemical potential
                    <a:math xmlns:a="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <a:msub>
                        <a:mi>μ</a:mi>
                        <a:mn>5</a:mn>
                      </a:msub>
                    </a:math>
                    , remains largely unexplored, in particular, whether the imbalance induces a parity-odd component in the wake. We address this within chiral kinetic theory with Berry curvature corrections, at finite
                    <c:math xmlns:c="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <c:msub>
                        <c:mi>μ</c:mi>
                        <c:mn>5</c:mn>
                      </c:msub>
                    </c:math>
                    and zero magnetic field. The screening sector responds to
                    <e:math xmlns:e="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <e:msub>
                        <e:mi>μ</e:mi>
                        <e:mn>5</e:mn>
                      </e:msub>
                    </e:math>
                    only weakly, and solely through the Debye mass. The chiral imprint instead resides in a parity-odd sector comprising an azimuthal field encircling the parton, a poloidal chromomagnetic field, and a circulating color current. All three are linear in

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>A major obstacle to data-driven oncology research is frequently the lack of substantial, well-annotated clinical and proteomic datasets, especially for conditions like endometrial cancer. Data-silo restrictions, privacy laws, and the high cost of mass spectrometry further limited access to real patient data. This paper presents SynthProteomics, an open-source, Gradio-based Python framework for creating realistic, unidentifiable synthetic datasets in the proteomic and clinical fields. A probabilistic, rule-based engine simulates clinical profiles, modelling interdependencies among patient characteristics such as age, cancer stage, and obesity. To ensure the data retained proper biological consistency, proteomic profiles were further validated against the Human Protein Atlas database and the published endometrial cancer literature in PubMed. SynthProteomics supports hypothesis testing, machine learning model training, and algorithm validation while also maintaining clinical plausibility. The generated data were evaluated with a Random Forest classifier, achieving 82 per cent accuracy on the synthetic held-out set and 74 per cent on the real cohort. SynthProteomics fills a crucial gap: no publicly available tool currently synthesises validated clinical and proteomic data for endometrial cancer research.</jats:p>
title: SynthProteomics: A Probabilistic Fuzzy Rule-Based Framework for Synthetic Clinical and Proteomics Data Simulation in Endometrial Cancer Research

items.abstract: <jats:p>This work analyzed the performance of a Support Vector Regression (SVR) model using four kernel functions (sigmoid, polynomial, linear and Radial Basis Function (RBF)) and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) algorithm to optimize the hyperparameters of the model. The results of cross validation showed that the RBF kernel made the best initial performance using the CV-RMSE measure, while the test results showed that the linear kernel performed better using the RMSE, MAE, MAPE and coefficient of Determination (R²). The optimization process identified substantial changes in the hyperparameters: the value of C was significantly increased, that of Gamma was increased and the value of Epsilon was reduced by 90%, which indicates that these hyperparameters underwent a recalibration to improve the model's predictive accuracy. Standard model results were compared with the PSO optimized model and found that the RMSE of the optimized model (4,653.33) was about 36.4% less than the standard model (7,320.49) thus showing the effectiveness of the optimization to reduce prediction errors. Additionally, graphical comparison showed good agreement between the actual and predicted prices for the optimized model at low to intermediate price levels, with some discrepancies at high and extreme price levels. According to the results, the combination of PSO algorithm and SVR model is effective in improving the precision of prediction and estimating the price of scrap.</jats:p>
title: Evaluating the Predictive Performance of a Support Vector Regression Model and Optimizing It Using Particle Swarm Optimization for Scrap Price Estimation

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We propose a model, consisting of an Long Short‐Term Memory Encoder‐Decoder backbone along with a novel late dynamic fusion mechanism for adaptively integrating learned representations from multisource hydrometeorological data for 7‐day‐ahead streamflow forecasting. This model is applied to both univariate (single‐flow gauge) and multivariate (multi‐gauge) streamflow forecasting in Severn Basin (UK), known for prolonged medium‐to high‐flow periods. Results show that the proposed dynamic fusion approach exceeded the attention‐based fusion, with an average improvement of 5.54% in Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and 3.55% in  for overall and high‐flow accuracy. Furthermore, the proposed approach outperforms traditional machine‐learning baselines, lowering overall MAE by up to 12.1% and high‐flow errors by up to 16.8%. Additionally, multivariate models are significantly faster in both training and inference by 76% and yield comparable accuracy to univariate models, but uncertainty analysis reveals that are more sensitive to the high‐flows than the latter. Overall, the model achieved a Nash‐Sutcliffe Efficiency of 0.76. Finally, the use of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (KernelSHAP) confirmed the dominant role of precipitation, past river flows, and the most recent timesteps in the underlying hydrologic process.</jats:p>
title: High‐Flow Forecasting With a Deep Learning‐Based Dynamic Feature Fusion Approach

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The Southern Annular Mode (SAM), the dominant mode of extratropical atmospheric variability in the Southern Hemisphere (SH), is conventionally represented as a single empirical orthogonal function (EOF) whose polarity and amplitude vary over time. Although highly informative, this framework favors high‐variance patterns and therefore may obscure differences among circulation patterns with similar SAM polarity. Here, we combine a convolutional autoencoder with hierarchical clustering of ERA5 monthly mean sea level pressure anomalies to develop a class‐based representation of SH circulation that does not prioritize such high‐variance patterns. Across 10 random initializations, the framework consistently identifies coherent SAM+ and higher‐amplitude SAM− classes. In nine of the 10 initializations, it also identifies a more frequently occupied, lower‐amplitude SAM− like class. This class is strongly correlated with empirical orthogonal function in the SAM− direction and differs significantly from zero over much of the domain, but is substantially more regionally asymmetric than the higher‐amplitude, strongly annular SAM− class. Transitions between the two SAM− like classes tend to occur more often than expected from their overall frequencies, although this enrichment is not statistically significant, whereas direct transitions between higher‐amplitude SAM− and SAM+ occur less often than expected. Seasonal analyses further reveal lower‐amplitude, non‐annular structures whose frequency and form vary throughout the year. These results suggest that SAM− variability may comprise both higher‐amplitude annular events and lower‐amplitude, regionally asymmetric events. The autoencoder framework therefore complements the conventional SAM index by distinguishing differences in amplitude, spatial structure, and temporal organization that are compressed within a single EOF pattern.</jats:p>
title: Beyond a Single Southern Annular Mode Pattern: Identifying Southern Hemisphere Circulation Classes With a Convolutional Autoencoder

items.abstract: <jats:p>Voltage-source inverters supply the permanent magnet synchronous motors (PMSMs) of electric vehicles and industrial drives, and their switches often fail. This paper evaluates machine learning and deep learning models for nine operating conditions of an inverter-driven PMSM (normal operation and two open-circuit, three short-circuit and three overheating faults), using a public 24-channel dataset sampled at 10 Hz. Each class was recorded as one contiguous block, so random splits place near-copies of test windows in the training set. A blocked 5-fold cross-validation with a guard band equal to the window length was used, and all model choices were made on chronological inner validation splits. Eighteen analytical classifiers and nineteen deep architectures with two ensembles were trained on features from five signal transforms and explained with LIME and SHAP. CatBoost reached 98.99 ± 2.01% accuracy and an ensemble of five Transformers 98.78 ± 2.13%. With a fixed, preliminary feature set, a random split raised the mean accuracy of the analytical models from 94.95% to 99.49%. The raw logs show that every class is a separate recording. The temperature channels alone gave up to 99.2% accuracy and the electrical channels alone at most 77.3%, and a 1 °C thermistor offset lowered CatBoost to 47.4%. The results therefore describe discrimination within these recordings, not transfer to new sessions.</jats:p>
title: Leakage-Free Evaluation of Machine Learning and Deep Learning Models for Fault Diagnosis of Inverter-Driven PMSM Drives

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The application of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) in pediatric neurosurgery is on the rise, especially in the field of neuroimaging. However, the literature on the application of AI/ML in pediatric neurosurgery is fragmented. In pediatric neurosurgery, there are challenges in the application of AI/ML, especially in terms of sample size, developmental considerations, and safety.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In order to systematically review the applications of AI in pediatric neurosurgery across the following domains: (1) diagnosis and image-based classification, (2) surgical planning and patient selection, and (3) prediction of treatment response and clinical outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A systematic literature search was performed on electronic databases like MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore from database inception to August 31, 2025, and was updated prior to manuscript submission. Human studies published in English language and conducted on children with neurosurgical conditions and age ≤ 18 years were included. The included studies should involve AI/ML and deep learning techniques for diagnosis, surgical planning, and outcome prediction in hydrocephalus, brain tumors, epilepsy surgery, traumatic brain injury, and neonatal brain injuries. Total 20 studies were included in this systematic review. The bias was evaluated with tools like QUADAS 2, PROBAST, and Cochrane RoB 2. GRADE was used to grade the evidence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among the 20 studies, 8 related to hydrocephalus, 6 to brain tumors, 2 to epilepsy surgery, and 4 to traumatic or hemorrhagic brain injury. Twelve studies evaluated diagnosis and segmentation, and eight focused on outcome prediction. Deep learning models demonstrated high performance in ventricular segmentation and tumor classification (Dice 0.85–0.95; accuracy 84–95%). In addition, prognostic models demonstrated moderate discrimination (AUC 0.70–0.90), though they frequently lacked external validation. One randomized study demonstrated that NLP-based alerts improved timely referral for epilepsy surgery compared with usual care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AI techniques show significant promise in pediatric neurosurgery, particularly for ventricular volumetry, tumor imaging, and surgical decision-making. Most published works currently rely on retrospective study designs, emphasizing a critical need for multicenter validation, calibration reporting, and prospective clinical trials before widespread implementation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical trial number</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Not applicable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Machine learning and deep learning applications in pediatric neurosurgery: a systematic review of diagnostic, prognostic, and decision support tools

items.abstract: <jats:p>This study used machine learning (ML) to predict and interpret the short-term compressive creep response of bamboo scrimber parallel to the grain using published experimental data. A database comprising 29 creep curves and 1982 data points was compiled from three published studies, with compressive strength parallel to the grain, load level, temperature, relative humidity, and loading time used as input features. Four ML models based on k-nearest neighbors, support vector regression, extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), and artificial neural network (ANN) algorithms were developed and evaluated. ANN achieved the highest testing accuracy, with a coefficient of determination of 0.999, a root mean square error of 0.01, and a mean absolute error of 0.01. XGBoost and ANN were selected as representative tree-based and neural network models for curve reconstruction and interpretation using Shapley additive explanations. Both models reproduced the general trends of the sampled creep curves, with ANN generating smoother predictions than XGBoost in the examined cases. Load level and temperature were identified as the most influential features in the model predictions. Relative humidity showed low apparent importance within the narrow range represented in the database, indicating a need for data covering broader humidity conditions. An ANN-based graphical user interface was developed to visualize and export predicted creep curves for exploratory estimation within the conditions represented in the database.</jats:p>
title: Prediction of Compressive Creep Parallel to the Grain in Bamboo Scrimber Using Machine Learning

items.abstract: <jats:p>The issue of predicting stock prices is no secret. This review looks at papers from 2018-2026 that look at various models both from a traditional ML perspective (random forests, gradient boosting, support vectors) and from a deep learning perspective (LSTM, graph networks, transformers) and how they can be applied to big data analytics. Overall deep models offer superiority on richer/higher frequency data whereas tree based models offer continual competitiveness on tabular data. However, evaluation can be very important and issues such as leakage and not considering transaction cost can occur. Section 6 provides some key findings. Section 7 details some open questions. Finally, there is a brief discussion of what is going on at a broader level within India regarding data analytics, AI adoption and financial institutions.</jats:p>
title: Big Data Analytics on Stock Price Prediction: A Comparative Study of Machine Learning and Deep Learning Models (2018-2026)

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Accurate prediction of fuel octane numbers, including Research Octane Number (RON) and Motor Octane Number (MON), is a critical technical requirement for reliable quantitative evaluation of fuel knocking propensity in combustion systems. Direct construction of predictive models for these properties from chemistry-derived kinetic features is hindered by the extreme high dimensionality of the raw simulation-generated input space, which leads to unstable training, redundant noise interference, and poor generalization for conventional machine learning architectures. Herein, we present a robust, kinetics-informed modeling framework that maps combustion simulation features to RON and MON values entirely in a compressed principal component space. The input to the model consists of features extracted from homogeneous, constant-volume kinetic simulations of each fuel, namely the initial pressure and temperature, the maximum mole fractions of the individual species and the times at which these maxima are attained, and the first- and second-stage ignition delay times. The workflow first applies Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to reduce the dimensionality of three distinct raw input feature sets, with nominal dimensions of 341, 2764, and 1355 for the Primary Reference Fuel (PRF), 15-alkane, and 346 multi-component blend datasets, respectively. The PCA-transformed low-dimensional features are then used to train two representative supervised learning architectures: Artificial Neural Network (ANN) and Kernel Support Vector Regression (KSVR). A systematic accuracy-versus-complexity comparison further demonstrates that the optimal selection between ANN and KSVR should be guided by explicit project priorities that balance achievable prediction accuracy, model parsimony, and computational training cost.</jats:p>
title: Chemical Kinetic Insights into Octane Numbers Using a Principal Component-Based Machine Learning Approach

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Lake Urmia has undergone severe contraction under interacting hydroclimatic and human pressures operating across multiple timescales. We developed an integrated multi-source framework combining satellite and reanalysis products, ground-based meteorological and hydrometric observations, groundwater and agricultural records, and groundwater-quality data with trend, change-point, lagged, Granger, and explainable machine-learning analyses. Lake surface-water area declined significantly, with a major change point in 2012. Ground-based precipitation showed the clearest short-term signal, with a significant positive association at a one-month lag and significant Granger-based temporal predictability after false-discovery-rate correction. XGBoost achieved the strongest held-out performance (R
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                     = 0.52, RMSE = 567.1 km
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    , MAE = 436.3 km
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    ). Its leading predictors were ground-based precipitation, atmospheric water vapor, total wells, water balance, and satellite/reanalysis wind speed. Climatic, hydrological, and five measured anthropogenic predictors accounted for 55.03%, 29.83%, and 15.14% of XGBoost SHAP attribution, respectively. Staged modelling increased held-out R
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    from 0.297 for climate only to 0.468 with hydrological predictors and 0.521 with anthropogenic predictors. Groundwater-quality mapping revealed marked spatial hydrochemical heterogeneity. These results indicate that short-term lake variability is most clearly associated with hydroclimatic conditions, while measured anthropogenic pressures provide additional longer-term model information.
                  </jats:p>
title: Multi-timescale climatic, hydrological and anthropogenic signals of Lake Urmia decline revealed by explainable machine learning

items.abstract: <jats:p>Accurate short-term forecasting of urban carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions is important for characterizing temporal emission patterns and evaluating the predictive capability of data-driven models. However, estimated daily urban CO2 emission series often exhibit nonlinear fluctuations and complex temporal dependencies, posing challenges for reliable forecasting. Kernel Extreme Learning Machine (KELM) provides a computationally efficient nonlinear regression framework, but its forecasting performance is sensitive to the selection of regularization and kernel parameters. To address this issue, this study proposes a Competitive Adaptive Dual-Strategy Zebra Optimization Algorithm (CADS-ZOA) and integrates it with KELM for hyperparameter optimization, establishing a CADS-ZOA-KELM model for urban carbon dioxide emission forecasting. First, a competitive dual-target guided foraging strategy is developed to enhance the diversity of search directions by incorporating competitive guidance from two target solutions and population differential information. Second, a success-feedback adaptive search strategy is introduced to dynamically adjust search parameters by combining individual search success rates with historical memories of successful parameter settings. Third, a diversity-aware dual-scale defense strategy is designed to adaptively balance global exploration and local exploitation according to population diversity. To evaluate the optimization performance of CADS-ZOA, comparative experiments are conducted against nine representative optimization algorithms on the 30-dimensional CEC2017 and the 10-dimensional and 20-dimensional CEC2020 benchmark suites, supplemented by Wilcoxon rank-sum tests and Friedman average ranking analysis. The experimental results show that CADS-ZOA achieves average ranks of 1.57, 2.45, and 1.65 across the three benchmark configurations. For practical forecasting applications, daily carbon dioxide emission data from Beijing covering January 1, 2020, to April 30, 2026, are employed, and the proposed CADS-ZOA-KELM model is compared with five forecasting models, namely KELM, SVR, LSSVM, GRU, and LSTM. In the reported forecasting comparison, CADS-ZOA-KELM achieves an MAE of 9.245 Kt, an RMSE of 12.180 Kt, a MAPE of 2.041%, and an R2 of 0.9082, obtaining the lowest reported prediction errors among the six evaluated models. Compared with conventional grid-search KELM, the MAE and RMSE are reduced by approximately 1.12% and 0.88%, respectively. However, the two hyperparameter selection methods were evaluated under unequal computational budgets, and the observed improvements are relatively modest. Therefore, the results demonstrate competitive one-day-ahead forecasting performance for the investigated estimated emission series but do not establish a practically significant advantage or direct benefits for urban carbon management.</jats:p>
title: Urban Carbon Dioxide Emission Forecasting Based on Machine Learning Methods for Low-Carbon Planning

items.abstract: <jats:p>Background/Objectives: High-dimensional transcriptomic biomarker studies are vulnerable to information leakage and unstable feature selection. This study aimed to develop and evaluate a stability-aware explainable machine learning framework for identifying epilepsy-associated transcriptomic biomarkers. Methods: GSE143272 was analyzed using 51 healthy controls and 34 drug-naive patients with epilepsy. The workflow combined descriptive differential expression, leakage-controlled nested cross-validation, repeated nested-selection stability, probe-to-gene consolidation, post hoc explainability, and exploratory functional enrichment. Discovery-derived candidates were fixed before cross-cohort/cross-tissue assessment in hippocampal GSE256068. Results: The primary pooled outer-fold ROC-AUC was 0.875 (bootstrap interval 0.793–0.945), with a balanced accuracy of 0.824. Repeated nested-selection analysis across 100 outer-training partitions revealed that the three most commonly selected genes among the 15 discovery-prioritized genes were ADCY7 (0.81), TNFSF14 (0.74), and FOXC2 (0.69). These rates are not indicative of independent biological replication, but rather of within-cohort model-selection recurrence. Fourteen prioritized genes were evaluable externally; seven had the same effect sign, although three had near-null external effects. FOXC2, TBXAS1, and MRPS31 were directionally concordant and FDR-significant. The fixed 14-gene directional score showed poor observed cross-context discrimination (AUC 0.356; stratified-bootstrap interval 0.173–0.565); the interval included 0.5, so the result does not establish inverse discrimination or equivalence to chance. Conclusions: The framework separates statistical association, predictive performance, feature-selection recurrence, explainability, and cross-context concordance. It identifies a recurrent within-cohort core with gene-specific, limited external concordance and requires independent peripheral-blood replication.</jats:p>
title: A Stability-Aware Explainable Machine Learning Framework for Peripheral Blood Transcriptomic Biomarker Discovery in Epilepsy

items.abstract: <jats:p>The study on consumer behavior deals with purchase intention followed by purchase decision and post purchase experience of consumption and evaluation, which can be received by manufacturer in the form of feedback. All purchase intentions do not transform into visible purchase decision because of several reasons or factors such as cognitive factors, emotional factors, situational, demographic and other factors. Certain components of these factors can be strategically dealt with by sales persons of automobile companies through fruitful communication, which is extremely useful to reduce confusion in minds of potential customers arising from perceived differences between desired and offered functionalities in the products. In this paper we propose a machine learning based method ML-ASA to assist sales persons of automobiles, in showrooms of various companies, to estimate purchase decision of potential customers and their probable choices of vehicle models.  ML-ASA computes probable purchase decision  based on a support vector machine or SVM  which outputs 1 if the customers purchase intention from the current manufacturer is strong.  Otherwise it returns 0. Also the essential set of attributes are identified which must be included in persuasion efforts from the sales person’s part. Vehicle models are demonstrated in decreasing order of popularity where popularity is  based on customers choice record in the showroom and prediction of sales records in the next quarter.  We have used auto-regressive moving average or ARMA model for sales prediction purpose of different vehicle models belonging to automobile companies Maruti Suzuki, Honda, Kia, Porsche, Tata, Mahindra, Hyundai, Bajaj and Toyota. Experiments are conducted using R 4.0.3 and results show that our model achieves high (>90%) accuracy, precision and recall.</jats:p>
title: From Purchase Intention to Purchase Decision - A Machine Learning Based Approach in Context of Automobile Industry of India

items.abstract: <jats:p>Machine-learning models frequently receive incomplete, noisy, ambiguous, or distribution-shifted observations. Probability-based predictors quantify stochastic variability but do not by themselves provide a linguistic representation of ambiguous feature boundaries or transparent rule-level reasoning. This article develops a proposed, uncertainty-aware fuzzy mathematical architecture integrating input membership representations, intuitionistic hesitation, reliability-weighted aggregation, Takagi–Sugeno rules, robust loss minimization, and decision abstention. It specifies assumptions, derives a boundedness result for normalized rule aggregation, and supplies a fully worked numerical example with synthetic values. Three original conceptual figures present the architecture, overlapping partitions, and uncertainty-to-response mapping. The work is theoretical and illustrative: no benchmark experiment, performance gain, or clinical/industrial validation is claimed. A reproducible evaluation protocol identifies how accuracy, calibration, coverage, resilience to corruption, and interpretability would be assessed in future empirical studies. The synthesis emphasizes complementary rather than interchangeable roles for fuzzy possibility, probabilistic uncertainty, and distributional robustness.</jats:p>
title: Fuzzy Mathematical Frameworks for Enhancing Machine Learning under Uncertain Conditions
