items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Water stable isotopes (δ²H, δ
                    <jats:sup>18</jats:sup>
                    O) are powerful tracers of water cycling in the groundwater–soil–plant–atmosphere continuum, yet most conventional approaches rely on destructive, labor-intensive sampling that provides only discrete temporal snapshots.
                    <jats:italic>In situ</jats:italic>
                    vapor-equilibration techniques coupled to laser spectroscopy now enable continuous monitoring of soil and xylem water isotopes, bypassing extraction artefacts and targeting the mobile water pool in both soils and plants. Building on more than a decade of methodological development, we contrast commercially available systems such as the water isotope probe (WIP) with the stem borehole equilibration (SBE) approach, highlighting their shared physical basis but differing costs, flexibility, and field practicality. We synthesize evidence that
                    <jats:italic>in situ</jats:italic>
                    datasets have provided unique ecohydrological insights-including dynamic root water uptake profiles, water age and storage effects, and hydraulic redistribution-and substantially improved the performance of site-scale soil–vegetation–atmosphere transfer (SVAT) and soil–plant–atmosphere continuum (SPAC) models, while noting that benefits for larger-scale climate models remain underexplored. We critically assess five persistent challenges: technical complexity and costs, reliable measurement at natural isotopic abundance, organic contamination and spectral interference, and ambiguity about the water pools sampled by different methods. We argue that carefully implemented
                    <jats:italic>in situ</jats:italic>
                    methods, supported by standardized calibration and post-processing workflows, explicit tests of isotopic equilibrium, and robust diagnosis and mitigation of organic contamination (e.g., micro-combustion modules), provide the most internally consistent means of linking soil and plant water isotope signals. Finally, we outline priorities for the community-including open processing protocols, coordinated long-term datasets, and closer collaboration with modelers-and recommend wider adoption of
                    <jats:italic>in situ</jats:italic>
                    monitoring because the potential gains in understanding root water uptake, transport, plasticity, and ecohydrological water cycling justify the remaining methodological effort.
                  </jats:p>
title: In situ xylem water isotope monitoring: from promise to practice

<jats:p>
                    This study presents new results from sulfur (
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">
                        <mml:mi>δ</mml:mi>

                    <jats:inline-formula>

                        <mml:mi>δ</mml:mi>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ¹³C), and oxygen (
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">
                        <mml:mi>δ</mml:mi>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ¹⁸O) isotope analyses of sulfide and carbonate minerals from the Mundonguara Cu- Ni -Au deposit in the Manica Greenstone Belt, Mozambique. Copper and nickel are key metals for electrification and battery technologies, respectively, placing such deposits at the core of the global energy transition and critical metals supply. Previous interpretations of the deposit as a syngenetic Cu-Ni system are challenged by integrated petrographic, structural, mineralogical, geochemical, and isotopic evidence supporting an epigenetic origin. Mineralization is structurally controlled, occurring as veins, patches, and schlieren dominated by chalcopyrite and pyrrhotite, with accessory cobaltite, pentlandite, native gold, and tellurides. Elevate Cu/Ni ratios and alteration assemblages (talc, chlorite, amphibole, carbonate, albite) indicate hydrothermal fluid circulation along shear zones, influenced by lithological and structural controls. Sulfur isotope values (
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">
                        <mml:mi>δ</mml:mi>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ³⁴S -0.4‰ to +4.0‰) point to a predominantly magmatic sulfur source, while carbon and oxygen isotopes from carbonates (
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">
                        <mml:mi>δ</mml:mi>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ¹³C -7.5‰ to -4.3‰,
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">
                        <mml:mi>δ</mml:mi>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ¹⁸O +6.5‰ to +8.5‰) suggest fluids of magmatic-hydrothermal origin with minor crustal input. Regional carbonate alteration in komatiites appears unrelated to ore formation and likely reflects earlier seafloor or metamorphic processes. These results redefine the genetic model of the Mundonguara deposit, as an atypical orogenic Au system enriched in Cu-Ni, expanding the range of Archean ore forming processes and providing new exploration criteria for critical and energy-transition metals in greenstone belts terranes.
                  </jats:p>
title: Sulfur, carbon and oxygen isotope constraints on the origin of the Mundonguara Cu-Au deposit, Manica, Mozambique

items.abstract: <jats:p>Man-made disasters are always shocking, especially when they involve loss of life. The shock is even greater when such disasters are attributed to failures in highly regulated organizations like Boeing, long known for engineering excellence and safety. In the spirit of pragmatic inquiry that considers attenuating the likelihood of disasters an urgent and important problem, we explore the underlying dynamics that can lead to such outcomes. We draw on an agent-based modelling approach within a system dynamics framework. We argue that operational and organizational complexity creates barriers to identifying failures that contribute to disasters. A key contributor to this dynamic is the weakening of regulatory oversight, as both regulators and operators fall into a “confidence trap” – a mistaken belief that past risk-taking success justifies continued risk-taking. This dynamic is exacerbated when the organization in question is perceived as “too big to fail,” which shields it from market selection mechanisms. To mitigate these factors, we propose two policy levers. First, we propose financial clawbacks that require executives to return part of their compensation in the event of a disaster. This aligns incentives of the regulator and executives by injecting the latter’s “skin in the game,” and attenuates the moral hazard problem. Second, we propose third-party monitoring and auditing that serve to mitigate regulatory oversight and better utilize expertise. Simulations indicate these levers significantly reduce the likelihood and impact of failures that lead to disasters, offering a robust logic of pursuit.</jats:p>
title: EXPRESS: Supercharging the Confidence Trap: Too-Big-to-Fail and Man-Made Disasters

<jats:p>
                    Traceability is essential for mitigating food fraud and ensuring regulatory compliance, requiring reliable markers to verify geographic origin. While environmental factors imprint unique isotopic signatures on agricultural products, management practices such as irrigation can complicate provenance assessments. This study evaluates the impact of irrigation source, volume, and timing on strontium isotope ratios (
                    <jats:sup>87</jats:sup>
                    Sr/
                    <jats:sup>86</jats:sup>
                    Sr) in
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">Vitis vinifera</jats:italic>
                    (Shiraz) grapes and vineyard soils within South Australia's Barossa zone.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    Analysis focused on the mobile, bioavailable fraction of the soil solution – the primary source for plant uptake – rather than bulk geology. Results demonstrate that bioavailable
                    <jats:sup>87</jats:sup>
                    Sr/
                    <jats:sup>86</jats:sup>
                    Sr signatures in both grapes and soils remain remarkably consistent across varied irrigation treatments and seasonal conditions. Furthermore, strontium ratios in grapes and soils align closely with each other and local groundwater, suggesting they serve as reliable mutual proxies. Unlike oxygen isotopes, which are sensitive to seasonal fluctuations, bioavailable strontium exhibits high temporal stability. This robustness underscores the utility of
                    <jats:sup>87</jats:sup>
                    Sr/
                    <jats:sup>86</jats:sup>
                    Sr as a dependable indicator of geographic origin, even in viticultural systems subject to intensive agricultural management. These findings strengthen the framework for using strontium isoscapes in global agricultural traceability.
                  </jats:p>
title: From soil to fruit: robust strontium isotope signatures for origin authentication in irrigated agriculture

items.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Digitalization is reshaping agricultural production through improvements in information access, production efficiency, market coordination, and factor mobility, yet its relationship with realized grain production may differ from its effects on productivity or production capacity. This study examines whether digital economy development is associated with provincial grain output in China and whether this relationship reflects changes in production scale, regional heterogeneity, and spatial interactions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A balanced panel of 31 Chinese provinces from 2011 to 2024 was analyzed using province and year fixed effects and province-clustered inference. Output decomposition, instrumented estimates, formal regional interactions and two-way fixed-effects spatial models were supplemented with alternative digital-index measurement, historical-exposure and time-trend sensitivity checks, weak-instrument-robust inference, and province-deletion diagnostics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The baseline digital-economy association with provincial grain output is significantly negative and concentrated in the sown-area dimension, with no significant association for grain yield or the grain-area share. The negative relationship persists with a pooled entropy-weight TOPSIS digital economy index but is less precisely estimated under equal weighting. Historical-telecommunications IV estimates remain negative under broad functional-region trend controls, while province-specific trends substantially weaken instrument relevance. Regional coefficient differences vary with the treatment of functional-region annual shocks. Negative direct spatial associations remain significant under alternative weight matrices, while positive indirect associations are matrix dependent.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings associate digitalization primarily with changes in provincial crop sown area and suggest possible regional compensation, without identifying physical interprovincial transfers or ecological effects. Sensitivity to measurement, historical trends and regional annual shocks warrants a cautious interpretation. Sustainable digital-agriculture strategies should balance grain-production responsibilities with ecological constraints, resource efficiency and production stability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Digital economy and grain production in China: production-scale adjustment, regional heterogeneity, and potential spatial reallocation

items.abstract: <jats:p>As live-stream e-commerce rapidly expands and gains popularity among consumers, many brand owners have supplemented their self-owned direct-selling channels with live-stream selling channels to utilize social network effects of key opinion leaders (KOLs). This dual-channel structure creates price discrepancy issues, prompting consumers to raise concerns about price fairness. Therefore, brand owners are motivated to coordinate pricing strategies, balancing cooperation and competition across channels. We build a game-theoretical model to investigate how consumers' peer-induced fairness seeking influences the price decisions of a brand owner (in the direct-selling channel) and the KOL (in the live-stream selling channel). Interestingly, we find that consumers' increased fairness concerns may paradoxically lead to increased prices in both channels, challenging the conventional expectation of price-cutting competition. We further demonstrate that consumers' fairness seeking may either benefit or harm both sellers, depending on the strength of network effects and various factors related to competition intensity. The non-monotonic impacts of consumer fairness seeking are driven by the brand owner's dueling strategic incentives to secure (or relinquish) its direct-selling business to compete with (or favor) the live-stream selling under different situations. Finally, we identify “win-win”, “lose-lose”, and “lose-win” outcomes that consumer fairness seeking can cause for the brand owner and KOL.</jats:p>
title: EXPRESS: The Role of Consumer Fairness Seeking in Live-Stream E-Commerce

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Rationale</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Coconut water is widely consumed in tropical regions, yet its stable isotopic composition and the processes controlling it remain insufficiently characterized. Characterizing these isotope values is important for improving our understanding of plant water dynamics and evaluating coconut water as a potential proxy for tropical environmental and hydrological conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Coconut water was collected from coconuts with varying filling status, size, maturity and tree height on Tanna Island (Vanuatu), including multiple fruits from individual trees. We determined stable hydrogen (δ
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      H) and oxygen (δ
                      <jats:sup>18</jats:sup>
                      O) isotopes of coconut water using isotope ratio mass spectrometry (IRMS) and evaluated them in relation to fruit development and environmental factors.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Coconut water isotopic values consistently plotted below the Global Meteoric Water Line, indicating a systematic offset from local meteoric water. Filled coconuts displayed more enriched isotopic compositions (δ
                      <jats:sup>18</jats:sup>
                      O: −3.1‰ to −0.2‰; δ
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      H: −26.4 to −3.9‰) compared to incompletely filled fruits. Tree height had only a minor influence, whereas fruit size was associated with isotopic enrichment, particularly for δ
                      <jats:sup>18</jats:sup>
                      O. Deuterium excess increased significantly with elevation, suggesting controls beyond the typical altitudinal isotopic depletion observed in precipitation.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These preliminary results identify coconut water as a distinct pool of plant water that integrates local precipitation signals with physiological fractionation processes during fruit development. The observed isotopic patterns show the potential of coconut water as a novel proxy for tropical ecohydrological processes and provide a foundation for future studies of plant‐water interactions in tropical environments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Isotope Composition of Coconut Water as an Indicator of Tropical Hydrological Processes

items.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Context</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Rumen methanogenesis represents a major source of agricultural greenhouse gas productions and a significant loss of dietary energy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Aims</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study evaluated the effects of fennel (Foeniculum vulgare Mill.) extract, supplied either as a bulk extract or as an oil-in-water nanoemulsion, at inclusion levels of 15, 30 and 45 μL/g dry matter (DM) on in vitro gas production kinetics, methane (CH4) and carbon dioxide (CO2) productions, nutrient degradability, and rumen fermentation characteristics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The incubation substrate was a total mixed ration (600 g/kg concentrate feed mixture, 300 g/kg berseem hay and 100 g/kg rice straw, DM basis). Treatments were arranged in a 2 × 3 + 1 factorial design with three incubation runs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Key results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Significant form × dose interactions were detected for asymptotic gas production (b), fractional rate of gas production (c), lag time, metabolizable energy, partitioning factor at 48 h and gas yield at 24 h (P &lt; 0.05). Nanosized nanoemulsion 30 μL/g DM produced the greatest fermentation response, yielding the highest b (384.2 mL/g DM), c (0.046 h−1), metabolizable energy (9.97 MJ/kg DM) and gas yield at 24 h (442.9 mL/g DM). In contrast, nanosized nanoemulsion 45 μL/g DM produced the lowest values for these variables, but the highest partitioning factor at 48 h. Both fennel extract forms reduced CH4 production relative to the control, with the nanoemulsion showing greater efficacy. Methane reductions reached 30.0% and 37.7% at nanosized nanoemulsion 30 μL/g DM and nanosized nanoemulsion 45 μL/g DM, respectively (P = 0.001). The nanoemulsion also increased CO2 production per gram of incubated DM compared with the bulk extract (P &lt; 0.001). In vitro DM, neutral detergent fiber and acid detergent fiber degradability, as well as fermentation pH, were significantly affected by the form × dose interaction (P = 0.001). Nanosized nanoemulsion 30 μL/g DM improved degradability, nanosized nanoemulsion 45 μL/g DM reduced it below control values and pH changed only slightly (6.77–6.97). Ammonia-N concentrations declined progressively with increasing fennel extract inclusion (P &lt; 0.001).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings indicate that nanoemulsification enhances the fermentation-modulating and antimethanogenic activity of fennel extract, with 30 μL/g DM providing the most favorable balance between improved fermentation and methane mitigation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Nanoemulsified fennel extract at 30 μL/g DM is a promising, natural phytogenic strategy for enteric CH4 mitigation that warrants confirmation under in vivo feeding conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Nanosized versus bulk fennel (Foeniculum vulgare) extract: comparative effects on in vitro rumen gas production kinetics, greenhouse gas productions, nutrient degradability and fermentation end-products

items.abstract: <jats:p>Urban development leads to the spread of urban functions into suburban areas and the displacement of agriculture from these areas. Livestock production is particularly vulnerable to these changes due to the nuisances it generates. The aim of this article was to assess changes in cattle and cow stocking rates in suburban areas located within a 50 km radius of Poland’s 11 largest cities between 2010 and 2020. Based on data from the Local Data Bank, the stocking densities of cattle and cows were calculated and compared across five 10-kilometre zones (rings) surrounding the urban centres under analysis. Research has shown that, as the distance from towns decreases, the population of the animal groups studied declines, and the process of herd elimination becomes increasingly pronounced. Among the most significant causes of the reduction in livestock numbers are the growing conflicts between farmers and new residents, the rise in the number of court cases concerning nuisances associated with livestock production, and the increasingly difficult conditions for farm development. The growing problems in neighbourly relations will not be fully resolved by the ‘Draft Act amending certain acts to protect the agricultural production functions of rural areas’, currently being debated in the Polish Sejm.</jats:p>
title: Changes in the Intensity of Cattle and Cow Production Around Poland’s Largest Cities

<jats:title>Summary</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Accurate oil production forecasting is of great importance for optimizing oilfield development and production decisions, reducing operating costs, and improving economic benefits. At present, deep learning (DL) methods have been widely applied to production forecasting. However, actual oilfield production data are typically nonlinear, noisy, and highly complex, which might mean that conventional DL methods are not always fully effective in capturing intricate nonlinear relationships; moreover, their performance in modeling pronounced fluctuations and abrupt production changes may require further optimization. To handle these challenges, this paper proposes a state space model (SSM)-attention-Kolmogorov-Arnold network (KAN) variant model (SSM-KAN), which integrates the SSM and KAN to predict oil production. In the proposed model, the SSM component extracts temporal features through efficient convolutional computation and focuses on key information via a multihead attention mechanism. Subsequently, the KAN serves as the decoder, performing nonlinear processing on the extracted features to achieve the final prediction. Instead of adopting conventional fixed activation functions, KAN employs learnable spline functions to strengthen its capability to model nonlinear relationships. In the experimental part, the proposed SSM-KAN model was validated using actual oilfield production data from the Volve oil field and an oil field in northern Russia. The results demonstrate that the SSM-KAN model achieves excellent prediction performance for production forecasting of three wells, with R2 values exceeding 0.96. Compared with multiple benchmark models, it reduces prediction errors by more than 20% while maintaining a compact model architecture and efficient inference.</jats:p>
title: Integrating State-Space Model and Kolmogorov-Arnold Network for Oilwell Production Forecasting

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec id="j_jdis-2026-0082_abs_001">
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      A bibliometric analysis of the scientific literature published in journals indexed in the SCOPUS database in the area of
                      <jats:italic>mathematics</jats:italic>
                      is presented. The data encompass documents published from 2008 to 2025, expanding and complementing previous studies that used different databases. The yearly production of articles, the number of articles per author, the size of different communities, Lotka’s laws for the journals, and yearly production by country are analyzed.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="j_jdis-2026-0082_abs_002">
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Yearly production in mathematics presents two very well-marked zones. We provide the best fitting functions for both zones. An analysis of productivity by author is also performed. We construct communities defined by the number of years that an author is considered productive. A similar analysis of different mathematical subareas is also presented. Bradford’s and Lotka’s laws are studied with the full mathematics production and by subareas.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="j_jdis-2026-0082_abs_003">
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>There are two well defined time intervals. In the first one, the production grows steadily and can be fitted by a polynomial, and in the second, the growth is no longer polynomial. The growth rate is much higher, with behavior approaching that of an exponential function. Similarly, communities of authors present different patterns in two very well-identified intervals. The number of authors with a few articles has increased, but the number of authors with more than 10 articles has also increased, although at a different rate. Productivity is increasing every year, and after a fall during the pandemic period, there is a resurgence with a very high growth rate. Productivity is increasing in almost all areas.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="j_jdis-2026-0082_abs_004">
                    <jats:title>Research limitations</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study focuses on a particular database, which, although well curated, has their own limitations. In addition, there are journals that belong to two or more areas and, therefore, are counted in each of them. Due to the fact that the production is analyzed yearly, there are zones where we need more data to confirm the fitting.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="j_jdis-2026-0082_abs_005">
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results show a significant change in how to discover and publish new mathematics. The size of the communities indicates that the number of researchers with only a few articles has increased. These researchers leave academia, and the job market and postgraduate programs are affected. Our article represents a quantification of this phenomenon and how it affects global production. It can be seen as a first attempt to study it in full generality and with a historical perspective.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="j_jdis-2026-0082_abs_006">
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Yearly production, studied since 1868, has increased in recent years like never before. It has changed from linear to polynomial growth, and recently, the growth has shifted to exponential. There is a price to pay: the number of authors who leave academia after their first or second article has increased. Finally, a ranking of countries by the number of articles produced during the period considered is presented, with China being the new leader.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: A Bibliometric Study of Scientific Production in Mathematics

items.abstract:
<jats:p>Background: Stem cells’ ability to differentiate into other cell types makes them unique. Physical activity may influence stem cell production and mobilisation, but evidence across different age groups and exercise types remains fragmented.
Objectives: This review examined the relationship between physical activity and stem cell production in children, young adults and the elderly.
Method: Relevant articles were searched in Google Scholar, EBSCOhost Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL), PubMed and Web of Science. Following article selection, methodological quality assessment and data extraction, 19 articles were included. Risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane Collaboration and ROBINS-I tools, while evidence quality was evaluated using the GRADE system.
Results: Increased physical activity was associated with increased stem cell production and mobilisation in children, adults and the elderly. This relationship was observed with both aerobic and anaerobic exercise and appeared independent of stem cell type. Endurance and resistance exercise were associated with increases through different physiological and adaptive mechanisms.
Conclusion: Regular physical activity, whether endurance or resistance training, enhances stem cell production and mobilisation across the lifespan, highlighting its potential benefits for tissue repair, functional capacity, health and well-being.
Clinical Implications: Physiotherapists can prescribe targeted aerobic and resistance programmes based on frequency, intensity, time and type principles to stimulate endogenous stem cell activity and support muscle repair. For older adults, progressively loaded, higher-intensity and longer-duration exercise may maximise functional outcomes, although regenerative responses may be attenuated by age-related changes. These findings support exercise-based strategies for promoting healthy ageing and contribute to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 3.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study investigates the vowel-length contrast in Seoul Korean (SK) and North Kyungsang Korean (NKK), integrating production and perception evidence to assess the state of sound change in the two varieties. In SK productions, only older women retain a durational contrast, while older men and all younger SK speakers show no detectable contrast. Older NKK speakers also maintain a robust durational contrast, but younger male NKK speakers exhibit a reduced contrast and younger women have none detectable. However, among NKK speakers, accentual categories are largely preserved; acoustic analysis of F0 shows that pitch differences between long- and short-vowel words are mediated by lexical accent category. Perception results diverge from production patterns, with NKK listeners showing higher identification accuracy than SK. When vowel duration and pitch-accent cues are placed in conflict, younger NKK listeners resolve the conflict in favor of pitch accent. These findings indicate a group-level production–perception dissociation and locate the source in perception. Because duration and pitch accent are lexically bundled in NKK, F0 is not an available dimension onto which the contrast can be reweighted. The change across generations is in the weight listeners assign to an already contrastive accentual cue as the secondary durational cue is lost.</jats:p>
title: Vowel-length merger in Korean according to variety, age, and gender: integrating production and perception evidence

items.abstract:
<jats:p>This study examined agricultural education and women’s empowerment through vegetable and 
poultry production in Bayelsa State. Guided by four research questions, the study adopted a 
descriptive survey research design. The population comprised women engaged in vegetable and 
poultry production across the eight Local Government Areas of Bayelsa State. A multistage 
sampling procedure was used to select 200 women from 16 communities in four purposively 
selected Local Government Areas. Data were collected using the Agricultural Education and 
Women’s Empowerment through Vegetable and Poultry Production Questionnaire (AEWEVPPQ), 
which was validated by experts and had a Cronbach’s Alpha reliability coefficient of 0.76 and 
above. Demographic data were analysed using frequency counts and percentages, while the 
research questions were answered using mean and standard deviation, with a criterion mean of 
2.50. The findings revealed that women’s access to agricultural education was low. Their 
knowledge and practical skills in vegetable production were high, particularly in nursery 
preparation, transplanting, planting, spacing and seed selection. However, their poultry
production skills were low overall, especially in brooding management, disease identification and 
biosecurity. Women’s participation in vegetable and poultry production was high, with substantial 
involvement in daily farm operations, labour management, cooperative activities and marketing, 
but limited access to credit and involvement in major financial decisions. The study concluded that 
although women were actively engaged in these agricultural enterprises, limited access to 
agricultural education, gaps in poultry-production skills and financial constraints restricted their 
empowerment. It recommended that relevant government agencies and agricultural cooperatives 
provide accessible, practical, gender-responsive training and improve women farmers’ access to 
credit.</jats:p>
title: Agricultural Education and Women Empowerment Through  Vegetable and Poultry Production in Bayelsa State

items.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Operations and supply chain managers are continuously pulled between efficiency to reduce costs and buffering for resilience. These endeavors are at the heart of Factory Physics, which theoretically defines the levers managers use to control the physics of an organization. However, organizations are also under pressure to incorporate environmental impacts into their decision-making due to consumer and regulatory pressures. With managerial decisions on inventory turnover and capacity utilization having direct environmental impacts, managers are thus challenged to consider environmental performance alongside economic consequences in an increasingly demanding environment. Taking a Factory Physics lens, this research focuses on the environmental impact of inventory turnover and capacity utilization, while considering potential nonlinearities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A high-dimensional fixed-effects approach is employed with a panel dataset of 4,638 operations and supply chain firms from 2002 to 2026.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results suggest that increasing inventory turnover and capacity utilization improve environmental performance. However, there is a nonlinearity: beyond a certain point, additional inventory turnover no longer improves environmental performance. A similar effect is found for capacity utilization when financial leverage is high. Extending this in a post hoc analysis, the findings suggest that capacity utilization is dominant in reducing environmental harm. Further, increasing inventory turnover only improves environmental performance in later stages of the process.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This research provides a holistic examination of the environmental implications of Factory Physics, considering the multiple levers managers use to manage Factory Physics and the potential for nonlinear outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Too lean? Exploring the nonlinear environmental implications of Factory Physics

items.abstract: <jats:p>Neurosporene is a key C40 carotenoid intermediate in lycopene biosynthesis, exhibiting remarkable antioxidant and biological activities, and holds promising prospects in the food, cosmetic, and pharmaceutical industries. Although Escherichia coli has been widely employed for the sustainable production of carotenoids, challenges such as imbalances in metabolic flux and spontaneous conversion of intermediates to lycopene hinder the efficient accumulation of neurosporene. In this study, we integrated strategies—including optimization of the expression pathway, refinement of fermentation conditions, and central carbon metabolism engineering—to construct an E. coli cell factory capable of high-efficiency neurosporene accumulation. By introducing the genes crtE, crtB, and crtI and comparing two bacterial hosts, we selected E. coli BL21(DE3) as the host strain for subsequent optimization. Using pHT01-Pgrac01 as the vector backbone, we optimized the operon gene order to crtIBE and strategically designed RBS to balance gene expression. Through response surface methodology and iterative single-factor optimization of fermentation conditions, the neurosporene titer increased to 2286.09 μg/L. Subsequently, employing the dual-plasmid genomic editing system pEcCas/pEcgRNA to knock out the bypass gene zwf, we redirected carbon metabolic flux toward product synthesis, elevating the titer to 3429.34 μg/L—approximately 1.5-fold higher than during the fermentation optimization phase. This strategy significantly enhanced the neurosporene biosynthetic capacity of E. coli, providing a valuable reference for the efficient microbial production of carotenoids.</jats:p>
title: Systematic Enhancement of Neurosporene Production in Escherichia coli Through Integrated Expression, Fermentation, and Metabolic Engineering

items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Racist nativism is increasingly becoming the guiding principle upon which immigration policy is written in the United States. More specifically, particular corners of anti-immigrant activism rely upon eco-fascism, or the “greening of hate,” where immigration (specifically from the developing world) is protested under the guise of environmental concern. We examine the publication record of the prominent Sociology journal
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">Population & Environment</jats:italic>
                    (
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">P&E</jats:italic>
                    ) during the editorship of Virginia Deane Abernethy in the 1980s and 1990s to argue that (1) the mainstreaming of racist nativist immigration policy in the United States has deep historical roots, and (2) those roots thread straight through one of Sociology’s significant environment and demography journals. Through a content analysis of
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">P&E’s</jats:italic>
                    publication record under Abernethy, we call attention to the ways that Sociology—and the process of scientific “knowledge” production more broadly—is in no way exempt from political and ideological influences that are used to justify the worst of America’s nationalistic, xenophobic impulses, and that mechanisms of Sociology as an institutionalized academic discipline has been weaponized to protect those who would manipulate the knowledge creation process to their own nefarious ends.
                  </jats:p>
title: The Production of Racist Nativism as Social Science Knowledge

items.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The proliferation of electronic goods has increased challenges for global e-waste; thus, reverse logistics (RL) and closed-loop supply chains (CLSC) in the electronics sector have become very challenging research areas. This study aims to provide a substantial bibliometric and systematic overview of the RL and CLSC research in electronics, with a particular emphasis on identifying potential barriers to implementation and synthesising findings into a conceptual framework for future empirical investigation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data analysis was performed using the PRISMA 2020 protocol, extracted from the Scopus database through searching the terms reverse logistics, closed-loop supply chain and electronics. The search occurred from 2010 to 2024 and after applying structured inclusion and exclusion criteria resulted in a final corpus of 94 peer-reviewed journal articles. Bibliometric methods, such as trends in publication, keyword co-occurrence, co-citation analysis and thematic mapping, were then used.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The volume of publications has grown sharply since 2019, with a combination of the regulators’ attention, the global e-waste crisis and COVID-19 supply chain disruption. Keyword analysis shows a new paradigm shift from operational efficiency to strategic sustainability. There are four dimensions where barriers to RL and CLSC introduction cluster: technical infrastructure gaps, policy and regulatory weaknesses, strategic and organisational resistance and market and consumer behaviour factors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Policymakers need to enhance extended producer responsibility (EPR) enforcement and implement market-based incentives. Electronics manufacturers should invest in a phased digital transformation, from RFID-based tracking to AI-enabled return forecasting and put design-for-disassembly principles front and centre in development.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In addition, introducing an original multi-dimensional Conceptual Framework of RL/CLSC Implementation in this paper synthesising drivers, barriers, enabling technologies and sustainability outcomes at technical, economic, environmental and social/political dimensions would lay a structure for future empirical studies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Reverse logistics in electronics industry: a bibliometric analysis, challenges and future research prospects

<jats:p>Purpose: This community engagement program aimed to strengthen Ina Chip’s fruit-chip production, packaging and labelling, and marketing practices.
Method: The program employed a participatory approach involving preparation, socialization, practical training, mentoring, and evaluation. Activities focused on fruit preparation and slicing, vacuum frying, oil removal, sealing, product labelling, and marketing development.
Practical Applications: The program provided practical guidance on production processes, packaging equipment, label development, and marketing practices. These activities were intended to help the partner improve production consistency, product presentation, and business development.
Conclusion: The program addressed three interconnected areas of microenterprise development: production, packaging and labelling, and marketing. Although the project report recorded the program’s output indicators as achieved, it did not provide quantitative evidence of changes in product quality, sales, or market reach. Further monitoring is needed to assess the sustainability and business impact of the intervention.</jats:p>
title: Strengthening Ina Chip Microenterprise through Production Improvement, Packaging Innovation, and Marketing Development

items.abstract:
<jats:p>China’s rapidly expanding video game sector has become a key site of AI-driven industrial transformation. The integration of AI is reshaping video game development through the emergence of human–AI collaborative workflows.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Drawing on the Frankfurt School’s critical theory of the culture industry, this study examines how generative AI is reshaping production processes and creative labour practices across the pre-production, production, and post-production stages of China’s video game industry. Based on semi-structured interviews with game professionals from major Chinese game studios, the study finds that AI integration reinforces the industrialisation and standardisation of cultural production, particularly through enhanced workflow efficiency and quality control. At the same time, it reconfigures creative labour by shifting workers’ responsibilities towards directing, supervising, and evaluating AI-assisted production processes. These developments illustrate the dual implications of AI adoption: while generative AI intensifies technological rationalisation, human creative judgement remains central to ensuring cultural specificity and context-sensitive creative outcomes. The study argues that human labour is not displaced but reconfigured within AI-enabled production, mediating the tension between industrial standardisation and culturally specific forms of video game production.</jats:p>
title: The new production logic? Exploring human-AI creative workflows in China’s video game development

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Drawing on the emotions-as-frames model (EFM), this study aims to examine the interaction between emotional framing and visual imagery in carbon pricing persuasion, focusing on the mediating role of message elaboration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study used a 2 × 2 between-subjects experimental design (emotion: hope vs fear; visual image: present vs absent) with a sample of 300 participants. Data were analyzed using analysis of variance (ANOVA) and analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) to test for main and interaction effects while controlling for climate change knowledge. The PROCESS macro was used to test for mediation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results indicated that fear framing was more persuasive than hope framing for behavioral intentions. The presence of a visual image in a fear-framed message showed a significant main effect on attitudes toward the climate change message. Furthermore, significant interaction was found between hope-framed messaging and visual imagery for attitudes toward the climate change message. Message elaboration, through evaluative processing, mediated the relationship between the emotional frames and the outcome variables. These effects remained robust after controlling for climate change knowledge.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study offers important contributions and provides a messaging framework for policy practitioners and communication specialists, suggesting that emphasizing risks through fear-framed messages paired with relevant visuals is most effective for driving behavioral intentions for carbon pricing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study advances the EFM by examining the interaction between emotion and a visual image, while accounting for the mediating role of message elaboration and the stability of these effects across varying levels of climate change knowledge.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Emotional framing and visual image in carbon pricing persuasion: the mediating role of message elaboration

<jats:p>Purpose: This community engagement program aimed to strengthen IGTKI Biringkanaya's institutional management and teachers' competence in developing inclusive sensory teaching materials for children with special needs.
Method: A participatory approach was implemented through needs mapping, training, demonstrations of appropriate technology, collaborative production, classroom mentoring, and monitoring and evaluation.
Practical Applications: The program involved 40 teachers from 11 early childhood education institutions. Teachers' mean knowledge score increased from 30% on the pretest to 90% on the posttest. The activities produced 20 sensory teaching materials, 20 integrated daily lesson plans, and a 97-page printed and digital ISBN-registered guidebook.
Conclusion: The program improved teachers' knowledge and practical capacity while establishing shared documentation and learning resources for IGTKI. Participants rated the activities highly and recommended advanced training covering planning through learning evaluation.</jats:p>
title: Strengthening Sensory Teaching Material Management and Production for Inclusive Education at IGTKI Biringkanaya

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We estimate the impact of cultural diversity on urban wage and rent premiums by means of hedonic regressions in a spatial equilibrium setting. Our estimates are based on a very large data set from Aotearoa New Zealand: complete unit record census data from 1981 until 2018 on individuals and dwellings in 110 urban areas. Various measures of cultural diversity are considered, including those that account for dissimilarity between groups. Controlling for observed and unobserved city characteristics, and for the potential endogeneity of diversity, we find that cultural diversity serves as a local positive production amenity and a weakly negative consumption amenity. The results are mostly robust to variation in the selection of samples of urban areas and census years; and to variation in the ways in which diversity can be quantified. We conclude that the presence of people from different cultural backgrounds enhances the profitability of urban firms but, at the same time, local populations exhibit a weak preference for living near others who are culturally like them.</jats:p>
title: Cultural Diversity as a Source of Local Urban Production and Consumption Amenities

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper aims to clarify the role of financial actors in sustainability transitions by developing and applying an archetype framework of financial agency logics. In transition studies, finance is often treated as a resource that flows towards promising innovations, rather than as a domain of agency shaping sustainability-related decision-making.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper adopts an abductive qualitative research design. An archetype framework is developed through engagement with sustainability transition theory and sustainable finance literature, and empirically explored through 13 semi-structured interviews with financial actors involved in Norwegian salmon farming production, complemented by 55 documents, including annual reports, sustainability strategies, investment guidelines and policy-related documents.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings reveal a misalignment between sustainability ambitions articulated in strategies and the logics guiding investment practices. While sustainability is commonly framed in line with sustainable logics, decision-making remains dominated by conventional orientations prioritising short-term profitability and narrowly defined risk. Transformative logics appear mainly in discursive commitments. Financial actors selectively mobilise overlapping logics depending on context, rather than conforming to a single archetype.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study is limited to a single sector and national context. Future research should test and refine the framework across sectors and geographies and examine how financial instruments and policy mixes shape the mobilisation of financial logics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The framework offers a diagnostic lens for practitioners and policymakers to examine how sustainability ambitions are interpreted and filtered within financial decision-making.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper introduces a novel archetype framework that operationalises financial agency in sustainability transitions, responding to a call for more knowledge on the role of finance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Between sustainability strategy and financial practice: archetypes of financial agency in Norwegian salmon farming

<jats:p>Reproductive inefficiency in Nili-Ravi buffaloes (Bubalus bubalis) presents a significant challenge to genetic progress and milk production in South Asia. In vitro embryo production is one of new technology but its media in indigenous Nili Ravi buffalo needs to be optimized to get promising results. This study explores the potential of Quercetin, a powerful antioxidant, to enhance in vitro oocyte maturation and embryo development, thereby improving reproductive outcomes. The objective was to evaluate the impact of varying Quercetin concentrations on in vitro oocyte maturation and in vitro embryo production. Total 200 oocytes were aspirated from ovaries of slaughtered female buffaloes and cultured in a maturation medium supplemented with Quercetin at concentrations of 0 µM, 5 µM, 10 µM, and 20 µM. Following fertilization, embryos were cultured to assess developmental progress. Results revealed that supplementation with 10 µM Quercetin significantly enhanced both in vitro oocyte maturation and blastocyst formation compared to the other concentrations (P≤0.05). 
The 10 µM concentration yielded the highest embryo development, underscoring its potential in improving oocyte maturation and facilitating successful in vitro embryo production, can be an effective strategy to enhance in vitro reproductive efficiency in Nili-Ravi buffaloes. This study lays the foundation for integrating Quercetin into in vitro maturation media of Nili Ravi buffalo breeding programs, with promising implications for genetic improvement and enhanced reproductive success.</jats:p>
title: QUERCETIN’S ROLE IN ENHANCING BUFFALO OOCYTE MATURATION AND IN VITRO EMBRYO PRODUCTION

items.abstract: <jats:p>Housing decarbonisation, affordability and social inclusion are often examined through separate technical and governance perspectives. This structured critical review considers modular construction, co-housing and zero-energy housing as interventions in production, governance and operational performance, respectively. The structured search identified 1095 records, and its initial reference register contained 96 entries; a bibliographic check subsequently identified one duplicate work. The review distinguishes source provenance from the evidential strength of individual claims and separates observations from named occupied projects from wider archetype-level studies. It also distinguishes product-stage, construction-stage and operational-energy measures to avoid comparing incompatible lifecycle boundaries. The reviewed literature describes production and waste-reduction opportunities associated with modular construction, governance and tenure mechanisms associated with co-housing, and measured operational-energy outcomes for selected zero-energy projects. However, available studies use different units, case-selection criteria and measurement methods, and the evidence base is geographically uneven. Missing evidence on measured affordability, participation and whole-life performance limits claims about actual comparative benefits. The proposed framework identifies complementary intervention mechanisms and testable research questions, not a ranking of measured housing performance or proof that combining the pathways creates synergistic benefits.</jats:p>
title: From Production to Governance to Performance: Modular, Co-Housing and Zero-Energy Housing as Pathways for Sustainable Human Settlements

items.abstract: <jats:p>Electro-optical and laser systems reach their specified performance only after assembly, alignment, and calibration, and the knowledge behind these operations accumulates in the prototype laboratory long before serial production begins. Drawings and specifications travel to the factory with the product, while the integration know-how stays with developers and integrators, leading to rework, unit failures, long test and calibration cycles, and a lasting dependence of production on the development team. This review systematizes approaches to transferring integration and calibration procedures from prototype development to serial production. An integrative review of recent research on optical packaging, alignment automation, production ramp-up, tacit knowledge transfer, work instructions, design for assembly, and multistage inspection supported a classification built on four criteria: the lifecycle stage at which transfer begins, the carrier of integration knowledge, the division of labor, and the control strategy during calibration. The analysis yields five classes, namely documentation handover, expert accompaniment, procedure codification, design anticipation, and equipment embedding, together with a mechanism that decouples mechanical assembly from integration. Firsthand integration practice illustrates the codification and design anticipation classes, as well as the decoupling mechanism. Transfer can become more predictable once integration requirements enter design reviews and calibration procedures include staged checkpoints that localize deviations, thereby opening a path toward shorter test and calibration cycles.</jats:p>
title: Systematization of Approaches to Transferring Integration and Calibration Procedures for Electro-Optical Systems from Prototype Development to Serial Production

                    The renewed increase of methane (CH
                    <jats:sub>4</jats:sub>
                    ) in the atmosphere since 2007 is an imminent threat to the stability of the climate system and undermines climate policy goals. A reversal in the trend of its carbon isotopic composition (
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">δ</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                    C
                    <jats:sub>CH4</jats:sub>
                    ) in the 21st century indicates a fundamental shift in the global CH
                    <jats:sub>4</jats:sub>
                    cycle. Here, we investigate the origin of this
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">δ</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                    C
                    <jats:sub>CH4</jats:sub>
                    trend by determining isotope source signatures of CH
                    <jats:sub>4</jats:sub>
                    emissions based on high and mid-northern latitude observations. A clear latitude gradient and seasonal cycle of the source signatures reflect the spatially and temporally varying contributions of the different sources, each with distinct signatures. We find a large shift in the source signature after 2007 between −3.6 and −5.1‰ at high northern latitudes, and a moderate change between −0.4 and −0.9‰ at mid-northern latitudes. The decrease in
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">δ</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                    C
                    <jats:sub>CH4</jats:sub>
                    source signature is likely caused by a shift from thermogenic and pyrogenic to microbial sources, accompanied by a likely decrease in the isotopic signature of the microbial emissions, possibly resulting from climate change. Our results suggest that current inverse models may underestimate the shift between fossil and microbial emissions at high northern latitudes, or that microbial methanogenesis pathways change much more strongly than currently believed. Source changes at high latitudes have a disproportionate contribution to the observed trend in atmospheric
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">δ</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                    C
                    <jats:sub>CH4</jats:sub>
                    .

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    We develop a systematic framework to quantify irreversibility in scalar Model A field theories with a generic non-Hermitian term driving the dynamics. Using the stochastic path-integral formalism, we perform a controlled small-noise expansion, allowing the computation of the entropy production rate (EPR) and violations of the fluctuation-dissipation theorem (FDT). We show that the local EPR is entirely determined by the anti-Hermitian part of the linearised Langevin equation. Around steady states, the non-Hermitian component produces linear corrections to FDT violations and contributes quadratically to the EPR. As an illustration of the applicability of our approach, we analyse a minimal non-Hermitian extension of the Ginzburg–Landau
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>
                        
                      </jats:tex-math>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">
                        <mml:mrow>
                          <mml:msup>
                            <mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi>
                            <mml:mn>4</mml:mn>
                          </mml:msup>
                        </mml:mrow>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    theory describing a non-reciprocal Ising model at coarse-grained scales, for which we obtain explicit expressions of the local EPR, showing that it localises at interfaces in non-uniform states. Our results provide a general characterisation of TRS breaking in non-Hermitian scalar field theories.
                  </jats:p>
title: Time irreversibility and entropy production in non-Hermitian Model A field theories

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Th17 cells (CD4+ T cells producing IL-17) are important for clearance of fungal infections and play a critical role in the development and exacerbation of numerous autoimmune diseases. Their differentiation, signalling pathways, cytokine production and metabolism are now well-characterised. As well as CD4+ T cells, certain CD8+ cells also produce IL-17 cytokines, and these have been named Tc17 cells. However, much less is known about their development, signalling or metabolism compared to their CD4+ counterparts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Here, we performed a series of in vitro and in vivo analyses of Tc17 cells as well as computational analysis of the published Tabula muris dataset, comparing Tc17 to IL-17- CD8+ T cells and to Th17 cells.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We show that murine Tc17 cells are generated in the presence of TGF-β and IL-6, and that cells produced by these culture conditions substantially reflect Tc17 cells seen in vivo; that is, with high expression of PD1, CD6, ICOS and increased NK1.1/CD161. Tc17 cells show phenotypic and functional differences to their Th17 counterparts, with increased production of IL-2 and IL-22 as well as an increased tendency to produce IL-17F as well as IL-17A. They also show a more glycolytic profile than Th17 cells relative to mitochondrial activity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This divergent phenotype and cytokine production suggests differential roles in vivo for these two cells.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: IL-17-producing CD8+ T cells differ in phenotype, metabolic profile and cytokine production to their Th17 counterparts

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Simulations were performed to investigate neutron-induced radioactivity in the iron (Fe) target and surrounding coolants (sodium-potassium alloy (NaK), lead (Pb), water (H
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O), liquid sodium (Na), and carbon dioxide (CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    )) by bombarding the target with 400 MeV carbon ions. Radionuclides produced within the target material and each coolant were evaluated over time using the FLUKA Monte Carlo code. The temporal evolution of all induced radionuclides was analyzed and visualized through time-dependent activity curves. Neutron yield was quantified at an incident energy of 400 MeV. It was observed that low-energy neutrons were the main cause of activation. During the shutdown of the accelerator,
                    <jats:sup>56</jats:sup>
                    Mn was observed with a high ratio inside the iron target, while
                    <jats:sup>41</jats:sup>
                    Ar,
                    <jats:sup>200</jats:sup>
                    Pb,
                    <jats:sup>11</jats:sup>
                    C, and
                    <jats:sup>24</jats:sup>
                    Na were identified as the primary contributors in the respective coolants: NaK, Lead, water, and liquid sodium. Specifically,
                    <jats:sup>11</jats:sup>
                    C was dominant in both water and CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    . From the start of irradiation to saturation, and with elapsed cooling time, growth and decay curves for each major induced element were summarized. A large amount of short-lived beta-decay radionuclides appeared while the accelerator was shut down; induced radionuclides with low activity were ignored due to low hazard. Considering the protection of radiation workers during maintenance or handling the equipment, research results show that lead (Pb) will produce the highest radiation effects when used as a coolant in a nuclear reactor, and it will require extra care as compared to water, gas, and other coolants included in this study.
                  </jats:p>
title: FLUKA-based assessment of induced radioactivity in iron target and surrounding coolants under 400 MeV carbon-ion irradiation

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Although heavy-ion beam irradiation has been applied to microalgae to develop strains for industrial applications, the effects of irradiation, including comprehensive mutation profiling, remain poorly characterized at the genome-wide level. In this study, we analyzed mutations using sequencing data from 12 strains of the haptophyte Tisochrysis lutea, isolated after carbon-ion beam irradiation. As previously reported, short insertions of several base pairs were the predominant mutation type in these mutants, but the underlying mechanism remains unknown. In this study, we identified insertion and excision events of Tc1-Mariner/Luffy transposons, whose target sites and terminal sequences were consistent with those of previously identified short insertions. Nearly all the 5-bp insertions, the most abundant type of short insertion, might have resulted from the insertion and subsequent excision of these transposons. We also found that the transposons were active even in the non-irradiated cells. In addition, we characterized single-base substitutions and structural variants and examined the relationship between irradiation dose and the number of mutations, although the dose dependence of mutation induction remained inconclusive. Our findings provide the first evidence that transposable elements contribute to short insertion mutations in T. lutea and expand our understanding of genome-wide changes in microalgae following heavy-ion beam irradiation. (199 words)</jats:p>
title: Genome-wide mutations and responses of transposable elements to heavy-ion beam irradiation in the haptophyte Tisochrysis lutea

items.abstract: <jats:p>Direct laser acceleration can generate high-current relativistic electron beams, yet their intrinsically large divergence severely limits beam transport and subsequent applications. In this work, a compact collimation scheme for direct-laser-accelerated electron beams is proposed and numerically investigated. By placing a wedge above the gas jet target, the gas flow is modified to form a millimeter-scale plasma region downstream of the jet, which acts as an integrated plasma lens for the accelerated electron beam. Numerical results show that, after passing through this plasma-lens region, the electron beam divergence can be reduced by approximately a factor of two. Owing to its simple configuration and ease of implementation, this scheme offers an effective route to improve the transport properties of electron beams without requiring complex target fabrication or stringent alignment. These results demonstrate that wedge-modified gas jet targets are promising for manipulating and applying electron beams in compact radiation sources and advanced accelerator systems.</jats:p>
title: Collimation of direct-laser-accelerated electron beams via a wedge-modified gas jet target

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Multiple myeloma, the second most common hematologic malignancy, remains incurable despite major therapeutic advances, highlighting an urgent need for novel therapeutic strategies. Proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) is involved in DNA replication and repair, chromatin remodeling, and cell-cycle progression, and increased PCNA expression has been associated with aggressive multiple myeloma phenotypes and poor clinical outcomes. Cancer cells express a posttranslationally modified, cancer-associated isoform of PCNA (caPCNA), potentially providing a selective therapeutic target. We evaluated the anti-myeloma activity of the novel caPCNA inhibitor AOH1996 alone and in combination with established anti-myeloma agents in vitro, in vivo, and ex vivo. AOH1996 inhibited the growth of many multiple myeloma cell lines in a dose-dependent manner, induced G2-phase accumulation and apoptosis, and reduced sphere- and colony-forming capacity. Combination treatment with bortezomib, venetoclax, melphalan, or cyclophosphamide enhanced anti-myeloma activity relative to single-agent treatment. AOH1996 treatment downregulated the expression of multiple tumor-associated genes and proteins, including EZH2, SOX2, CDK4, CDK6, and BCL2 family members and inflammatory and prosurvival cytokines. RNA and miRNA analyses demonstrated the suppression of several oncogenic miRNAs—including miR-21, miR-30a, miR-99a, miR-100, miR-142, miR-191, and miR-222—along with the upregulation of the tumor-suppressive miRNA miR-145. Forced expression of miR-145 inhibited multiple myeloma cell growth and enhanced sensitivity to AOH1996, implicating miR-145 as a mechanistic mediator of PCNA inhibition’s antitumor effects. In xenograft models, AOH1996 significantly enhanced the antitumor activity of bortezomib and venetoclax without apparent toxicity. Ex vivo studies demonstrated selective activity against primary multiple myeloma cells and CD138+ plasma cells, with minimal effects on normal peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Collectively, these findings support caPCNA as a promising therapeutic target in multiple myeloma and provide a strong preclinical rationale for further clinical investigation of AOH1996-based therapeutic strategies.</jats:p>
title: Proliferating Cell Nuclear Antigen as a New Therapeutic Target in Multiple Myeloma

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is the most common primary malignant brain tumour seen in adults, where treatment is focused on tumour control and quality of life. The median survival of relapsed glioblastoma following progression after 1st line treatment is widely considered to be around 6 months reflecting limited treatment options and poor response at relapse. Results from the BRIOCHE trial investigating second line re-irradiation (35Gy/10#), with a comparison to single agent Lomustine are awaited. This study reports the re-irradiation experience of a regional cancer centre.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We retrospectively reviewed records for patients with GBM who received re-irradiation (35Gy/10#) in any line of treatment following Stupp or Perry protocol 1st line treatment. Patient demographics, MGMT status, treatment detail and response were recorded. Progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS), measured from decision to treat, censored at time of evaluation were calculated.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>11 patients received re-irradiation. The cohort was 55% male, median age 63 years. 91% of patients underwent initial resection (with the remaining biopsy only) and 27% of the patients were MGMT methylated according to pyrosequencing (10% or higher). 82% of patients initially underwent STUPP treatment as opposed to PERRY. Re-irradiation was delivered in the 3rd line setting for the majority (73%). All patients completed the 10 fractions of radiotherapy and no radio-necrosis was observed. Median PFS and OS were 5.3 months (PFS 1.4-9.8 months and OS 1.4-15.7 months). 2 of the longer survival patients had radiotherapy as 4th line treatment and went on to receive further therapy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this small cohort of patients receiving re-irradiation for relapsed GBM, median OS and median PFS were 5.3 months despite use predominantly in 3rd+ line settings. Our data is limited by small patient numbers. We await the upcoming results of BRIOCHE study but these findings highlight the need for larger trials in re-irradiation beyond 2nd line treatment, with focus on quality-of-life effects.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: EP09.26 Real world experience of re-irradiation in relapsed Glioblastoma

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Hypo-fractionated stereotactic radiotherapy (HFSRT) may enhance anti-PDL1 immunotherapy efficacy in recurrent glioblastoma by promoting immunogenic cell death. After establishing the safety of HFSRT combined with Durvalumab in a phase I trial, we present the results of the randomized phase II STERIMGLI trial (NCT02866747).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Eligible patients with recurrent glioblastoma (WHO 2016 classification) and tumor volume ≤35 mm were randomized 1:2 to receive HFSRT alone (24 Gy in 3 fractions over 5 days, Arm A) or the same HFSRT plus Durvalumab 1500 mg on day 5, then every 4 weeks until progression or 12 months (Arm B). The primary endpoint was overall survival (OS) from randomization. With 100 patients and 77 events, the study had 85% power to detect an HR of 0.57 (one-sided, 10%-level test). Longitudinal blood samples were collected for ancillary analyses for all patients included in arm B.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Between February 2018 and April 2023, 102 patients (median age 61.5 years old, range [26-87]) were randomized (n = 34 and 68 in Arm A and B). Baseline characteristics were balanced, except for more prior targeted therapy in Arm B (22.1% vs 2.9%) and more IDH-mutated in Arm A (15.6% vs 6.1%). Treatment was well tolerated, 12.4% of patients experienced grade 3 treatment-related adverse events (no grade 4 or 5). After a median follow-up of 34.1 months, 78 deaths were reported, median OS was 13.3 months in Arm A vs. 16.1 months in Arm B (Hazard Ratio (HR)=0.77, 80%CI = [0.56;1.06], one-sided p = 0.146). In multivariate analysis, adjusted HR for prognostic factors was 0.41 (80%CI = [0.28;0.60]). Among patients with IDH-wildtype glioblastoma (WHO 2021), median OS was 10.9 vs. 16.1 months (HR = 0.54, 80%CI = [0.39;0.76], one-sided p = 0.010). The median intracranial progression-free interval assessed by investigators with RANO criteria was 2.3 vs. 3.5 months (HR = 0.91, 80%CI = [0.68;1.23], one-sided p = 0.349). No major significant differences in either Health-related quality of life assessed using the EORTC QLQ-C30 and BN20 questionnaires or cognitive function evaluated using the MoCA test were observed between the two treatment arms during the follow-up. Cytokines profile associated with response to HFSRT and Durvalumab combination will be presented.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Re-irradiation with HFSRT (24 Gy/3 fractions) combined with Durvalumab is safe and improves overall survival in patients with recurrent glioblastoma</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: JS07.5.A Hypo-fractionated Stereotactic re-irradiation (HFSRT) plus Durvalumab vs HFSRT re-irradiation alone for patients with a recurrent glioblastoma: results of the comparative randomized phase II STERIMGLI trial
