<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The standard of care for recurrent high-grade glioma (HGG) is currently insufficient. Various treatment options have been explored, including re-irradiation (re-RT). While the results appear promising, they are primarily derived from retrospective studies. The purpose of the present trial is to assess the dosimetric characteristics and clinical outcomes of recurrent HGG patients undergoing re-RT at a single institution.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Adult patients with a diagnosis of high-grade glioma (HGG) according to the 2021 fifth edition CNS classification, who had an interval time (IT) from their previous radiotherapy (RT) of six months or more, were included in this study. All patients had primary brain tumors at diagnosis and experienced recurrent disease during follow-up, either in the primary field or out-of-field (classified as type I and type II based on the ESTRO/EORTC consensus). We retrospectively reviewed clinical and dosimetric data from 21 patients who were treated between January 2021 and December 2025. Re-treatment was carried out using either fractionated stereotactic radiotherapy (in 18 patients) or conventional fractionated radiotherapy (in 3 patients). After the second course of radiotherapy, we calculated the cumulative dose using EQD2Gy at the organ at risk, according to Re-COG (Reirradiation Collaborative Group) recommendations. The primary endpoint of this study was overall survival (OS) following both the primary and secondary courses of RT.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The median age of patients was 53 years, with a range of 18 to 69 years. The median follow-up duration was 32 months, during which 10 patients had died at the last follow-up. The median time between the two treatment courses was 26 months, with a range of 11 to 54 months. The primary course prescription doses were 54 Gy for 6 patients and 60 Gy for the others. The mean volume of the planning target tumor (PTV) was 367 cc for the first course (range: 164 to 3208 cc) and 164 cc for the second course (range: 8 to 1358 cc). The median maximum cumulative doses received were 102.7 Gy for the brain, 64.9 Gy for the brain stem, 59.8 Gy for the chiasm, 31.5 Gy for the right optic nerve, and 23.3 Gy for the left optic nerve. The two-year overall survival rate was 84%, with a median survival time of 33 months (range: 14 to 61 months) after the primary course and 5 months (range: 1 to 32 months) after the secondary course. The one-year survival rate after the second course of radiation therapy was 27%. No grade ≥3 toxicities were observed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Re-irradiation for high-grade glioma is feasible and offers acceptable local control with low toxicity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: EP09.01 The dosimetric analysis and clinical outcomes of re-irradiation for recurrent high grade glioma

items.abstract: <jats:p>Wound healing is a complex, dynamic biological process that relies on the integration of cells, soluble mediators, the extracellular matrix, and an adequate blood supply. Systemic conditions, such as diabetes mellitus, vascular insufficiency, and chronic inflammatory states, can compromise this process and lead to wounds that are difficult to heal. In this context, photobiomodulation (PBM) has been widely studied as an adjunctive therapy. Specifically, Intravascular Laser Irradiation of Blood (ILIB) has attracted interest because of its potential systemic, rather than merely local, effects. This study aimed to analyze, through an integrative literature review, the available evidence on the use of ILIB and its photobiological foundations in the wound-healing process. The synthesis indicates that the proposed mechanisms of ILIB include the modulation of mitochondrial activity, nitric oxide release, reduction of oxidative stress, improvement of blood rheological parameters, and cytokine modulation. Although experimental and in vitro studies support the biological plausibility of these effects, the clinical literature specifically addressing ILIB and wound healing remains scarce, heterogeneous regarding dosimetric parameters, and largely of low methodological quality. It is concluded that ILIB is a biologically plausible and potentially promising adjunctive approach; however, randomized, controlled clinical trials with standardized protocols are required before firm recommendations can be established.</jats:p>
title: O uso do laser ILIB na cicatrização: uma revisão integrativa da literatura
The use of ILIB laser in wound healing: an integrative literature review

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Medulloblastoma (MB) is one of the most common malignant pediatric central nervous system (CNS) tumors, accounting for approximately 6.3% of CNS tumors in patients aged &lt; 19 years. While initial multimodal therapy achieves 70-80% 5-year overall survival (OS), recurrence occurs in 20-30% of patients and remains the primary cause of mortality. Currently, management of relapse is challenging with no established standard of care. Re-irradiation (reRT) is an emerging salvage option, but its efficacy and risk of toxicity remain poorly defined. Therefore, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the efficacy and safety of reRT in recurrent MB.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A systematic search was conducted across MEDLINE, Web of Science, Embase, Scopus, and CENTRAL up to October 2025, in accordance with PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO: CRD20251161747). Eligible studies included ≥ 5 recurrent MB patients treated with reRT. Primary outcomes were OS, progression-free survival (PFS), and treatment-related toxicities. Random-effects models were used to pool survival probabilities and risk ratios (RRs) using R software.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Twenty studies involving 559 patients were included, with sample sizes ranging from 7 to 84 patients. ReRT doses ranged from 14.5 to 59.4 Gy. Pooled analysis of three comparative studies revealed that reRT significantly improved OS compared to patients not receiving reRT at 1-year (RR: 0.51; 95% CI: 0.32-0.82), 2-years (RR: 0.53; 95% CI: 0.40-0.71), and 5-years (RR: 0.86; 95% CI: 0.76-0.98), with no observed heterogeneity (I² = 0%). For patients receiving reRT, the pooled OS from relapse was 78% (95% CI: 64-88%; I² = 56%), 64% (95% CI: 48-77%; I² = 65.6%), 45% (95% CI: 37-54%; I² = 0%), and 28% (95% CI: 18-41%; I² = 50.1%) at 1-, 2-, 3-, 5-years, respectively. The pooled radiological response rate, reported by five studies, was 50% (95% CI: 37-62%; I² = 0%). The pooled incidence of radiation necrosis was 9% (95% CI: 3-21%; I² = 63.4%) across 10 studies, with all reported events limited to grades 1 and 2. Sensitivity analysis confirmed the robustness of this finding.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest that reRT is a feasible and effective salvage strategy for recurrent medulloblastoma, demonstrating a significant survival benefit. Although the risk of radiation necrosis exists, it is generally low-grade. However, further comparative studies and clinical trials, as well as studies with more homogeneous treatment groups, are needed to provide more definitive evidence and to optimize treatment parameters, including radiation dose and patient selection based on molecular subgroups.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: EP09.18 Efficacy and safety of re-irradiation in recurrent medulloblastoma: a systematic review and meta-analysis

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Glioblastoma (GBM) is an aggressive cancer requiring deeper understanding and new therapeutic approaches. The tumoral microenvironment guide cancer cell progression. Our previous studies demonstrated that astrocytes (ACs) enhance GBM proliferation, as evidenced by analyses of clinical samples and experimental studies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>HTS screening (14000 compounds) was performed on co-cultured GBM cells and astrocytes. Tumor growth and self-renewal capacity were assessed via cell proliferation and tumor-sphere formation assays (Luc-GFP system). Human GBM specimens were analyzed using multiplex profiling to detect FASN+GFAP+ astrocytes and Ki67+ proliferative cancer cells. Mitochondrial transfer from ACs to GBM cells was quantified using confocal imaging and FACS. FASN inhibitors potency screening was used to correlate FASN cellular activity and co-culture activity. Non-FASN inhibitory hits were explored by Proteome Integral Solubility Alteration (PISA) Assay for target identification.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Primary screening identified approximately 130 specific hits. Bioinformatic analysis indicated fatty acid synthase (FASN) as an enriched target. FASN knockdown in astrocytes significantly reduced their support of GBM proliferation and self-renewal. Selected compound from screening showed reduced or no activity in co-cultures with FASN KD astrocytes. Strong correlation was observed between cellular FASN inhibitory potency and growth-inhibitory activity among FASN inhibitors. Free fatty acid supplementation rescued GBM growth in co-cultures with FASN-knockdown astrocytes but not in wild-type astrocyte co-cultures. FASN knockdown reduced mitochondrial transfer from astrocytes to GBM cells, while MIRO knockdown suggested mitochondrial transfer is essential for FASN-mediated AC-supported growth. PISA analyses of hits not targeting FASN also indicated effects on fatty acid metabolism. Preliminary multiplex staining demonstrated positive correlation between FASN-positive astrocytes and Ki67+EGFR+GBM cells in human samples.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Screening results, tissue profiling, and knockdown experiments collectively identify astrocyte-derived FASN and fatty acid metabolism as critical components of astrocyte-driven GBM growth. These findings are being developed through mechanistic studies, expanded human GBM profiling, and studies in in orthotopic mouse models using FASN-knockdown astrocytes and FASN inhibitors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: P02.01.B Astrocyte-expressed FASN as a novel candidate drug target for glioblastoma

items.abstract: <jats:p>This Perspective article presents the development and practical implementation of cybersecurity requirements for nuclear power plants (NPP) instrumentation and control (I&amp;C) systems in Ukraine. Particular attention is given to NP 306.2.237-2022 “Cybersecurity Requirements for Instrumentation and Control Systems of Nuclear Power Plants to Ensure Nuclear and Radiation Safety” (NP 306.2.237-2022) as the key regulatory instrument establishing a specialized approach to cybersecurity of NPP I&amp;C systems. The paper examines the integration of cybersecurity requirements into the nuclear and radiation safety framework, the implementation process for I&amp;C system developers and the operating organization, and the main technical, methodological, and organizational challenges encountered during implementation. The adoption of specialized, safety-oriented cybersecurity regulations is an essential step toward protecting nuclear I&amp;C systems, but their practical effectiveness depends on translating general requirements into technically justified measures compatible with nuclear safety functions. On this basis, priorities for further development are proposed, and lessons of potential relevance to other countries are outlined.</jats:p>
title: Cybersecurity requirements for nuclear power plant instrumentation and control systems in Ukraine: challenges and future directions for implementation

items.abstract: <jats:p>Autism is defined through social-communication differences and restricted or repetitive patterns, but these domains are often explained separately. Informational Engagement Kinetics (IEK) proposes a clinical process framework for asking how an informational target gains control, becomes integrated and stabilized, is released, and is followed by a usable successor. Its central hypothesis is amplified and history-dependent target selectivity: controlled differences in person–target–context compatibility should produce larger differences in recruitment, stabilization, release, and successor construction in autistic than comparison participants, while prior occupancy should predict additional transition effects after current compatibility is controlled. A compact candidate specification states the minimum causal relations required for the hypotheses without claiming validated parameters, biomarkers, or a new diagnostic subtype. Its clinical contribution is a structured kinetic map of high-value targets, common competitors, entry supports, overload signatures, stabilizing conditions, release barriers, and effective transition bridges. This map helps distinguish outwardly similar presentations of non-response, rigidity, inattention, and distress. Six falsifiable hypotheses are proposed, including randomized-exposure studies using novel targets, survival analysis of release, and distributional analysis of dwell time. IEK is offered as an autism-centered process theory whose value depends on incremental prediction beyond monotropism, uncertainty, executive, predictive-processing, and decision-accumulation accounts.</jats:p>
title: Informational engagement kinetics in autism: a clinical framework for target recruitment, stabilization, release, and successor construction

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Diffuse midline glioma (DMG) remains a uniformly fatal pediatric brain tumor, in part due to the restrictive nature of the blood-brain-tumor barrier (BBTB), which limits therapeutic delivery. Although radiation therapy remains the standard of care, its effects on tumor-associated vasculature and subsequent drug delivery are poorly understood. To address this gap, we leveraged a patient-derived microvascular model of the DMG-BBTB to investigate how clinically relevant radiation doses alter vascular integrity and influence nanoparticle transport.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We have established a microvascular model of the DMG-BBTB, where tumor cells, endothelial cells, astrocytes, and pericytes are seeded into microfluidic devices and self-assemble into perfusable three-dimensional microvascular networks. Devices containing DMG cells or tumor-free BBB controls were exposed to a single dose of 0.25 Gy, 1 Gy, 2 Gy, 4 Gy, or no x-ray irradiation. Vascular responses were assessed 1-24 hours post-irradiation. Barrier integrity and permeability were quantified by perfusing fluorescently labeled dextran to evaluate paracellular transport following radiation. Nanoparticles were either co-perfused with dextran to assess permeability coefficients or administered for extended dosing to evaluate live trafficking and tumor targeting over time.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Radiation effects were examined across multiple timepoints and doses, revealing dose- and time-dependent alterations in vascular integrity and marker expression unique to the DMG-BBTB. One such marker, P-selectin, featured expression that was highest upregulated on DMG-BBTB vasculature at 1 hour after 2 Gy radiation exposure compared to later timepoints, with expression localized primarily on the luminal surface of microvascular branch points. To assess the targeting potential of this vascular alteration, fluorescent lipid-based nanoparticles functionalized to bind P-selectin were formulated via layer-by-layer assembly and administered to devices. P-selectin targeting nanoparticles featured time-dependent differences in permeability in irradiated DMG-BBTB devices as well as association in DMG-BBTB tumor and endothelial cells compared to nonirradiated, nontumor, or untargeted nanoparticle controls.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In summary, we developed a high-fidelity microvascular model of the DMG-BBTB and demonstrated its utility by examining the effects of radiation on barrier integrity and screening nanoparticle formulations for targeted delivery. We found that P-selectin is upregulated in irradiated DMG microvasculature, and P-selectin-targeting nanoparticles offer a promising delivery strategy for DMG following radiation. This integrative preclinical platform provides a framework for investigating combinatory radiation and nanomedicine strategies for DMG.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: P10.21.A Targeted nanoparticle delivery following low-dose irradiation in a microvascular model of pediatric diffuse midline glioma

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The standard of care for glioblastoma involves maximal safe resection, followed by concomitant chemoradiotherapy and six cycles of adjuvant temozolomide (TMZ). The clinical benefit of extending TMZ treatment remains controversial due to a lack of consistent evidence. We evaluated the impact of prolonged TMZ therapy on overall survival.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A population-based retrospective cohort study was conducted using administrative health data to emulate an intention-to-treat target trial comparing extended TMZ (12 cycles) with the standard six-cycle regimen. Adults with glioblastoma (2016 WHO classification) who received surgical resection or biopsy in Ontario (2010-2023) followed by completion of six cycles of adjuvant TMZ after chemoradiation (≥54Gy/30 fractions or 34Gy/15 fractions for elderly patients) were included. To mitigate immortal time bias, time zero was defined at completion of the standard treatment. Confounding was addressed using inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), with propensity score calibration for the molecular markers (MGMT promoter methylation, IDH mutation) unmeasured for some participants. Hazard ratios (HRs) were estimated using weighted Cox models. Sensitivity analyses included 1) a per-protocol analysis, 2) a time-dependent treatment model, and 3) excluding those who died ≤ 28 days of time-zero. Stratified analyses were also performed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>775 patients were included (standard: n = 364; extended: n = 411); 65% male (standard: 63%; extended: 67%) with a median age of 60 (standard: 61; extended: 59). IPTW achieved covariate balance across treatment groups (all standardized differences &lt;0.05). Median overall survival was longer in the extended group (9.9 vs 7.8 months; log-rank p = 0.08) with an unadjusted HR of 0.87 (95% CI: 0.75-1.02). Extended TMZ was associated with lower risk of death in the intention-to-treat (HR: 0.84; 95% CI: 0.76-0.93) and per-protocol analyses (HR: 0.74; 95% CI: 0.62-0.87), as well as among IDH wildtype patients (HR: 0.84; 95% CI: 0.75-0.95). The time-dependent model (HR: 0.85; 95% CI: 0.77-0.96) and analysis excluding those who died ≤ 28 days of time-zero (HR: 0.85; 95% CI: 0.77-0.95) showed similar results. Effect estimates were consistent when stratified by age (≥65, &lt;65) and MGMT status. There was an interaction between radiotherapy and treatment on survival (p = 0.04), with a greater effect of extended TMZ in patients who received hypofractionated radiation (HR: 0.67; 95% CI: 0.52-0.85) than standard radiation (HR: 0.88; 95% CI: 0.78-0.99). A similar pattern was observed in the IDH-wildtype subgroup (interaction p = 0.06).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A survival benefit for extended adjuvant TMZ was demonstrated in the primary and sensitivity analyses, with consistent results in most stratified models. These findings support the consideration of prolonged adjuvant TMZ for glioblastoma patients.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: EP12.33 Safety and effectiveness of extended temozolomide chemotherapy in glioblastoma patients, a target trial emulation

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy has transformed the treatment of haematological malignancies but has shown limited efficacy in solid tumours such as glioblastoma, where antigen heterogeneity and immunosuppressive tumour microenvironments drive therapeutic failure. Multi-target CAR strategies offer a means to overcome antigen escape, yet the expanded combinatorial space presents a major barrier to rational therapeutic prioritisation, and multi-antigen targeting alone may be insufficient to achieve durable tumour control.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Here, we performed cell-surface proteomics of adult and paediatric brain tumours to identify recurrently expressed antigens and generated a panel of ten corresponding CAR constructs. Using a protein barcoding strategy (Pro-Code) to track CAR combinations at single-cell resolution, we systematically interrogated multi-CAR pools in vitro and in orthotopic glioblastoma xenograft models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Although multi-target CAR pools exhibited robust activation and expansion following repeated antigen stimulation in vitro, they failed to provide consistent tumour control in vivo, highlighting the requirement for additional immunomodulatory support.To address this, we developed a bispecific PD-L1×CD137 immunomodulatory antibody and evaluated its capacity to augment multi-target CAR T cell therapy. While PD-1 checkpoint blockade alone did not improve efficacy, PD-L1×CD137 treatment dramatically enhanced CAR T cell engraftment and converted a rationally selected multi-CAR pool into a curative therapeutic regimen, achieving rapid and complete clearance of established orthotopic brain tumours.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Together, these findings demonstrate that effective solid tumour CAR T cell therapy requires both multi-antigen targeting and tumour-directed co-stimulatory reinforcement, and provide a scalable framework for prioritising therapeutic combinations to overcome the efficacy barrier in brain cancer.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: OS01.5.A Tumour-directed PD-L1×CD137 bispecific immunomodulation unlocks curative multi-target CAR T cell therapy in glioblastoma

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Pilocytic astrocytoma (PA) is a slow-growing, typically benign brain tumor. Stereotactic irradiation is considered one of the most effective methods for the tumor control. The safety of this approach to the treatment of benign tumors remains a subject of considerable discussion in the literature.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We present the treatment outcomes of 410 patients with PA. There were 300 (73.2%) pediatric patients (under 18 years of age) and 110 (26.8%) adults. Among 152 patients (37%), the tumor was located in the optic pathway. Brainstem tumors occurred in 133 (32.4%). Other sites: subcortical ganglia — 57 (13.9%), cerebellum — 44 (10.7%), cerebral hemispheres — 24 (5.9%).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In 24 (5.9%) cases, patients received chemotherapy according to the SIOPP protocol prior to radiotherapy. Radiotherapy was the primary treatment for newly diagnosed tumors in 63 (15.4%) patients. In 141 (34.4%) patients, radiotherapy was performed because there are residual tumors after surgery. In 206 patients, the treatment was administered for continued tumor growth (recurrence), 69 (16.8%) patients showed growth of the residual tumor after the first surgery; 94 (22.9%) patients underwent two or more surgeries due to tumor recurrence; and 24 (5.9%) patients experienced continued growth after chemotherapy. In the majority of cases (292 (71.2%) patients), stereotactic radiotherapy was delivered using standart fractionation (1,8 Gy per fraction). Hypofractionated radiotherapy was used in 61 (14.9%) patients. The median total prescribed dose for standart fractionation was 54 Gy (range, 45.3-66 Gy), with a median clinical target volume (CTV) of 19.2 cm³ (range, 0.91-237 cm³). For hypofractionated radiotherapy, the median total prescribed dose was 28 Gy (5,5 Gy per fraction), with a median CTV of 11.51 cm³ (range, 0.1-36.9 cm³). Radiosurgery was used in 57 (13,9%) patients with a median dose 18 Gy. Among the 391 patients (95,4%) with available follow-up data. All patients achieved a follow-up of 48 months after irradiation. . Five-year overal survival 99%. Partial response was observed in 51.6% of cases, a complete response in 7.2%, stable disease in 21.5% of cases. 67 (16.3%) patients developed pseudoprogression followed by spontaneous regression or partial removal/emptying of cysts. Recurrences (4 local and 4 distant) occurred in 8 (2%) patients. Finally, five-year progression-free survival was achieved in 97,5% cases. No secondary tumors were detected in any patient.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Stereotactic irradiation is an effective method of treatment for PA in patients with residual tumors and patients with progressive disease.With the available follow-up period, we did not identify any serious complications that may justify postponing the radiation treatment. Further study of the results of stereotactic irradiation and revision of the indications for this treatment method are required.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: EP10.07 Outcomes of stereotactic irradiation for pilocytic astrocytoma: the largest single-center study

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM), classified as a grade IV astrocytoma by the World Health Organization, is one of the most aggressive and heterogeneous malignant brain tumors, accounting for a large proportion of central nervous system malignancies. Recent advances in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) have enabled characterization of gene expression at single-cell resolution, providing deeper insight into tumor heterogeneity. Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), which regulate gene expression at multiple levels, have been increasingly implicated in cancer development, progression, and therapeutic resistance. However, the functional roles of many lncRNAs in GBM remain poorly understood.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In the computational phase, publicly available scRNA-seq datasets from 14 GBM patients were analyzed to evaluate the expression of 12,133 disease-associated lncRNAs at single-cell resolution. Among these, LINC01551 was identified as a potential oncogenic regulator. Correlation analyses with highly variable genes were performed to identify putative target genes and GBM-related pathways associated with LINC01551. In the experimental phase, CRISPR-Cas9-mediated knockout of LINC01551 was performed in normal human astrocytes and multiple GBM cell lines, followed by transcriptomic profiling (RNA-seq) to investigate its functional role and regulatory network.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>LINC01551 was identified as a key lncRNA associated with GBM malignancy. Significant interactions were observed between LINC01551 and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT)-related genes, including SOX2, EGFR, PTN, and PTPRZ1, suggesting its involvement in tumor progression through EMT-associated mechanisms. Computational analysis indicated that LINC01551 may regulate at least 154 genes in GBM tissue. RT-qPCR validation confirmed that 48 of these genes were significantly upregulated in U87MG cells compared to normal astrocytes and exhibited significant expression changes following LINC01551 CRISPR-Cas9-mediated knockout.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study identifies LINC01551 as a potential key regulator in GBM pathogenesis. CRISPR-based functional analyses combined with transcriptomic profiling provide a framework for elucidating its regulatory gene network and biological roles in both normal and malignant brain cells. Elucidating the contribution of LINC01551 to GBM progression through regulation of multiple protein-coding genes, particularly via EMT-related mechanisms, may offer insights into therapeutic target identification and support the development of more effective treatments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: EP18.25 Functional role of lncRNA LINC01551 in glioblastoma and its target gene network

items.abstract: <jats:p>Laser doping is one of the routes available for forming a selective emitter on boron-diffused n-type silicon, but the power range within which the process is both dopant-effective and repairable had not been delimited. This work follows a laser-doped selective emitter from 30 to 40 W and asks what a subsequent oxidation can and cannot undo. Morphology, reflectance, sheet resistance and electrochemical capacitance-voltage profiles were taken at a fixed point of the fabrication sequence, and symmetric test structures were measured before and after the oxidation so that the repair step could be separated from the presence of the selective emitter. Between 30 and 35 W the oxidation recovers most of the recombination that the laser introduces and lowers the peak surface concentration to 8.4–9.1 × 1018 cm−3, a behavior consistent with boron segregation into the growing oxide and with the annealing of part of the laser-induced defects. At 40 W the pyramids collapse and ablation pits open, and the same oxidation partially repaired only about 14% of the saturation current density, against 40%–43% at the two lower powers. Cells printed with the 35 W emitter reach an average efficiency of 25.60% against 25.26% for the homogeneous reference.</jats:p>
title: Laser-Power-Dependent Damage and Post-Oxidation Repair in Laser-Doped Selective Emitters for High-Efficiency TOPCon Solar Cells

items.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Thulium fiber laser (TFL) has been proposed as an alternative to holmium:yttrium-aluminum-garnet (Ho:YAG) laser for endoscopic lithotripsy, but its incremental benefit over contemporary Ho:YAG systems remains uncertain.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to May 2026. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing TFL with Ho:YAG laser lithotripsy for upper urinary tract stones were included. Continuous outcomes were pooled as mean differences (MDs), and dichotomous outcomes were pooled as odds ratios (ORs). Subgroup analyses were performed according to stone-free rate (SFR) definition, stone location, and use of Modulated Oscillating Pulse Energy System (MOSES) 2.0 technology. Additional exploratory analyses examined stone burden, imaging modality, surgical modality, and study initiation period.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Twelve RCTs involving 1383 patients were included. TFL was associated with shorter total operation time (MD = −6.65 minutes, 95% confidence interval [CI]: −9.52 to −3.79) and lasering time (MD = −3.92 minutes, 95% CI: −5.65 to −2.20). Complete SFR favored TFL (OR = 1.70, 95% CI: 1.13–2.54), whereas SFR allowing clinically insignificant residual fragments (CIRFs) did not (OR = 1.71, 95% CI: 0.86–3.37). Hospital stay, postoperative stenting, ureteral perforation, mucosal injury, and Clavien–Dindo grades I–III complications were comparable. In exploratory comparisons using MOSES 2.0, TFL showed no significant advantage in operation time or SFR.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>TFL appears to improve lithotripsy efficiency and complete stone clearance without increasing most complications. Its advantage is less clear when small residual fragments are accepted or when the comparator uses MOSES 2.0 technology.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Thulium Fiber Laser vs Ho:YAG Laser Lithotripsy for Upper Urinary Tract Stones: An Updated Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials

items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Chronic diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) pose a severe clinical hurdle, largely because of the resilience of polymicrobial biofilms. When
                    <jats:italic>Staphylococcus aureus</jats:italic>
                    and
                    <jats:italic>Pseudomonas aeruginosa</jats:italic>
                    occupy the same wound environment, they can form a drug-tolerant biofilm in which context-dependent cooperation, regulated in part by species-specific quorum sensing (QS) systems, contributes to persistence. Single-target treatments do not address the regulatory programmes of both organisms. This perspective proposes, but does not implement a computational strategy that combines machine learning, multi-task virtual screening, and a staged experimental cascade to prioritize dual-acting QS inhibitors. We hypothesize that the Gram-negative LasR receptor and the Gram-positive AgrA regulator, although structurally unrelated, share enough pharmacophore-level ligandability for a single small molecule to inhibit both. Such dual inhibition of two species-specific QS pathways is distinct from direct disruption of interspecies signaling, which would require separate evidence. We distinguish established evidence from hypothesis and proposed methodology, set out a convergence test and falsifiable go/no-go criteria, and discuss data harmonization, model validation and wound-specific constraints. If the hypothesis holds, such a compound could act as an antivirulence adjuvant that may enhance the activity of conventional antibiotics under selected conditions and support wound healing.
                  </jats:p>
title: A proposed multi-task machine learning strategy for dual-target quorum sensing inhibitor discovery in diabetic foot ulcer biofilms

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Radiotherapy is the only established treatment option for meningioma beyond surgical resection. Technology progress in radiation oncology during the past decades includes proton beam irradiation for selected cases. The efficacy of proton compared to photon beam radiotherapy for meningioma has not been studied in detail.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Patients and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Multi-center retrospective cohort study of patients with histopathologically diagnosed meningioma, who were treated by radiotherapy at three centers between 2000-2020. Demographics and clinical parameters were retrieved from electronic patient charts. Magnetic resonance imaging scans were analyzed for tumor size, extent of resection and progression-free survival per the Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology working group criteria. Categorical variables were compared by the chi square test, continuous variables by the Mann-Whitney-U Test and survival by the logrank test. Multivariate analyses of progression-free survival was done by Cox regression, accounting for age, sex, gross total versus partial resection, tumor grade, and second line versus first line radiotherapy as well as irradiation modality.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We identified 217 meningiomas in 190 patients. The median age at diagnosis was 55 years (range: 22-84) and 146 patients (67%) were female. There were 99 grade 1 (46%), 83 grade 2 (38%) and 35 grade 3 meningiomas (16%). Sixty-seven meningiomas (31%) exhibited parenchymal infiltration of the brain. A gross-total resection prior to radiotherapy was achieved in approximately one third of patients (N = 73, 34%). Radiotherapy was conducted as photon beam irradiation in 166 meningiomas (76%), of which 132 were treated by normofractionated stereotactic irradiation (mean dose 56.4 Gy, range 20-32 fractions), 13 by hypofractionated stereotactic irradiation (mean dose 24.1 Gy, range 3-7 fractions) and 16 by single fraction radiosurgery (mean dose 20.4 Gy, range 1-6 fractions). Proton beam irradiation was conducted as normofractionated irradiation in 53 of 54 meningiomas (mean 56.9 Gy, range 20-35 fractions). Demographics and clinical parameters were balanced between patients who underwent photon versus proton beam radiotherapy. Median progression-free survival of patients treated by normofractionated photon versus proton beam radiotherapy was similar among patients with grade 1 (p = 0.59) or grade 2 (p = 0.50) meningiomas. All but one of the 35 grade 3 meningiomas were treated by photon beam radiotherapy, and the median progression-free survival was 17.0 months (range 3.7-63.5). No difference in progression-free survival between proton versus photon beam irradiation was observed in the multivariate Cox model (HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.23-1.62, p = 0.34).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>There was no difference in the efficacy of photon and proton beam radiotherapy for meningioma patients with similar demographic and treatment factors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: EP09.02 Proton versus photon beam radiotherapy for meningioma: A retrospective efficacy analysis by irradiation modality

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The ion temperature (Ti) clamping effect, which severely constrains the improvement of energy confinement in electron-heated plasmas, has been systematically investigated in EAST. The core ion temperature is universally clamped at approximately 1.25 keV under electron cyclotron resonance heating (ECRH) and lower hybrid wave (LHW) scenarios with plasma current Ip ≤ 550 kA. Experimental results show that under high plasma current (600 kA) and high density conditions, the energy confinement time exceeds the electron-ion collision time, enabling efficient collisional ion heating and breaking the clamping effect with a maximum core ion temperature up to 2 keV. In contrast, the clamping effect persists at Ip ≤ 550 kA even when the energy confinement time becomes comparable to the electron-ion collision time, indicating additional mechanisms beyond simple time-scale matching. Furthermore, pulsed argon (Ar) impurity injection at 400 kA effectively elevates the core ion temperature by approximately 80% to 1.8 keV, exceeding the clamping threshold. This enhancement is accompanied by a significant reduction in ion thermal diffusivity and a transition of the dominant turbulent instability modes from TEM and ETG dominance to ITG and ETG dominance, demonstrating a pronounced improvement in ion channel confinement. These findings provide important experimental evidence for understanding ion heating and energy confinement physics in electron-heated plasmas, and support the development of advanced operational scenarios for future fusion devices.</jats:p>
title: Experimental investigation of ion temperature clamping effect in electron-heated plasmas on EAST

                    N
                    <jats:sup>6</jats:sup>
                    -methyladenosine (m
                    <jats:sup>6</jats:sup>
                    A) regulation is essential to RNA fate and leukemic cell-state maintenance, but genetic dependency does not necessarily establish a tractable drug target. This focused review evaluates the pharmacological targeting of three m
                    <jats:sup>6</jats:sup>
                    A regulators—METTL3, FTO and ALKBH5 in acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Unlike broader surveys of epitranscriptomic therapeutics across cancers, we compare the strength of genetic evidence, chemical target engagement, antileukemic activity and translational readiness for each target. METTL3 has the most convincing chemical proof of concept: STM2457 inhibits its catalytic activity, induces differentiation and apoptosis, and reduces leukemia burden in preclinical models. FTO-directed compounds, including R-2-hydroxyglutarate, FB23-2 and CS1/CS2, support pharmacological exploration, although activity against dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH) complicates mechanistic attribution. ALKBH5 sustains leukemia stem-cell programs, but selective inhibitors remain insufficiently validated. We also examine METTL3 inhibition combined with venetoclax and emerging protein-degradation or delivery approaches. The principal barriers are chemical selectivity, differences between AML and normal hematopoiesis, molecular-subtype dependence and inadequate pharmacodynamic biomarkers. We propose an AML-specific evidence framework that distinguishes target dependency from compound-specific efficacy and prioritizes mechanistically validated combinations over broad claims of clinical readiness.
                  </jats:p>
title: Pharmacological targeting of METTL3, FTO and ALKBH5 in acute myeloid leukemia: target validation, therapeutic resistance and translational challenges

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Pervious concrete (PC) serves as a highly porous pavement material enabling water infiltration, stormwater runoff reduction, and groundwater recharge. PC properties are often governed by factors such as aggregate shape, size, and pore characteristics, cement content, water–cement ratio, and additives. Although machine learning (ML) has transformed the construction industry by predicting conventional concrete properties, studies on PC with additives remain limited. Thus, the major objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness of ML models and algorithms in predicting the target properties of PC mixtures, including compressive strength (CS), porosity, and permeability, based on random forest (RF), gradient boosting (GB), and artificial neural network (ANN) using a master database of 350 data points covering 78 mixtures. An independent 36-point external validation set was used to assess model generalizability. The input parameters used for developing the models included water-to-cement ratio, aggregate-to-cement (a/c) ratio, density, and additives such as silica fume and crumb rubber. Performance metrics indicated that RF and GB outperformed ANN during CS prediction, with test coefficient of determination (R2) of 0.79 and 0.80, and root mean square error of 2.04 and 1.97 MPa, respectively. Further, mixture-level out-of-fold R2 of 0.45 (RF) and 0.44 (GB) represented the unbiased estimates. All three models predicted porosity and permeability with good to excellent accuracy (R2 = 0.83–0.98). Furthermore, SHapley Additive exPlanations-based feature importance analysis revealed that density dominated CS prediction, and the a/c ratio governed porosity and permeability, thereby corroborating the distinct physical mechanisms controlling the mechanical and hydraulic performance of PC. All three ML models predicted the target PC properties with very good to excellent accuracy; however, the RF model showed the narrowest expected difference range (d3s) for predicted PC properties. It is envisioned that the proposed algorithms in this study can be readily applied in practice by entering component quantities in the same format as the training dataset. Overall, this research study contributed to comprehending the PC properties better and will serve as the foundation for a computational and statistical framework in the future to facilitate a paradigm shift toward developing environmentally sustainable and resilient roadway infrastructure materials/systems.</jats:p>
title: Assessing the Effectiveness of Machine Learning Models in Predicting the Target Properties of Modified Pervious Concrete Mixtures

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Hydrothermal systems have long been proposed as plausible cradles for the chemical origin of life, yet how hydrothermal minerals shape the synthetic potential of prebiotic chemical networks remains poorly understood. Here, we construct a six-layered computational mineral-promoted chemical reaction network (M-CRN) by integrating experimentally validated reactions promoted by minerals into a classical chemical reaction network. We combine machine-learning-assisted pathway analysis with thermodynamic assessment to quantify how these minerals alter the accessibility, connectivity, and energetic properties of prebiotic chemistry. The M-CRN contains 114,476 molecules, including 26 intermediates associated with five proposed primordial metabolic cycles and 10 amino acids selected as target molecules. Compared with a network without minerals, the M-CRN provides more than twice as many enumerated pathways for 12 target molecules, enables access to 14 otherwise inaccessible target molecules, and shortens the synthetic routes to four targets. Metal sulfides also broaden the carbon sources available for assimilatory fixation and chain elongation; under modeled Miller-type conditions, mineral-promoted reactions are more frequent in the network than corresponding non-mineral pathways. These network-level effect suggest that metal sulfides could enhance organic synthesis under resource-limited conditions, with potential implications for the dilution challenge in hydrothermal environments. Mineral-promoted reactions preferentially contribute to the formation of sulfur-containing organic molecules with higher free energies and more diverse subsequent transformations, linking network expansion to potentially energy-rich chemistry. These findings identify hydrothermal metal sulfides as key organizers of prebiotic reaction networks and provide a framework connecting mineral-mediated geochemistry to the emergence of metabolic precursors.</jats:p>
title: Hydrothermal minerals expand the accessible prebiotic chemical space: Insights from computational reaction networks

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Glioblastoma (GBM) is a highly aggressive brain tumor with poor patient survival. A key feature of GBM progression is extensive remodeling of the brain extracellular matrix (ECM), which drives tumor growth, invasion, and therapy resistance. Heparan sulfate proteoglycans play a central role in regulating pro-tumorigenic signaling pathways. Heparanase (HPSE), the enzyme responsible for cleaving heparan sulfate (HS), has emerged as an important cancerpromoting factor. Increased HPSE activity enhances invasion and angiogenesis, and elevated HPSE expression has been associated with accelerated GBM growth and reduced patient survival.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We investigated metalloshielding as a strategy to interfere with HS remodeling and thereby inhibit the effects of HPSE in GBM. We evaluate the polynuclear platinum complex TriplatinNC, which crosses the blood-brain barrier without compromising its integrity, for its ability to modulate the tumor microenvironment through dual mechanisms involving both DNA binding and HS inhibition. Cell viability (IC₅。), HPSE expression, and cell cycle distribution were assessed in vitro. In vivo efficacy was examined using a patient-derived GBM xenograft mouse model.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>TriplatinNC demonstrated potent, concentrationdependent growth inhibition across patientderived GBM cell lines. Treatment also significantly reduced HPSE levels in GBM cells, suggesting an ability to interfere with ECMdriven tumor progression. Additionally, TriplatinNC induced prolonged G0/G1 cell cycle arrest in GBM cells. In vivo, TriplatinNC treatment resulted in reduced tumor growth and prolonged overall survival in the xenograft model.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings identify TriplatinNC as a promising HPSEtargeting therapeutic candidate for GBM and support ECMfocused approaches as potential additions to current treatment strategies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: EP02.04 Modulating heparanase as a therapeutic strategy to target glioblastoma

items.abstract: <jats:p>Glioblastoma (GBM) creates a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment in which L-arginine metabolism serves as a central regulatory node. This review synthesizes current evidence on two mechanistically distinct but converging arginine pathways: epigenetic silencing of argininosuccinate synthetase 1 (ASS1) and argininosuccinate lyase (ASL) renders GBM cells arginine-auxotrophic and dependent on extracellular arginine uptake, whereas arginase-1 (Arg1) expressed by tumor-associated myeloid cells, predominantly polymorphonuclear myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), depletes extracellular arginine and impairs T-cell proliferation and effector function. Additional themes include hypoxia-driven histone lactylation in neutrophil Arg1 induction and polyamine-supported myeloid cell survival. Arginine deprivation therapy with ADI-PEG20 or pegylated arginase induces autophagy, impairs β-actin arginylation, and enhances radiosensitivity through epigenetic silencing of DNA repair genes; combinations with radiotherapy or CDK inhibitors show synergistic activity in preclinical GBM models, and arginase inhibition enhances the efficacy of PD-1 blockade in murine gliomas, whereas direct evidence for arginine-depleting enzymes combined with checkpoint blockade in GBM remains lacking. Because activated T cells themselves require arginine, we further consider the trade-off between tumor cell starvation and T-cell function, including the condition-dependent contribution of citrulline salvage, myeloid reprogramming, and local versus systemic arginine pools, with implications for patient selection based on tumor ASS1/ASL status and myeloid Arg1 signatures. Remaining challenges include intratumoral heterogeneity in urea cycle enzyme expression, adaptive metabolic plasticity, and the limited translational fidelity of rodent models; future directions require patient-specific metabolic profiling and integrated strategies that simultaneously target tumor cell auxotrophy and myeloid-mediated immunosuppression.</jats:p>
title: Arginine metabolism as a therapeutic target in glioblastoma immunosuppression

                    <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      How top-down goals and bottom-up saliency interact over time remains a central debate in visual search. Recent models, such as the Attentional Dwelling Account and the Priority Accumulation Framework, propose that attentional capture by salient, non-matching cues (e.g., abrupt onsets) increases under difficult search conditions (longer reaction times (RTs)), challenging the classical view of transient capture. To test whether this difficulty-dependent modulation generalizes across cue types, we conducted two visual search experiments using target-matching color cues across both feature and singleton search, manipulating task difficulty via color similarity. Across both search types, we observed the inverse of the onset-cue pattern: spatial cueing effects (valid vs. invalid) were pronounced during easy search (short RTs) but virtually eliminated during difficult search (long RTs). These findings indicate that target-matching peripheral cues exert a transient influence, modulating early attentional selection but dissipating before prolonged visual search decisions conclude. Consequently, while attentional dwelling and priority accumulation accounts capture the dynamics of non-matching onset cues, they do not generalize to feature-matching color cues. We conclude that cue type, specifically whether a cue shares defining features with the target, fundamentally determines how task difficulty modulates the time course and magnitude of attentional capture. The data and analysis scripts are available at
                      <jats:ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="10.17605/OSF.IO/2CXHE" ext-link-type="doi">https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/2CXHE</jats:ext-link>
                      .
                    </jats:p>

                    <jats:p>
                      The following software was used: MATLAB 2022 a (The Mathworks, Natick, MA, USA) with the Psychtoolbox (Brainard, 1997; Kleiner et al., 2007) was used to run the experiment. Statistical analyses were performed using R 4.4.2 (R Core Team, 2024) and RStudio 2025.09.1 (Posit team, 2025). The pre-processed data and the analysis code in R are available on the Open Science Framework at
                      <jats:ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="10.17605/OSF.IO/2CXHE" ext-link-type="doi">https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/2CXHE</jats:ext-link>
                      . The study’s design and its analysis were not preregistered. The program code used to run the experiments is available on request. Please send an email to dirk.kerzel@unige.ch.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Significance statement</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper re-evaluates current priority accumulation and attentional dwelling frameworks. While these models propose that search difficulty increases attentional capture, our findings suggest a more nuanced dynamic: for target-matching color cues, capture appears transient and dissipates as difficulty grows. By showing that the relationship between difficulty and capture depends on cue type, this work highlights important boundary conditions and helps reconcile diverging accounts of attentional control.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: When difficulty helps and when it hurts: Target-matching cues yield transient capture while mismatching cues lead to dwelling

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The effectiveness of shielding concrete in nuclear and medical facilities depends primarily on its density and radiation attenuation capacity. This study investigates the use of steel slag and direct reduced iron (DRI), two locally available industrial by-products, as heavyweight aggregates for enhancing gamma radiation shielding performance of concrete. An experimental program was conducted on concrete cube specimens and prismatic beams prepared with full replacement of conventional dolomite coarse aggregate and natural sand by slag-, iron powder-, and DRI-based aggregates. The main study variables were aggregate type and water-to-cement (w/c) ratio (0.40 and 0.50) resulting in a total of twelve mixtures. A conventional concrete mix containing dolomite and sand was used as the control specimen for comparison. The investigation included physical characterization (specific gravity and water absorption), mechanical testing (compressive and flexural strength), UPV measurements before and after irradiation, and gamma attenuation assessment through determination of the linear attenuation coefficient (LAC) and half-value layer (HVL). Concrete specimens with varying thicknesses were exposed to a Cesium-137 (Cs-137) gamma source emitting photons at 662 keV under narrow-beam transmission geometry. Results showed that heavyweight mixes incorporating slag and DRI achieved significantly higher LAC values and lower HVL compared to the control concrete. The best-performing mix exhibited an HVL of 2.09 cm, approximately 48% lower than the control mix, demonstrating superior shielding efficiency. This improvement was primarily attributed to the use of high-density slag and iron-based aggregates, which constituted the most influential variable governing radiation attenuation performance. Slag-based mixes also maintained or improved mechanical strength, while short-term irradiation (7 days) caused no significant internal integrity changes. These findings confirm that steel industry by-products can serve as sustainable and cost-effective alternatives to conventional heavyweight aggregates for structural gamma radiation shielding applications.</jats:p>
title: Enhancement of gamma radiation shielding performance of heavyweight concrete using slag and Direct Reduced Iron (DRI)

items.abstract: <jats:p>Background: Diffuse-type (DGC) and intestinal-type gastric cancer (IGC) differ in pathogenesis. Because pepsinogen (PG)-based screening detects gastric atrophy, its applicability to early DGC remains uncertain. We compared serologic profiles between early DGC and IGC and evaluated biomarker performance for early DGC. Methods: We analyzed 452 patients with early gastric cancer (236 IGC and 216 DGC) and 2117 endoscopically normal controls. PGI, PGII, gastrin-17 (G-17), and Helicobacter pylori IgG were measured in patients. Clinicopathologic and biomarker characteristics were compared between subtypes, and receiver operating characteristic analysis was performed for early DGC versus controls. Results: Patients with DGC were younger (median 56.0 vs. 65.0 years) and more often female (50.5% vs. 21.6%) than those with IGC (both p < 0.001). PGI (98.7 vs. 77.7 µg/L, p < 0.001), PGII (16.6 vs. 11.9 µg/L, p < 0.001), and G-17 (5.3 vs. 3.8 pmol/L, p = 0.031) levels were higher in DGC, whereas intestinal metaplasia was more prevalent in IGC (78.0% vs. 52.8%, p < 0.001). The PGI/PGII ratio showed modest overall discrimination for early DGC (area under the curve [AUC], 0.710), increasing in women and younger subgroups to 0.818 in women aged <40 years. Conclusions: Early IGC and DGC show distinct demographic and serologic profiles. Relatively preserved PGI, PGII, and G-17 levels in early DGC suggest that atrophy-based screening may not fully capture this subtype. Sex- and age-stratified application of the PGI/PGII ratio is a potential approach for identifying early DGC, particularly in younger women.</jats:p>
title: Differential Biomarker Profiles Between Early-Stage Diffuse-Type and Intestinal-Type Gastric Cancer

items.abstract: <jats:p>Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the anatomical accessibility of a standardized simulated inferior alveolar nerve block (IANB) needle pathway in individuals with skeletal Class I, II, and III malocclusions using three-dimensional cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT)-derived mandibular models. The primary objective was to compare simulated anatomical accessibility among skeletal classes, while the secondary objective was to evaluate differences in the distal displacement required in initially unsuccessful simulations. Materials and Methods: CBCT images of 90 individuals (30 in each skeletal class), classified according to the sagittal maxillomandibular relationship using the A-point–nasion–B-point (ANB) angle, corresponding to 180 mandibular sides, were retrospectively analyzed. Three-dimensional mandibular models were reconstructed using Mimics 20.0 software. A standardized IANB needle path was simulated on each model to evaluate direct accessibility to the mandibular foramen without contacting the lingula. In unsuccessful simulations, the required distal displacement was measured. Generalized estimating equations (GEEs) for logistic regression and linear mixed-effects models were used to assess differences among skeletal classes, accounting for within-patient correlation between bilateral observations and adjusting for age, sex, and side. Bonferroni correction was applied to pairwise comparisons. Results: Simulated anatomical accessibility rates were 60.0%, 63.3%, and 40.0% in skeletal Classes I, II, and III, respectively, with an overall simulated failure rate of 45.6% (82/180 sides). GEE logistic regression revealed no statistically significant overall association between skeletal classification and simulated anatomical inaccessibility (p = 0.081). Although Class II demonstrated lower odds of simulated anatomical inaccessibility than Class III in the GEE coefficient comparison (adjusted OR = 0.364, 95% CI: 0.143–0.929; p = 0.034, unadjusted for multiple comparisons), no pairwise differences remained statistically significant in the separate Bonferroni-adjusted estimated marginal means analysis (Class II vs. Class III, p = 0.090). Age, sex, and mandibular side were not significantly associated with simulated anatomical inaccessibility (all p > 0.05). Conclusions: Although numerical differences in simulated anatomical accessibility rates and required distal displacement were observed among skeletal classes, neither outcome showed a statistically significant overall association with skeletal classification in the adjusted analyses. Further clinical studies are needed to determine whether these simulation-based anatomical findings have implications for actual IANB success.</jats:p>
title: Simulated Inferior Alveolar Nerve Block Accessibility of the Mandibular Foramen Across Skeletal Classes

items.abstract: <jats:p>Background/Objectives: The right ventricular ejection fraction (RVEF) is used with clinical thresholds, and deep learning models measure it after training on expert contours (labels). When these labels are refined, the models are re-evaluated by contour overlap. However, the overlap does not show whether the threshold decisions change. Methods: Here, label-change impact assessment (LCIA) is proposed, from the label update to the audit at a clinical site. Level 1 compares the two label sets. Level 2 evaluates a model trained on the original labels against both. In Level 3, the model is retrained on each label set with the same initial state, batches and dropout, so that any RVEF shift is caused by the labels. The RVEF range for the two label sets flags each decision, which depends on the labels. LCIA is evaluated with 5 models on the 150 patients (50 for testing) of the Automated Cardiac Diagnosis Challenge (ACDC), and the nnU-Net is also tested on 320 external patients. Results: The two label sets overlap almost completely (median Dice similarity coefficient 0.976), but the category at the 45 % threshold changes for 18 of the 150 patients. A model trained on the original labels misclassifies 13 of 50 test patients against the refined labels (4 against its own), and its overlap decreases only from 0.92 to 0.90. In four architectures, retraining moves the RVEF by a median of 3.4 to 4.7 percentage points, against 1.9 to 3.4 points between training runs. In a site audit, 11 of the 50 test decisions are flagged. Conclusions: A label refinement that is not visible in the overlap can reclassify patients at clinical thresholds without any warning. LCIA detects these patients before a model is updated, and in an audit, it refers them to the clinician.</jats:p>
title: When Reference Labels Change: A Framework for Assessing Deep Learning Measurement of Right Ventricular Ejection Fraction

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Radiation-induced contrast enhancement (RICE) and radiation-induced optic neuropathy (RION) are rare but relevant side effects following proton beam therapy for brain tumors. RICE represents a radiation-related disruption of the blood-brain barrier. RION describes radiation-induced damage to the optic nerve. While dose-dependent risk factors have been reported, individual patient-related risk factors remain largely unclear. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the incidence of RICE/RION and to identify potential cardiovascular risk factors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 115 patients (87 females, 28 males) with skull base meningiomas treated with proton beam therapy at the Heidelberg Ion-Beam Therapy Center between 2015 and 2022 were included. Follow-up consisted of clinical assessment and contrast-enhanced MRI. RICE was graded according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE), version 5.0. The incidence of RICE/RION was determined, and potential clinical risk factors (cardiovascular risk factors, including smoking, arterial hypertension, obesity, and hypercholesterolemia) were analyzed using univariable and multivariable logistic regression. Additionally, time-to-event analyses were performed using Kaplan-Meier estimates and Cox proportional hazards models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The median prescribed dose was 54 Gy (range 50-54 Gy), delivered in 25-30 fractions. After a median follow-up of 37 months, 22 patients (19%) developed at least one event, with a median time to event of 10 months, including 13 patients (11%) with RICE only, 7 patients (6%) with RION only, and 2 patients (2%) with both. In univariable logistic regression, diabetes mellitus was significantly associated with an increased risk of RICE/RION (OR 8.8, 95% CI 2.0-46.4, p = 0.005). This association remained significant after adjustment for age and periventricular PTV location (OR 7.19, 95% CI 1.53-39.07, p = 0.014). Consistent findings were observed in time-to-event analyses, where diabetes remained an independent predictor of RICE/RION (HR 4.86, 95% CI 1.51-15.68, p = 0.008). In exploratory analyses, a non-significant trend towards an increased risk of RION with higher maximum chiasma dose was observed, with additional spatial analyses ongoing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>RICE and RION represent rare but clinically relevant complications following proton beam therapy for meningiomas. Diabetes mellitus was identified as a strong and independent risk factor for their development. These findings highlight the importance of patient-related factors, particularly diabetes, for individualized risk assessment and follow-up management. This work was supported by the Mildred Scheel Doctoral Fellowship (German Cancer Aid).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: EP09.09 Diabetes mellitus as an independent risk factor for radiation-induced contrast enhancement and optic neuropathy after proton beam therapy in meningioma patients

items.abstract: <jats:p>Background/Objectives: Evidence on complete blood-count-derived inflammatory indices in patients with suspected coronary artery disease who have not received lipid-lowering or antiplatelet therapy remains limited. We examined the associations of the systemic inflammation response index (SIRI), systemic immune-inflammation index (SII), and pan-immune-inflammation value (PIV) with coronary plaque, particularly in younger patients. Methods: This cross-sectional study included 614 patients with no history of lipid-lowering or antiplatelet therapy who underwent coronary computed tomography angiography. Associations with plaque were assessed overall and by age group (younger: men < 55 years and women < 65 years). Results: After adjustment for conventional risk factors, SIRI and PIV were associated with coronary plaque (odds ratios per 1-SD increase in the log-transformed index: 1.39, 95% CI 1.13–1.69, and 1.32, 95% CI 1.08–1.60, respectively), whereas SII was not. SIRI had the highest area under the curve among the three indices (0.628). Among 325 younger patients, all three indices were associated with plaque in the main models, although the association for SII was no longer statistically significant after additional adjustment. In this group, plaque prevalence increased from 31.7% to 64.2% across SIRI quartiles. None of the associations was statistically significant in older patients, and there was no significant interaction with age, whether modeled categorically or continuously. The indices did not distinguish non-calcified or mixed plaque from calcified plaque. Conclusions: SIRI and PIV were independently associated with coronary atherosclerosis, but their modest discriminatory performance limits their use as stand-alone diagnostic markers.</jats:p>
title: Systemic Inflammatory Indices and Coronary Atherosclerosis on Computed Tomography Angiography in Patients Naive to Lipid-Lowering and Antiplatelet Therapy

items.abstract: <jats:p>Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic and preliminary prognostic value of preoperative serum cystatin-4 (CST4), a cysteine protease inhibitor involved in tumor invasion and extracellular matrix remodeling, in patients with prostate cancer (PCa). Materials and Methods: Serum CST4 levels were measured in 135 men with PCa who underwent radical prostatectomy (RP) and in 40 healthy controls with normal prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels and no evidence of cancer. Fasting serum samples were analyzed using sandwich ELISA. PSA and PSA density (PSAD) were also recorded. Diagnostic performance was assessed via ROC analysis and logistic regression. Results: Preoperative CST4 levels were significantly higher in the PCa group than in controls (1.91 ± 2.64 vs. 0.50 ± 0.28 ng/mL; p = 0.030). CST4 demonstrated modest diagnostic accuracy (AUC = 0.613; cut-off = 0.645 ng/mL; sensitivity 48.9%, specificity 87.5%; p = 0.03), whereas PSA (AUC = 0.994; p < 0.001) and PSAD (AUC = 0.971; p < 0.001) showed excellent discrimination. In multivariable logistic regression, both PSA and CST4 were statistically associated with PCa status (p < 0.05). In additional model comparisons, adding CST4 improved discrimination beyond PSAD (p = 0.023), but not beyond PSA (p = 0.130). Higher CST4 levels were observed in patients with RP Gleason score ≥ 7 (p = 0.035) but were not significantly associated with pathological stage, margin status, or D’Amico risk groups. Conclusions: Serum CST4 levels were higher in patients with PCa than in healthy controls, but discriminatory performance was limited. Additional diagnostic benefit beyond PSA has not been established. Larger studies in representative diagnostic populations, incorporating serum and tissue-level analyses, are needed to clarify CST4’s biological and clinical relevance.</jats:p>
title: Assessing Serum Cystatin 4 Levels as a Potential Biomarker in Prostate Cancer Patients Undergoing Radical Prostatectomy: A Case–Control Study

items.abstract: <jats:p>Background/Objectives: Anatomic staging leaves prognostic heterogeneity in advanced melanoma. We evaluated whether four tissue microRNAs add prognostic information beyond stage and routine clinical variables. Methods: In this prospective cohort study, adults with unresectable stage III or IV cutaneous melanoma beginning first-line anti-PD-1-based therapy were evaluated during January 2022–January 2026 at two independently recruiting centers (development center, n = 287; validation center, n = 191). A fixed, equally weighted directional score combining miR-200a-3p, miR-335-5p, miR-451a, and miR-29b-3p was added to an anatomic-stage model and a clinical Cox model including age, performance status, lactate dehydrogenase, and treatment regimen. Development models were applied without refitting to the validation cohort. Discrimination, prediction error, and calibration were evaluated at 24 months. Results: There were 171 development and 111 validation deaths. Validation Uno concordance increased from 0.708 with the clinical model to 0.780 with the panel (difference 0.072, 95% CI 0.041–0.108), and the Brier score decreased from 0.187 to 0.145. The validation association model yielded an adjusted hazard ratio of 2.83 per standardized score unit (95% CI 2.17–3.69). The extended model calibration slope was 1.16 (95% CI 0.94–1.38). Associations had consistent directions across clinical subgroups, and incremental discrimination persisted with assay perturbation and single-marker omission. Conclusions: The four-miRNA panel added prognostic information beyond clinical staging and routine variables in the validation cohort. Assay standardization, further external validation, and evaluation of clinical utility are required.</jats:p>
title: Added Prognostic Value of a Four-MicroRNA Panel Beyond Clinical Staging in Advanced Melanoma: A Development and Validation Study

items.abstract: <jats:p>Background and Clinical Significance: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) is a rare systemic vasculitis that can cause severe cardiac involvement, including eosinophilic myocarditis, myocardial fibrosis, and ventricular dysfunction. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging plays an important role in identifying myocardial injury and monitoring its evolution over time. Case Presentation: We report the case of a 39-year-old woman with antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-negative EGPA, presenting with severe eosinophilia, elevated cardiac biomarkers, and acute myocardial dysfunction. Initial CMR in July 2017 demonstrated severe left ventricular systolic impairment (left ventricular ejection fraction [LVEF], 24%), myocardial oedema, extensive heterogeneous late gadolinium enhancement (LGE), and pericardial effusion. Repeat imaging in September 2017 showed improvement in LVEF to 43%, a reduction in LGE extent, and resolution of the pericardial effusion. Long-term follow-up CMR in February 2026 demonstrated an LVEF of 45%, persistent left ventricular dilatation, and residual subendocardial LGE involving the inferoseptal and inferolateral segments. These findings illustrate the evolution from acute inflammatory myocardial injury to persistent structural abnormalities despite partial functional recovery. Conclusions: This case highlights the value of serial CMR in assessing myocardial involvement in EGPA over an extended follow-up period. Although ventricular systolic function improved and the extent of LGE decreased during the early phase, residual myocardial enhancement and progressive ventricular dilatation persisted nearly nine years after the initial presentation. These observations suggest that improvement in ventricular function does not necessarily indicate complete structural recovery and support the role of long-term imaging surveillance in patients with EGPA-related cardiac involvement.</jats:p>
title: From Acute Eosinophilic Myocarditis to Chronic Myocardial Fibrosis in Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis

                    , there is a 3.385 to 2.402 eV energy band gap narrowing (for indirect ones), indicating structural changes and raised non-bridging oxygen (NBO) content. Urbach energy decreases, suggesting reduced disorder, while refractive index, dielectric constant and molar refraction rise due to elevated NBO concentration. Reflection loss increases, optical transparency declines, and the metallization factor confirms the glasses’ insulating behavior. The reduction in optical electronegativity indicates an enhanced electron-donating capacity, along with an increase in polarizability. Moreover, the prepared glasses’ radiation shielding features were studied over the wide 0.015–15 MeV energy range. The glass sample doped with Er
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    shows superior effective atomic number and linear attenuation coefficient. The half-value layer confirms that Er
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    -infused glass provides the best shielding with minimal thickness. The results from this work emphasize doping’s influence on the features of optical and shielding, positioning Er
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    -enriched glass as a robust photonic and nuclear radiation protection application candidate.
                  </jats:p>
