items.abstract: <jats:p>Electrolyte disturbances are among the most frequent laboratory abnormalities in emergency department (ED) and hospitalized patients. This narrative review summarizes current evidence on the epidemiology, pathophysiology, recognition, acute management and prognostic value of disorders of sodium, potassium, calcium and magnesium. We discuss the diagnostic approach in the ED, including laboratory pitfalls, the role and limits of the electrocardiogram, and the selective use of point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) when the clinical and laboratory assessment of volume status in hyponatremia remains inconclusive, and we propose an unvalidated POCUS-assisted diagnostic approach. We outline guideline-based emergency treatment and the current debate on correction limits in hyponatremia, in which observational data link faster correction to lower mortality but also to a higher risk of osmotic demyelination and do not justify relaxing current safeguards. Cohort studies show a graded, U-shaped association between sodium and potassium levels and mortality, extending into the borderline range, although much of this risk reflects the underlying disease. We review emerging predictive tools, including artificial intelligence applied to the electrocardiogram and risk scores for overcorrection, which require prospective validation. Finally, we identify knowledge gaps, notably the scarcity of prospective ED-specific data, the uncertain causal role of electrolyte disturbances and the need for trials comparing correction targets.</jats:p>
title: Electrolyte Disturbances in Emergency and Hospital Medicine: Clinical Recognition, Acute Management and Prognostic Value

items.abstract: <jats:p>Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) is susceptible to contributions from instrumentation, fixtures, grounding, shielding, and electromagnetic disturbances. This study examined enclosure and transformer-state sensitivity across two campaigns comprising 388 passive dummy-circuit spectra and 104 Samsung INR18650-25R cell spectra. Assessment combined relative complex-impedance deviations, replicate-based Type-A uncertainty, instrument accuracy-contour screening, and fixed-order, 24-RC KK-compatible residual analysis. With an energized but unloaded transformer, Campaign A dummy measurements yielded maximum deviations of 22.30% at 100 µV, 2.05% at 1 mV, and 0.274% at 10 mV, with the strongest response near 49.867 Hz. Campaign B reproduced the amplitude-dependent pattern across four repetitions per transformer state, but corresponding maxima were reduced to 5.31%, 0.460%, and 0.112%, demonstrating variable rather than fixed interference magnitude. Galvanostatic dummy deviations remained comparatively small. For the cell, plain-table transformer-state deviations were 0.163% at 49.867 Hz in Campaign A and 0.061–0.249% across Campaign B excitation settings; none of the Campaign B values exceeded the Type-A repeatability-based detection threshold. Campaign B maxima reached 2.01–2.19% at 79.5–100 kHz, where instrument and fixture contributions limit interpretation. Enclosure comparisons identified no consistently superior configuration under these conditions, while sequential cell-voltage evolution limited causal attribution. Thus, disturbance detectability depends on the complete measurement chain, and dummy-circuit findings cannot be quantitatively transferred to cylindrical-cell EIS.</jats:p>
title: Measurement Chain Artefacts and Faraday Shielding in Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy

items.abstract: <jats:p>Foam concrete and equivalent classes of highly porous cementitious materials operate as fundamental components within modern construction. These applications heavily leverage their optimal strength-to-weight ratios alongside exceptional thermal insulation capacities. However, their specific spatial geometry, intrinsically formed by randomly distributed cellular structures and macro-voids, generates substantial obstacles for objective mechanical analysis. Under external loading paradigms, every individual cavity functions as an aggressive local stress concentrator. Critical strain gradients actively generate along the perimeters of these microstructural heterogeneities, initiating localized micro-cracking sequences. Optical diagnostics mapping these internal mechanisms utilizing classical Digital Image Correlation (DIC) frequently encounter algorithmic limitations. Traditional optical flow methodologies (e.g. the Farneback algorithm) rely heavily on spatial averaging of displacement fields, which invariably results in severe artificial smoothing of displacement vectors strictly along the pore and crack boundaries. To circumvent this methodological deficiency, the present research implements a tailored Structure-Adaptive Digital Image Correlation (SA-DIC) framework adjusted for foam concrete kinematics. The pipeline deploys an edge detection scan to construct a rigid binary mask outlining structural discontinuities. By integrating a geometric connectivity function, the calculation strictly blocks spatial averaging from crossing localized structural boundaries, thereby preserving physically authentic strain jumps. Method verification was conducted based on a real physical experiment: uniaxial compression of a foam concrete specimen equipped with a high-contrast speckle pattern, recorded in 4K resolution at 60 frames per second. The analysis demonstrated that the SA-DIC algorithm reduces the baseline instrumental noise floor by 19.3 % (verified via a Zero-Strain Test on stationary frames). During the active compression phase and macro-crack opening, the application of the SA-DIC method successfully reduced the level of fictitious strains within the intact matrix of the foam concrete by 25.1 % compared to the standard averaging protocol.</jats:p>
title: Structure-Adaptive Digital Image Correlation for Diagnostics of Structural Inhomogeneity in Foam Concrete

items.abstract: <jats:p>Background/Objectives: Multimodal deep learning for glaucoma detection often combines fundus imaging with optical coherence tomography (OCT), yet it is unclear when fusion adds information beyond OCT alone and how such models behave under domain shift. We compared joint and late fusion of scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (SLO) and OCT and their cross-domain transfer. Methods: Models trained on GAMMA (color fundus photographs and macular OCT; 99 cases) were applied without retraining to the Harvard-FairVision glaucoma test split (3000 patients; SLO and OCT). Unimodal and multimodal models were then trained on FairVision (6000 training and 1000 validation patients). Four candidates (OCT-only, concatenation and cross-attention fusion, and late fusion with a cross-fitted SLO weight of 0.15) were locked with their calibration and thresholds and evaluated once on the same test split. Results: Cross-domain transfer yielded areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) of 0.635–0.653. In-domain OCT-only reached a test AUROC of 0.876. Neither jointly trained cross-attention fusion (ΔAUROC −0.0045; 95% confidence interval (CI) −0.0110 to 0.0021) nor concatenation fusion (+0.0009; 95% CI −0.0056 to 0.0074) improved on OCT-only. Late fusion yielded a small ranking improvement (+0.0059; 95% CI 0.0033 to 0.0087; Holm-adjusted p = 0.0012), but a sensitivity gain at matched specificity was not established. Post hoc analyses identified lower AUROC among Black patients and a higher false-positive rate among normal eyes. Conclusions: OCT carried most of the diagnostic information. Standard joint fusion did not add value. Low-weight late fusion improved ranking slightly on a previously accessed test split; this requires independent confirmation and does not establish clinical benefit. Fusion claims require strong unimodal and late-fusion baselines and external validation.</jats:p>
title: When Does Multimodal Fusion Help? Cross-Domain Transfer, Joint Fusion, and Late Fusion of SLO and OCT for Glaucoma Detection Under an Analysis-Locked Evaluation

items.abstract: <jats:p>Background/Objectives: Pubertal development assessment relies on multimodal evidence such as clinical text, laboratory tests, ultrasound, and X-ray. In clinical practice, inference costs vary across evidence sources, while real-world data often suffer from missing modalities and uneven sample distributions. To address these challenges, we develop a cost-efficient adaptive expert-selection framework that maintains diagnostic performance under resource constraints. Methods and Materials: We propose PACE-MoE (Plan-Adaptive Cost-Efficient Mixture-of-Experts), a two-stage dynamic MoE architecture. Stage 1 invokes only a symptom expert for low-cost screening. In Stage 2, candidate expert plans are generated via structural masking and stochastic combinatorial sampling, filtered under modality and resource constraints, and scored by a resource-aware deep reinforcement learning (DRL) router to select the highest-scoring feasible plan. Predictions from both stages are combined via logit-space weighting. We evaluated the model on 1249 pubertal development cases (970 females, 279 males), which include clinical text, laboratory tests, ultrasound, and X-ray with partial modality missingness, using five-fold cross-validation and additional ablation, resource configuration, and robustness experiments. Results: PACE-MoE reduced the normalized expert-invocation proxy cost from 3.7297 to 1.4836 (a 60.2% reduction) compared with Always-Upgrade (which invokes the complete expert set for every case), while maintaining a comparable F1-score (0.8255 vs. 0.8368). At 90% optional-modality missingness, with clinical text retained, the F1-score was 0.7079 and the Mean Cost was 0.6513. Conclusions: PACE-MoE provides a two-stage dynamic MoE framework for cost-aware pubertal development assessment, reducing the normalized expert-invocation proxy cost while maintaining comparable diagnostic performance. Due to the single-center retrospective data and proxy-based cost modeling, multi-center validation remains necessary.</jats:p>
title: PACE-MoE: A Plan-Adaptive Mixture-of-Experts Framework for Cost-Aware Multimodal Pubertal Development Assessment Under Modality and Resource Constraints

items.abstract: <jats:p>The development of decentralized viral diagnostics requires sensing platforms that are portable, low-cost, and compatible with reduced material and energy demands. Sustainable and biodegradable materials provide potential substrates for such systems, but their integration with functional sensing components and point-of-care architectures remains fragmented. This review examines sustainable and biodegradable materials for viral biosensing, focusing on cellulose and its derivatives, bacterial cellulose, chitosan, alginate, silk fibroin, gelatin, starch, and biodegradable synthetic polymers. Their physicochemical properties, processability, mechanical performance, moisture sensitivity, and degradation characteristics are discussed in relation to biosensor fabrication. The review then considers metal and metal-oxide nanoparticles, carbon-based nanomaterials, quantum dots, graphene-derived materials, and MXenes as functional components for electrical, electrochemical, optical, fluorescence, and colorimetric transduction. Particular attention is given to the distinct roles of the sensing components, where molecular specificity is provided by antibodies, aptamers, nucleic-acid probes, or other recognition elements, while functional nanomaterials primarily support charge transport, signal generation, catalytic activity, or interfacial organization. Paper-based, microfluidic, flexible, and emerging wearable architectures are evaluated for low-volume and decentralized viral detection. Smartphone-based analysis, artificial intelligence and machine learning, and Internet of Medical Things connectivity are also discussed as complementary technologies for signal interpretation and data communication. Current limitations include moisture sensitivity, material variability, assay stability, matrix effects, reproducibility, manufacturing scalability, clinical validation, and the environmental impact of non-biodegradable components within complete devices. This review emphasizes the need to assess sustainability at the device level rather than considering the substrate in isolation. It integrates sustainable materials, sensing nanomaterials, device architectures, and digital technologies within a device-oriented framework, distinguishing material-level sustainability from the environmental and practical performance of complete viral diagnostic systems. Future development should therefore focus on integrating biodegradable materials with functional transducers, low-energy fluidics, flexible architectures, and appropriate digital readout while maintaining analytical and clinical reliability.</jats:p>
title: Sustainable and biodegradable materials for flexible point-of-care biosensing with applications in viral diagnostics

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Lightweight, multifunctional materials that combine electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding with sustainable energy generation are critical for the next generation of flexible electronics. Incorporating 10 phr (parts per hundred rubber) of reduced graphene oxide (rGO) into natural rubber (NR) foam counterintuitively reduced the density by 59.5% compared to that of unfilled foam, which is an outcome driven by rGO-controlled heterogeneous nucleation that simultaneously minimizes cell wall thickness and maximizes the expansion ratio. The resulting foam has a density of 0.34 g/cm3 and a compressive modulus of 5.21 MPa. These microstructural features create a percolating conductive network within the thin cell walls, co-optimizing electromagnetic interference shielding and triboelectric energy harvesting via the morphological structure, thereby helping to confine the rGO network within the cell walls. This microstructure independently provides a conductive pathway for EMI attenuation and charge-trapping density for the triboelectric output. Consequently, the foam demonstrated a specific shielding effectiveness of 94.1 dB.cm2/g and a triboelectric nanogenerator power density of 4.30 W/m2. The charge value recorded for the currently developed system was 107 nC, while the maximum charge density observed was 43 µC/m2, indicating superior performance compared to existing materials. This work establishes a scalable material platform that integrates EMI shielding with self-powering capabilities, offering a unique solution toward interference-resilient, energy-autonomous, flexible electronics.</jats:p>
title: Lightweight Natural Rubber–Reduced Graphene Oxide Foam Architectures Enabling Simultaneous Electromagnetic Interference Shielding and Self-Powered Flexible Electronics

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Herein, we numerically present a nano-beam produced by two dielectric semi-cylinders. The nano-beam is distributed at the gap of the two dielectric semi-cylinders. Both the full length at half maximum and the full width at half maximum of the nano-beam can be less than
                    <jats:italic>λ</jats:italic>
                    /2. The properties of the nano-beam can be tuned by changing the refractive index of the semi-cylinder and the gap length of the two semi-cylinders. When the two semi-cylinders (radius: 1.5
                    <jats:italic>μ</jats:italic>
                    m; the refractive indices of the top and bottom semi-cylinder: 2.5 and 3.3 respectively; the gap: 270 nm) are illuminated by a plane wave with a wavelength of 532 nm, the maximum intensity of the nano-beam can reach nearly 32.4 times that of the incident wave. Finally, the influences of unaligned semi-cylinders and an oblique incident wave on the properties of the nano-beam are investigated. And we discuss the influences of the resonances of the bottom semi-cylinder on the nano-beam. Our results provide a novel optical device for generating a high-intensity nanoscale beam.
                  </jats:p>
title: Nano-beam generated by two dielectric semi-cylinders

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to map the existing literature on bone cancer by examining diagnostic approaches, treatment strategies, and emerging research trends to identify knowledge gaps and provide directions for future research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Bone cancer remains a significant clinical challenge because early diagnosis and effective treatment continue to be difficult. Recent advances in artificial intelligence, medical imaging, precision medicine, and computational modeling have introduced new approaches to the diagnosis and management of bone cancer. This review examines the current evidence related to diagnostic methods, therapeutic interventions, and recent developments in bone cancer research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Inclusion Criteria</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This scoping review included peer-reviewed studies involving patients with bone cancer across different age groups and demographic settings. Eligible studies examined diagnostic methods, treatment strategies, or emerging research trends and reported findings with potential clinical relevance. Only studies published in English were included.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A comprehensive literature search was conducted using PubMed, Google Scholar, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, Ovid-Embase, Ovid-Medline, and Scopus. Studies addressing the epidemiology, pathophysiology, diagnosis, and treatment of bone cancer were screened and analyzed. The selected literature was evaluated to identify major themes, recent advances, and existing research gaps.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The review identified substantial progress in diagnostic imaging, biomarker discovery, and therapeutic approaches, including chemotherapy, radiotherapy, surgery, targeted therapy, and artificial intelligence-assisted techniques. The findings also highlighted the increasing role of personalized medicine and computational approaches in improving diagnostic accuracy and treatment planning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Although significant progress has been achieved in the diagnosis and treatment of bone cancer, important challenges remain, particularly in early detection and therapeutic optimization. Future research should focus on integrating advanced diagnostic technologies, personalized treatment strategies, and metastasis-directed approaches to improve patient outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Mapping the landscape of bone cancer diagnostics, treatments, and emerging trends: a scoping review

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>DNA methylation profiling has transformed classification of central nervous system (CNS) tumors, leading to improved diagnostics and altered management of patients compared with histopathology-based diagnostics. However, array-based workflows take several weeks in the clinical setting and are centralized due to the need of simultaneously running 8 samples. Nanopore whole-genome sequencing (WGS) with modified-base calling enables rapid, local generation of sparse genome-wide methylomes together with copy-number profiles and mutations from the same dataset. Recent studies show that low-coverage nanopore WGS can be employed to generate methylation-based classifications, achieving same-day to next-day turnaround times. Concurrently, real-time frameworks such as MethyLYZR update predictions as data streams off the sequencer, demonstrating high accuracy within minutes in the intraoperative settings, while ROBIN pipelines integrate multiple classifiers for rapid methylome calls. Nanopore classification has also been extended to liquid biopsy (CSF/cfDNA), supporting minimally invasive diagnostics and monitoring. A bedside-capable epigenomic assay that compresses time-to-result from weeks to hours-days can directly influence patient care in both pediatric and adult neuro-oncology.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To compare the performance of nanopore sequencing with methylation arrays and assess concordance across cohorts and classifiers, we analyzed 21 pediatric and 18 adult CNS tumour samples with both methodologies. For nanopore analysis, each sample was run on a single PrometION p2 Solo flow cell for 72 hours, generating on average 100 Gb of data per sample. The data was preprocessed using Dorado for basecalling and alignment, and Modkit was used for aggregating methylation calls.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Overall, the methylation values generated from both methods showed high correlation, R2=0.973. Copy number alteration plots were comparable but due to the higher resolution of the nanopore data, also smaller alterations could be identified. Methylation-based classification using MNP-flex and individual classifiers implemented in ROBIN (nanoDX/panNanoDX [RapidCNS2], Sturgeon, and a repository-provided random forest classifier) yielded concordant diagnostic entities across both methods for both cohorts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Nanopore WGS provides rapid, local methylome and CNV profiling with higher structural resolution, delivering results in hours-days. For both pediatric and adult CNS tumours, methylation values closely matched arrays (R²=0.973), and concordant classifications were observed across multiple independent classifiers, supporting nanopore as a robust and clinically actionable alternative to array-based diagnostics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: EP05.11 Brain tumor diagnostics using nanopore sequencing

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Brain tumor diagnosis involves specific molecular testing based on the 2021 WHO classification. Liquid Biopsies deciphering genetic hallmarks are of increasing importance in neurooncology. Here we present the Neuro Liquid Biopsy Board that resembling a classical tumor board integrates data from cell-free DNA sequencing (cfDNAseq) of cerebrospinal fluid together with clinical, imaging and tissue data for optimized diagnosis and treatment decision making.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>372 prospectively acquired patient samples were submitted and 288 patients with brain tumors or suspicion of a brain tumor passing quality control have been discussed in the Neuro Liquid Biopsy Board from May 2024 until March 2026. Samples were included from 13 centers and next generation sequencing-based cfDNAseq from cerebrospinal fluid was conducted centrally. Data were discussed with neurooncologists, neuropathologists, neuroradiologists and CSF specialists and recommendation for further diagnostics and treatment was given to the responsible clinician.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>From 288 patients discussed, 233 were from Heidelberg University Hospital, 31 from Mannheim University Hospital, 17 from further centers in Germany and six from centers outside Germany. Median turnaround time from lumbar puncture to board decision was 14 days. A brain tumor with characterizing genomic variants was identified in 124 out of 288 samples and in 62 samples a WHO analogue exact diagnosis was made. The most common CSF-based tumor diagnoses were glioblastoma, astrocytoma, diffuse midline glioma H3K27 altered and oligodendroglioma. There were no false positives.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A Neuro Liquid Biopsy Board for structured evaluation and interdisciplinary interpretation of results from cell-free DNA sequencing is feasible in a clinical meaningful timeframe and can aid brain tumor diagnosis and treatment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: P05.11.A The Neuro Liquid Biopsy board - Brain tumor diagnostics from cerebrospinal fluid

items.abstract: <jats:p>Background/Objectives: Early assessment of response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) may facilitate treatment evaluation in breast cancer. We evaluated the performance of PET SUV-based and MRI-derived magnetization transfer ratio (MTR) metrics for early prediction of NAC response. Methods: From January 2019 to December 2021, 30 women with newly diagnosed breast cancer (mean age, 46.6 ± 11.2 years) scheduled for NAC underwent hybrid FDG PET/MR. Participants received two examinations: study 1 before NAC, and study 2 during early NAC (mean, 18.2 ± 4.6 days after NAC initiation). PET metrics included SUVmax of the index tumor (SUVlesion) and SUVs measured in ipsilateral and contralateral normal breast parenchyma (SUVipsi, SUVcontra). MTR metrics included MTRlesion encompassing the SUVmax site, with MTRipsi and MTRcontra in normal breast parenchyma. Ratios (SUVlesion/ipsi, SUVlesion/contra, MTRlesion/ipsi, MTRlesion/contra) were also calculated. Treatment response was categorized as residual cancer burden (RCB) 0–I (group 1) or II–III (group 2). ROC analysis with leave-one-out cross-validation was performed. Results: Group 1 showed greater reductions in imaging metrics, whereas group 2 showed smaller reductions or increases (percent changes: all Δ%SUV metrics, p ≤ 0.001; Δ%MTRlesion and Δ%MTRlesion/ipsi, p ≤ 0.013). SUV-based metrics generally demonstrated higher diagnostic performance than MTR metrics (AUC, 0.652–0.864 vs. 0.656–0.756), with the highest AUC among individual metrics observed for Δ%SUVlesion/ipsi. Selected hybrid SUV-MTR metrics showed numerically higher AUCs than the corresponding individual metrics, with the highest AUC (0.919) achieved by Δ%MTRlesion/ipsi combined with SUVlesion at study 2. Conclusions: In this exploratory pilot study, SUV-based metrics showed higher overall diagnostic performance than MTR-based metrics for early prediction of NAC response. Selected hybrid metrics yielded numerically higher AUCs than individual metrics; these preliminary findings require validation in larger cohorts.</jats:p>
title: PET and Magnetization Transfer MRI for Early Prediction of Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy Response in Breast Cancer

items.abstract: <jats:p>Background: Sarcoidosis is a highly heterogeneous disease, leading to differences in clinical practices across countries. This study aimed to identify similarities and differences in diagnostic, therapeutic, and follow-up practices for sarcoidosis across European countries. Methods: Within the Joint Action on REspiratory Diseases (JARED) project, we conducted a multinational, cross-sectional study using a key informant expert survey. The structured survey comprised 48 questions on adult sarcoidosis diagnostics and management. Representatives of all 15 JARED project countries completed the electronic survey. Results: Sarcoidosis and/or interstitial lung disease centres are present in 12 countries, but only 7 have national guidelines for diagnosis and treatment. In most countries, bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and endobronchial ultrasound-guided lymph node biopsy are performed. The use of bronchoscopic lung biopsies, particularly cryobiopsies, varies considerably. To assess the extent and activity of the disease, almost all countries perform extended pulmonary function testing, but there are variations in the use of hypercalcaemia and hypercalciuria tests. Positron emission tomography is routinely used in only 4 countries. Around half of the patients are treated with corticosteroids. In most cases, treatment is initiated when an organ other than the lungs is affected or when severe impairment of pulmonary function is present. The follow-up intervals range from 1 to 12 months. The monitoring strategies vary based on the radiological stage of sarcoidosis or the disease’s severity. Conclusions: Our survey highlights substantial variation in sarcoidosis management across Europe, underscoring the need for updated, evidence-based recommendations on diagnostic strategies, treatment initiation and duration, and long-term follow-up.</jats:p>
title: Marked Variation in the Diagnosis and Management of Sarcoidosis Across Europe: Results from a Multinational Expert Survey

<jats:p>
                    At muon colliders, muon decays naturally produce intense electrons and positrons with unique features, namely high energies, high repetition rates, and small intrinsic uncertainties, that are unavailable at existing accelerator facilities. We quantitatively study the feasibility of extracting such particles in two representative future muon collider designs, IMCC and
                    <a:math xmlns:a="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <a:mi>μ</a:mi>
                      <a:mi>TRISTAN</a:mi>
                    </a:math>
                    . Using Monte Carlo simulations with the corresponding design parameters, we study the spatial, angular, and energy distributions of decay electrons and positrons in the curved sections of the collider ring. We find that typical deflections of 0.1–10 mrad can be achieved even for high-energy electrons carrying large energy fractions (
                    <c:math xmlns:c="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <c:mrow>
                        <c:mo>≃</c:mo>
                        <c:mn>0.6</c:mn>
                        <c:mi>–</c:mi>
                        <c:mn>1.0</c:mn>
                      </c:mrow>
                    </c:math>
                    ) of the muon beam energy, with the ring bending magnets (or magnets providing an equivalent field) effectively serving as a “preseptum magnet” that partially deflects the beam before the main septum magnet, suggesting that the extraction scheme could be practically feasible. Exploiting the distinct beam properties of IMCC and
                    <e:math xmlns:e="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <e:mi>μ</e:mi>
                      <e:mi>TRISTAN</e:mi>
                    </e:math>
                    , we propose complementary search strategies—missing energy and momentum searches for dark matter at
                    <g:math xmlns:g="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <g:mi>μ</g:mi>
                      <g:mi>TRISTAN</g:mi>
                    </g:math>
                    and visible-decay searches for axionlike particles and light scalars at IMCC—which probe parameter space beyond the reach of current and other proposed experiments.
                  </jats:p>
title: Muon collider experiments as electron and positron beam sources: Case studies of new light-particle searches

items.abstract: <jats:p>Increasing attention has been paid to precast steel–concrete composite structures owing to their eco-friendliness, fast construction and reliable quality. Ultra-high-performance concrete (UHPC), with low self-weight and outstanding mechanical performance, greatly optimises the performance of precast steel–concrete composite beams. In this paper, the authors propose a novel demountable precast steel–UHPC composite beam with bolt shear connectors designed for disassembly and systematically study its flexural performance and design methodology. Three full-scale specimens are tested to analyse failure modes, load–deflection responses, interfacial load–slip characteristics and strain distribution, revealing the structural cooperative working mechanism. A refined finite-element model is built and calibrated against test results to clarify the internal load transfer mechanism, and parametric analyses are conducted to quantify how key design variables affect flexural behaviour. Theoretical formulas for flexural capacity are derived and verified by way of experimental and numerical data. Combining the generalised strain energy density and the Mann–Kendall criterion, a method is put forward to identify the flexural characteristic values for deeper mechanical interpretation. This research offers solid theoretical and technical references for the engineering design and application of precast steel–UHPC composite structures.</jats:p>
title: Bending performance and design of a demountable precast steel–UHPC composite beam

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Medulloblastoma (MB) is the most common primary malignant tumor of the central nervous system (CNS) in children but remains rare in adults, resulting in limited clinical data for the adult population. Standard treatment typically includes maximal safe tumor resection followed by craniospinal irradiation (CSI) with a boost to the primary site, with or without concomitant chemotherapy and subsequent maintenance therapy. This study evaluates clinical outcomes and treatment-related toxicity following proton beam therapy (PBT) in adult patients with MB.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Patients ≥ 18 years with primary MB treated with PBT between January 2017 and March 2024 and enrolled in the prospective registry study ProReg (DRKS00004384) were evaluated in this analysis. Adverse events were documented according to CTCAE v4.0 and v5.0 before, during, and after PT. The overall survival (OS), progression free survival (PSF) and higher grade toxicity (≥ grade 3) were analyzed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Forty-two patients (26 males, 16 females; median age 26.7 years (range, 18.3-49.5 years)) were evaluable. Histopathological subtype was classic (n = 26) or desmoplastic/extensive nodularity (n = 12), respectively. Complete tumor resection was achieved in x (?) patients (71.4%). At diagnosis, 27 patients (64.2%) presented with localized, non-metastatic disease. 21 patients (50%) were classified as high risk ( 15 patients had metastatic disease (M1-M3), and 6 patients had residual tumor &gt;1.5 cm²) The median total CSI dose was 36 Gy (RBE) (range, 23.4-40 Gy (RBE)), and the median cumulative local dose was 54 Gy (RBE)(range, 38-68 Gy (RBE)) in single fraction doses of 1.0-1.8 Gy (RBE)(median single dose was 1.8 Gy (RBE). Boost irradiation was delivered to the posterior fossa (n = 29) or the tumor bed (n = 13), respectively. Concomitant chemotherapy was administered in 27 patients (61.9%). The median follow-up time after first diagnosis was 4.4 years (range, 0.6-8.9 years). Disease recurrence was observed in nine patients (CNS recurrences (n = 6) , and extra-CNS metastases in bone and/or lymph nodes (n = 3). Four patients died due to disease progression (n = 3) or due to pulmonary embolism (n = 1). PFS and OS rates at 4-year were 76.1% and 91.3%, respectively. Acute higher-grade toxicities included meningitis (n = 2), intracranial hypertension (n = 1), and hematologic toxicity (n = 1). PBT was stopped in one patient at 38 Gy due to shunt infection and meningitis. Late higher-grade toxicities comprised vascular events (n = 1), concentration deficits (n = 2), hearing impairment (n = 2), fatigue (n = 1), anorexia (n = 3), and cognitive disturbances (n = 6).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>PBT in adult MB patients demonstrated good feasibility, acceptable toxicity, and promising tumor control. These findings should be confirmed with longer follow-up.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: EP09.24 Proton Beam Therapy for Adult Medulloblastoma: Un update of a Single-Institution Experience

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This work presents a physics-informed synthetic waveform
  generation and HDL replay validation framework for radiation
  detector readout development. The proposed workflow connects Monte
  Carlo energy deposition modelling, detector-informed waveform
  synthesis, ADC digitization, readout metric analysis and HDL-ready
  replay vector generation within a single reproducible chain.  The
  framework is demonstrated using a NaI(Tl)-based scintillation
  detector reference case for 59.5 keV gamma rays.  Geant4-generated
  deposited energy records are used as the physical input for
  producing truth-labelled NaI(Tl)-like waveform windows, which are
  subsequently digitized at ADC resolutions of 8, 10 and 12 bits. This
  structure allows quantization effects to be separated from detector
  response and noise effects while preserving event-level reference
  information.  For the simulated waveform dataset, energy
  reconstruction is dominated by analog noise and gain variation
  rather than ADC bit-depth, with non-zero-event energy RMSE values
  ranging from approximately 0.86 keV to 1.03 keV over the tested
  noise conditions. The generated ADC vectors are exported for HDL
  replay validation using Icarus Verilog, where the trigger decision,
  peak count and peak index outputs agree with software reference
  labels with zero mismatches across the tested ADC configurations.
  These results establish functional consistency for the tested
  synthetic inputs. The waveform model has not been validated against
  measured NaI(Tl) calibration data, and its synthetic-to-real
  transferability remains unassessed.  A supplementary Vivado
  implementation comparison on an Artix-7 target identifies a severe
  timing violation in the original RTL and demonstrates internal
  timing closure at 250 MHz after explicit arithmetic pipelining.
  The revised 12-bit block achieves worst setup and hold slacks of
  +0.223 and +0.086 ns, respectively, with eight added clock
  cycles of latency; external interface timing and physical board
  operation remain unvalidated.</jats:p>
title: Physics-informed synthetic waveform generation and HDL replay validation for radiation detector readout development

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To report the first evidence of efficacy of interleukin-6 (IL-6) blockade with tocilizumab in radiation-induced brachial plexopathy (RIBP), a rare and disabling late complication of radiotherapy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A single patient with a history of deltoid sarcoma treated with surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy was evaluated decades later for progressive upper limb weakness and paresthesias. Clinical examination, nerve conduction studies/electromyography (NCS/EMG), and brachial plexus MRI were consistent with diagnosis of RIBP. After failure of bevacizumab, the patient received compassionate tocilizumab.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Tocilizumab (162 mg every four weeks for three cycles) was well tolerated and led to partial clinical improvement, including increased muscle strength (≥1 point on MRC scale) and reduced paresthesias. MRI showed decreased contrast enhancement, and NCS/EMG demonstrated functional improvement. Benefits persisted at 18 months.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This case highlights a potential disease-modifying role of IL-6 blockade in RIBP, including in late-stage or treatment-refractory cases. It supports further investigation of tocilizumab as a therapeutic option and suggests IL-6 as a relevant target in radiation-induced plexopathy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: EP08.03 Tocilizumab in Radiation-Induced Plexopathy

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The ion temperature (Ti) clamping effect, which severely constrains the improvement of energy confinement in electron-heated plasmas, has been systematically investigated in EAST. The core ion temperature is universally clamped at approximately 1.25 keV under electron cyclotron resonance heating (ECRH) and lower hybrid wave (LHW) scenarios with plasma current Ip ≤ 550 kA. Experimental results show that under high plasma current (600 kA) and high density conditions, the energy confinement time exceeds the electron-ion collision time, enabling efficient collisional ion heating and breaking the clamping effect with a maximum core ion temperature up to 2 keV. In contrast, the clamping effect persists at Ip ≤ 550 kA even when the energy confinement time becomes comparable to the electron-ion collision time, indicating additional mechanisms beyond simple time-scale matching. Furthermore, pulsed argon (Ar) impurity injection at 400 kA effectively elevates the core ion temperature by approximately 80% to 1.8 keV, exceeding the clamping threshold. This enhancement is accompanied by a significant reduction in ion thermal diffusivity and a transition of the dominant turbulent instability modes from TEM and ETG dominance to ITG and ETG dominance, demonstrating a pronounced improvement in ion channel confinement. These findings provide important experimental evidence for understanding ion heating and energy confinement physics in electron-heated plasmas, and support the development of advanced operational scenarios for future fusion devices.</jats:p>
title: Experimental investigation of ion temperature clamping effect in electron-heated plasmas on EAST

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Xanthogranulomatous sialadenitis is a rare chronic inflammatory disease of the parotid gland that can mimic malignant tumors through its clinical, radiological, and intraoperative findings. This case report presents a rare parotid gland mass that, despite exhibiting benign features in preoperative evaluations, raised suspicion of malignancy intraoperatively and was ultimately diagnosed as xanthogranulomatous sialadenitis based on histopathological examination. A 68‐year‐old female patient presented to our clinic with a complaint of swelling in the left parotid region. A superficial parotidectomy was planned. During the operation, the mass was observed to be adherent to the facial nerve. Although this suggested a malignant infiltrative process, the definitive diagnosis was xanthogranulomatous sialadenitis. This case demonstrates that xanthogranulomatous sialadenitis should be kept in mind in the differential diagnosis of parotid masses, and that confirmation of a definitive pathological diagnosis is crucial, especially in masses adherent to the facial nerve, before irreversible surgical interventions are performed.</jats:p>
title: A Rare Case Mimicking Parotid Gland Malignancy: Xanthogranulomatous Sialadenitis

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In the follow-up of glioma patients, differentiating treatment-associated changes from tumor progression on MRI is challenging. In the Netherlands, this diagnostic uncertainty often leads to watchful waiting, delayed treatment, and patient distress. So far, research on new diagnostic tests has primarily focused on accuracy, while patient perspectives remain largely unexplored. This qualitative study aimed to explore glioma patients’ perspectives on diagnostic uncertainty and the implementation of tests aimed at reducing uncertainty.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 10 diffuse glioma patients (31-70 years old; 50% female) treated at the UMC Utrecht, the Netherlands. Two independent coders analyzed interview transcripts thematically to identify key themes in patient perspectives.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Four themes were found: (1) Most patients experienced diagnostic uncertainty, which was stressful for themselves and their loved ones. (2) A new test was considered meaningful if it provided early certainty. Patients wanted certainty to guide treatment, and even without therapeutic options, a certain diagnosis could optimize quality of life by living more consciously. (3) All patients wished to participate in decision-making regarding undergoing new tests, with variable preferences regarding the amount of information to be received. (4) Patients expressed the need for continuity of care, honest communication, and immediate disclosure of test results. These study results are discussed in a multidisciplinary expert group.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Patients value faster certainty from new diagnostic tests, both to guide treatment and improve survival and quality of life, and to optimize quality of life when no therapeutic options remain. Integrating this emphasis on quality of life into diagnostic research may stimulate patient-centered test implementation, ultimately improving neuro-oncological care. Possible implications for diagnostic clinical practice are discussed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: EP12.24 Patient perspectives on diagnostic uncertainty and novel diagnostic tests in neuro-oncology

items.abstract: <jats:p>Background/Objectives: Multimodal deep learning for glaucoma detection often combines fundus imaging with optical coherence tomography (OCT), yet it is unclear when fusion adds information beyond OCT alone and how such models behave under domain shift. We compared joint and late fusion of scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (SLO) and OCT and their cross-domain transfer. Methods: Models trained on GAMMA (color fundus photographs and macular OCT; 99 cases) were applied without retraining to the Harvard-FairVision glaucoma test split (3000 patients; SLO and OCT). Unimodal and multimodal models were then trained on FairVision (6000 training and 1000 validation patients). Four candidates (OCT-only, concatenation and cross-attention fusion, and late fusion with a cross-fitted SLO weight of 0.15) were locked with their calibration and thresholds and evaluated once on the same test split. Results: Cross-domain transfer yielded areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) of 0.635–0.653. In-domain OCT-only reached a test AUROC of 0.876. Neither jointly trained cross-attention fusion (ΔAUROC −0.0045; 95% confidence interval (CI) −0.0110 to 0.0021) nor concatenation fusion (+0.0009; 95% CI −0.0056 to 0.0074) improved on OCT-only. Late fusion yielded a small ranking improvement (+0.0059; 95% CI 0.0033 to 0.0087; Holm-adjusted p = 0.0012), but a sensitivity gain at matched specificity was not established. Post hoc analyses identified lower AUROC among Black patients and a higher false-positive rate among normal eyes. Conclusions: OCT carried most of the diagnostic information. Standard joint fusion did not add value. Low-weight late fusion improved ranking slightly on a previously accessed test split; this requires independent confirmation and does not establish clinical benefit. Fusion claims require strong unimodal and late-fusion baselines and external validation.</jats:p>
title: When Does Multimodal Fusion Help? Cross-Domain Transfer, Joint Fusion, and Late Fusion of SLO and OCT for Glaucoma Detection Under an Analysis-Locked Evaluation

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sex-based disparities in oncology are increasingly recognized, yet their role in neuro-oncology remains unclear. While diagnostic delay is often used as a surrogate of inequality, it may fail to capture the complexity of the diagnostic pathway. We aimed to evaluate sex-related differences in both diagnostic timing and healthcare utilization in glioma patients.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a retrospective study of 117 patients with low-grade (LGG) and high-grade gliomas (HGG). The diagnostic pathway was assessed using time to diagnosis and number of pre-diagnostic consultations. Clinical presentation, tumor characteristics, and overall survival were compared between sexes using non-parametric tests and Kaplan-Meier analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Women required more pre-diagnostic consultations than men (mean 2.4 vs. 1.8; p = 0.045). However, no significant differences were observed in time to diagnosis or in the proportion of patients experiencing delays &gt;15 days (25.6% vs. 24.3%; p = 0.879).Clinical presentation was driven by tumor biology rather than sex, with seizures predominating in LGG and focal deficits in HGG (p = 0.012). No sex-related differences in presenting symptoms were identified. Overall survival was comparable between sexes (log-rank p = 0.224), despite a non-significant trend towards longer survival in women.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Although no differences were observed in diagnostic timing or outcomes, the higher number of pre-diagnostic consultations in women may suggest a more complex diagnostic pathway. This finding raises the possibility of subtle sex-related differences in healthcare access or referral patterns, which may not be fully captured by time-based metrics alone. Further research is warranted to better characterize potential sex-related differences in the diagnostic process.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: EP12.63 Beyond Diagnostic Delay: Evaluating Sex-Related Differences in the Diagnostic Pathway of Glioma Patients

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Neuroepithelial tumors with PLAGL1 fusion represent a recently defined methylation class characterized by distinctive epigenetic features and frequent histopathological features consistent with ependymal differentiation, predominantly affecting young children. Different fusion partners have been described, most commonly EWSR1 and FOXO1, but their biological impact remains poorly understood. Further molecular insights from this rare entity are needed to deeper understand the heterogeneous spectrum of fusion-positive neuroepithelial tumors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Bulk RNA sequencing was performed on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded samples of supratentorial ependymoma-like tumors lacking ZFTA or YAP1 fusions. Transcriptional profiles were analyzed in tumors harboring PLAGL1 fusions. Differential expression (DE) analysis and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) were performed, including comparisons with reference cohorts of ZFTA and YAP1 fusion-positive supratentorial ependymomas to identify fusion-specific transcriptional programs. DNA methylation profiling was used for tumor classification and clustering.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this retrospective cohort, PLAGL1 fusion was identified in 22 tumors, including EWSR1::PLAGL1 (n = 16) and PLAGL1::FOXO1 (n = 6). Dimensionality reduction analyses showed distinct clustering both at the epigenetic and the transcriptomic levels according to fusion partner. EWSR1::PLAGL1 tumors showed a strong activation of progenitor/mesenchymal-like programs, with high expression of homeobox genes HOXD3 and HOXD8. GSEA analysis revealed enriched oxidative phosphorylation compared to PLAGL1::FOXO1 tumors, with increased expression of the mitochondrial regulator PPARGC1A. In contrast, PLAGL1::FOXO1 tumors displayed a more pronounced astro-glial differentiation, with an enrichment of ciliogenesis-related pathways and elevated GFAP expression. These tumors also showed increased expression of MTOR, suggesting potential involvement of mTOR signaling.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Neuroepithelial tumors with PLAGL1 fusion are biologically heterogeneous and exhibit fusion partner-specific developmental and metabolic states. EWSR1::PLAGL1 tumors are characterized by a HOXD-associated developmental activation and metabolic reprogramming, whereas PLAGL1::FOXO1 tumors display a more differentiated transcriptional phenotype. These findings support the existence of distinct biological states within the PLAGL1-fusion spectrum and warrant further investigation for refined classification and potential therapeutic targeting. Ongoing studies aim to correlate these molecular features with clinicopathological characteristics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: P14.06.B Fusion partner drives developmental and metabolic divergence in ependymoma-like neuroepithelial tumors with PLAGL1 fusion

                    If strange quark matter (SQM) is absolutely stable, hadronic neutron stars (NSs) and strange quark stars (QSs) may coexist in the so-called two-families scenario. A key issue is explaining how hadronic NSs can survive as long-lived metastable objects, rather than promptly converting into stable QSs. Since all NSs are born as hot protoneutron stars (PNSs), a necessary condition for their existence is that the conditions for conversion, triggered by the nucleation of the first critical SQM droplet, are not reached in every PNS. We investigate the thermal nucleation of critical SQM droplets under representative PNS conditions, accounting for flavor-composition fluctuations and finite-size effects on color superconductivity by suppressing pairing in droplets smaller than the diquark coherence length. We define the nucleation conditions as the thermodynamic state at which a critical SQM droplet is expected to nucleate statistically within the characteristic dynamical timescale of the system. items.abstract: <jats:p>This Perspective article presents the development and practical implementation of cybersecurity requirements for nuclear power plants (NPP) instrumentation and control (I&amp;C) systems in Ukraine. Particular attention is given to NP 306.2.237-2022 “Cybersecurity Requirements for Instrumentation and Control Systems of Nuclear Power Plants to Ensure Nuclear and Radiation Safety” (NP 306.2.237-2022) as the key regulatory instrument establishing a specialized approach to cybersecurity of NPP I&amp;C systems. The paper examines the integration of cybersecurity requirements into the nuclear and radiation safety framework, the implementation process for I&amp;C system developers and the operating organization, and the main technical, methodological, and organizational challenges encountered during implementation. The adoption of specialized, safety-oriented cybersecurity regulations is an essential step toward protecting nuclear I&amp;C systems, but their practical effectiveness depends on translating general requirements into technically justified measures compatible with nuclear safety functions. On this basis, priorities for further development are proposed, and lessons of potential relevance to other countries are outlined.</jats:p>
title: Cybersecurity requirements for nuclear power plant instrumentation and control systems in Ukraine: challenges and future directions for implementation

items.abstract: <jats:p>We investigate the Landau-Zener description of resonant axion-photon conversion in neutron star magnetospheres. We find that this picture often fails for axion conversions to millimeter-to-optical band photons due to the characteristic resonance width exceeding the size of the conversion region. This comparison of scales yields a simple criterion for evaluating the validity of the Landau-Zener formula. We verify this criterion numerically, and show that when invalid, the Landau-Zener conversion probability may significantly deviate from the numerical result. In light of these findings, we revise constraints on axions from neutron star optical-band polarization searches.</jats:p>
title: Landau-Zener formula and resonant axion conversion in neutron star magnetospheres

items.abstract: <jats:p>To address insufficient feature representation and the insufficient utilization of auxiliary information in images degraded by complex haze, this paper proposes a Multi-depth Enhanced Adaptive Fusion Polarization-guided Network (MEAF-P-Net). The network enhances dehazing feature representation through multi-depth feature fusion and introduces a Polarization-Guided Fusion Module (PGFM) that utilizes polarization features at different resolutions to assist image restoration. Experiments are conducted on a synthetic visible-light dehazing dataset and a synthetic polarization dehazing dataset constructed from PolarLITIS. For RGB image dehazing, the MEAF backbone achieves a PSNR of 31.40 dB and an SSIM of 0.933, which are 1.89 dB and 0.0201 lower than those achieved by ED-Former, respectively. For polarization-based dehazing, MEAF-PGFM achieves a PSNR of 29.56 dB, an SSIM of 0.9592, and an MAE of 0.0332. Compared with DuRP, MEAF-PGFM improves PSNR by 6.01 dB and SSIM by 0.1193, while reducing MAE from 0.0673 to 0.0332. Furthermore, ablation experiments involving different fusion strategies and polarization features at different resolutions demonstrate the effectiveness of PGFM.</jats:p>
title: A Multi-Depth Enhanced Adaptive Fusion Polarization-Guided Network for Image Dehazing

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Epithelioid glioblastoma (eGB), IDH-wildtype, is a rare aggressive GB variant with poor prognosis (median OS 10-14 months). NTRK fusions are very rare in adult GB, and clinical experience with NTRK inhibitors in CNS tumors is limited. At relapse after NTRK inhibition, no standard strategy exists. We report a case of eGB harboring a NOS1AP-NTRK1 fusion with exceptional response to sequential NTRK-targeted therapy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In January 2021, a 68-year-old woman presented with progressive right-sided hemiparesis. Brain MRI revealed a left frontal lesion, treated with subtotal resection in April 2021. Histopathology confirmed eGB, IDH-wildtype, NOS1AP-NTRK1 fusion-positive, and BRAF V600E-wild-type. Baseline functional status was KPS 80%. First-line therapy consisted of standard radiochemotherapy with concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide from April to October 2021. Upon progression in November 2021, she received larotrectinib. After further progression in September 2022, treatment was switched to lomustine plus bevacizumab, which was ineffective. She then received the second-generation TRK inhibitor repotrectinib in November 2022, followed by cabozantinib in March 2023.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Initial radiochemotherapy yielded a partial radiographic response, with progression-free survival (PFS) of 6 months. Larotrectinib resulted in marked clinical and radiological improvement, including partial recovery of right upper limb function and reduction of perilesional edema (PFS: 10 months). Lomustine + bevacizumab was ineffective (PFS: 2 months). Repotrectinib achieved partial stabilization and improved clinical status (PFS: 4 months), followed by progression. Cabozantinib provided transient control (PFS: 2 months). Final progression occurred in May 2023, with multifocal bifrontal and supracallosal lesions confirmed by MRI and PET, associated with clinical decline (KPS 50%). The patient died in June 2023, 29 months after diagnosis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sequential NTRK-targeted therapy can produce exceptional and durable responses in NTRK1 fusion-positive eGB. Larotrectinib was initiated after progression based on the presence of a NOS1AP-NTRK1 fusion, targeting constitutive TRKA activation and downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT signaling, resulting in rapid antitumor effects. Upon progression, repotrectinib, a CNS-penetrant second-generation TRK inhibitor, was selected to overcome potential resistance mutations and maintain pathway inhibition. As disease progressed, cabozantinib, a multikinase inhibitor targeting MET and VEGFR, was used to address bypass signaling and tumor angiogenesis. This case highlights the importance of mechanism-based sequencing, molecular profiling, and CNS-active agents in rare, targetable glioblastoma subtypes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: EP12.80 Exceptional response to sequential TRK inhibition in an epithelioid glioblastoma with NOS1AP-NTRK1 fusion

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Key Content</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      <jats:list list-type="bullet">
                        <jats:list-item>
                          <jats:p>Ultrasound is the primary imaging modality of ovarian tumours, and diagnostic algorithms can be used to aid diagnosis.</jats:p>
                        </jats:list-item>
                        <jats:list-item>
                          <jats:p>Mucinous ovarian tumours (MOTs) account for 10%–15% of epithelial tumours and are often unilateral and multilocular.</jats:p>
                        </jats:list-item>
                        <jats:list-item>
                          <jats:p>In this article, we aim to review the current ultrasound models for diagnosis of ovarian tumours, the ultrasound features of different mucinous tumours and the surgical management of MOTs.</jats:p>
                        </jats:list-item>
                      </jats:list>
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Learning Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      <jats:list list-type="bullet">
                        <jats:list-item>
                          <jats:p>To appreciate the challenge of the ultrasound diagnosis of ovarian tumours and understand the role of Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI), International Ovarian Tumour Analysis (IOTA) simple rules, Logistic Regression models (LR1 and LR2), Assessment of Different Neoplasias in the adneXa model (ADNEX) models and Ovarian Adnexal Data and Reporting Systems (ORADS) and subjective impression in this.</jats:p>
                        </jats:list-item>
                        <jats:list-item>
                          <jats:p>To appreciate the new emerging role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the ultrasound diagnosis of ovarian tumours.</jats:p>
                        </jats:list-item>
                        <jats:list-item>
                          <jats:p>To learn about the histopathological and ultrasound features of MOTs including the mucinous ovarian collision tumours.</jats:p>
                        </jats:list-item>
                        <jats:list-item>
                          <jats:p>To have an awareness of the surgical management of MOTs in pre‐ and post‐menopausal women.</jats:p>
                        </jats:list-item>
                      </jats:list>
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Mucinous Ovarian Tumours: A Diagnostic and Management Conundrum

items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Eosinophilic disorders are a heterogeneous group of neoplastic and non-neoplastic conditions, characterized by increased eosinophils in the peripheral blood which can sometimes lead to eosinophil-driven organ damage and dysfunction. Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine-kinase fusion genes (MLN-TK) are a group of hematologic neoplasms resulting from the formation of abnormal fusion genes that encode constitutively activated tyrosine kinases. The
                    <jats:italic>FIP1L1::PDGFRA</jats:italic>
                    fusion gene is the most common genetic abnormality detected in MLN-TK and ten rarer
                    <jats:italic>PDGFRA</jats:italic>
                    partners have also been documented at the time of writing. Here we identified a novel
                    <jats:italic>CUX1::PDGFRA</jats:italic>
                    fusion in an adult male with MLN-TK using targeted RNA sequencing. This represents the twelfth
                    <jats:italic>PDGFRA</jats:italic>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy is commonly used to evaluate children with gastrointestinal symptoms, but its diagnostic yield varies by indication. In addition, normal macroscopic findings may not exclude histopathological disease. This study aimed to evaluate the indications for upper gastrointestinal endoscopy in children in one centre and to determine the diagnostic yield of macroscopic endoscopic findings, with histopathology used as a reference standard.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methodology</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a retrospective cohort study of children aged ≤14 years, who underwent diagnostic upper gastrointestinal endoscopy 2016 through 2021. Children who underwent therapeutic endoscopy or had incomplete endoscopic or histopathological documentation were excluded. Demographic, clinical, laboratory, endoscopic, and histopathological data were extracted from medical records. Descriptive statistics and comparative analyses were performed. The diagnostic performance of macroscopic endoscopic findings was assessed by calculating sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value using histopathology as the reference standard.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 398 children screened, 374 met inclusion criteria. The mean age was 8.9 ± 3.6 years, and 190 (50.8%) were female sex. The most common indications were abdominal pain or dyspepsia (37.4%), dysphagia (20.3%), and suspected celiac disease (12.8%). Abnormal macroscopic findings were present in 256 (68.4%) children and were associated with older age (P = 0.025) and dysphagia (77.6%; P = 0.043). Abnormal histopathological findings were identified in 249 (72.4%) children and were strongly associated with abnormal macroscopic endoscopy (P &lt; 0.001). Higher IgA tissue transglutaminase levels (P = 0.001) and C-reactive protein levels (P = 0.028) were also associated with abnormal endoscopic findings. Using histopathology as the reference standard, macroscopic endoscopy had a sensitivity of 77.9%, specificity of 54.7%, positive predictive value of 81.9%, and negative predictive value of 48.6%. Fifty-five patients had abnormal histopathology despite normal macroscopic endoscopic findings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Diagnostic upper gastrointestinal endoscopy demonstrated a high yield in this paediatric tertiary-care cohort. Older age and dysphagia were associated with abnormal macroscopic findings, while suspected celiac disease showed particularly high histopathological yield. However, normal macroscopic endoscopy did not reliably exclude histopathological disease, supporting the continued role of biopsy sampling in selected children, particularly those with persistent symptoms, suspected celiac disease, inflammatory markers, or growth-related indications.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The diagnostic yield of upper gastrointestinal endoscopy in paediatric patients: retrospective tertiary-care centre study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Bevacizumab (BEV)-induced stroke-like lesions, also known as bevacizumab-related imaging abnormalities or gelatinous radionecrosis, are necrotic lesions characterized by marked restricted diffusion following BEV administration in brain regions exposed to a radiation dose ≥60 Gy. Histopathologically, these lesions might differ from the collagenous thickening and fibrinoid necrosis typical of traditional radiation necrosis, instead presenting as atypical gelatinous necrotic tissue possibly induced by chronic hypoxia. Their occurrence in the absence of bevacizumab remains exceptional and poorly understood.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We report the case of a 60-year-old male with a history of primary progressive multiple sclerosis (diagnosed eight years prior), in whom routine MRI follow-up revealed a left parieto-occipital lesion, suggestive of high-grade glioma. A biopsy was performed, and the final pathological examination confirmed an IDH-wildtype diffuse glioma with a TERT promoter mutation and a probable chromosome 10 loss. The patient received 12 cycles of temozolomide followed by radiochemotherapy with concurrent temozolomide. Serial MRI, multimodal imaging, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, and a second biopsy were performed during follow-up.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Initial treatment was well tolerated, with radiological stability. Two years after completing the radiochemotherapy, MRI revealed a progressive necrotic lesion in the corpus callosum, characterized by the absence of neoangiogenesis and marked diffusion restriction, suggestive of gelatinous necrosis (Fig. 1). The lesion was unresponsive to corticosteroid therapy. Given the rarity of this radiological diagnosis in the absence of BEV exposure, and the alternative diagnosis of tumor progression, a biopsy was performed. Histological examination (Fig. 2) showed extensive necrosis without viable tumor cells, with features compatible with gelatinous necrosis, confirming the radiological suspicion. Bevacizumab was initiated in May 2024, resulting in transient improvement, followed by further decline and transition to palliative care approximately one year later.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This case highlights that gelatinous radionecrosis may occur independently of BEV exposure and suggests a potential increased vulnerability in patients with multiple sclerosis, possibly related to chronic inflammation and microvascular alterations. While no direct causal relationship between radiotherapy and multiple sclerosis has been established, radiation-induced demyelination and MS-like lesions have been reported. Radiological suspicion of these post-treatment lesions, along with histopathological confirmation, is essential for accurate diagnosis and management.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: EP03.08 Gelatinous Radionecrosis Without Bevacizumab in a Patient with High-Grade Glioma: A Diagnostic Pitfall

items.abstract: <jats:p>Three-dimensional reconstruction remains challenging for slender flexible structures when external visual observation is unavailable or restricted. Fiber Bragg grating (FBG) sensors provide continuous local geometric information, but small errors in curvature and torsion can accumulate during spatial integration and produce global directional drift. This study proposes an FBG–inertial measurement unit (IMU) optimization framework in which sparse IMU tangent observations correct continuous FBG-derived curvature–torsion fields. Low-dimensional Gaussian basis functions represent smooth corrections, and a weighted objective enforces IMU tangent consistency, FBG geometric consistency, bounded correction amplitude and spatial smoothness. Experimentally characterized curvature-calibration residuals and bending-direction deviations were propagated through 40 simulated curves, while measured IMU attitude errors were introduced into the tangent observations used for weight selection and ablation. For combined curvature and bending-direction perturbations, the across-curve averages of the empirical 95th-percentile mean centerline-position and endpoint-position deviations were 0.470 cm and 1.021 cm, respectively. Physical validation used one 3.0 m flexible specimen with a fixed sensor layout, 16 quasi-static configurations from four shape categories and five independent acquisitions per configuration. The overall mean position error decreased from 5.61 cm for FBG-only reconstruction to 2.71 cm with the proposed method, and the endpoint-position error decreased from 9.81 cm to 4.54 cm, corresponding to reductions of 51.67% and 53.76%, respectively. In a leave-one-IMU-out analysis, the four three-IMU variants yielded mean errors of 4.13–4.52 cm and endpoint errors of 5.31–5.92 cm; all remained below the corresponding FBG-only errors. Under the tested quasi-static conditions, sparse tangent constraints reduced accumulated reconstruction error while retaining local FBG geometric information and remained effective after removal of any single optimization IMU, although performance depended on IMU placement.</jats:p>
title: Sparse Tangent-Constrained FBG–IMU Fusion for Three-Dimensional Shape Reconstruction of Flexible Structures

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We present a new computational approach based on Nuclear-Electronic Orbital and Subsystem Density Functional Theory. The resulting NEO-sDFT methodology enables quantum chemical calculations of large molecular systems composed of thousands of atoms while also describing selected protons quantum mechanically. A key feature of the associated program implementation is its flexibility in assigning quantum protons to subsystems, allowing different embedding schemes to be employed within a unified framework. The accuracy of NEO-sDFT is assessed by computing energies of water clusters of growing size. Deviations from reference Nuclear-Electronic Orbital Density Functional Theory results amount to only a few meV for water dimers near the equilibrium separation and are comparable to those of conventional Subsystem Density Functional Theory for larger clusters. The favorable computational scaling of NEO-sDFT is further showcased through calculations on water clusters of increasing size, with up to 303 protons being treated quantum mechanically. Our results demonstrate that NEO-sDFT is an accurate and efficient approach for incorporating nuclear quantum effects into large-scale simulations, providing a foundation for future applications to proton transfer processes in biochemical systems.</jats:p>
