items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Pediatric CNS tumor epidemiology in Armenia remains poorly characterized. Institutional cohort analyses are important for understanding tumor distribution, diagnostic discrepancy, and healthcare delivery challenges in real-world practice. As a leading national center for hematology and oncology in Armenia, Yeolyan Center provides a valuable institutional setting for evaluating these patterns in a consecutive pediatric CNS tumor cohort.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Retrospective analysis of 186 consecutive pediatric CNS tumor cases recorded at Yeolyan Center, Armenia (1995-2021). Data collected included demographics, anatomical tumor location, presenting symptoms, diagnostic discrepancy (defined as any change in pathology, anatomical site, or classification between initial and final diagnosis), time from symptom onset to diagnosis, and clinical outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 186 cases, 55.9% were male with mean age 7.2 years. The most frequent tumor locations/categories were cerebellar (n = 55, 29.6%), retinoblastoma (n = 25, 13.4%), fourth ventricle (n = 21, 11.3%). Diagnostic discrepancy occurred in 72% of cases (134/186). Common presenting symptoms included headache/vomiting (44.6%), visual impairment (44.1%), strabismus (20.4%), and waddling gait (17.7%). Mean/median time to diagnosis varied: cerebellar tumors (3.2/1.0 months), retinoblastoma (6.0/3.0 months), third/fourth ventricle combined (2.6/2.0 months), fourth ventricle alone (2.2/2.0 months). Outcomes: complete response (n = 54), remission/ stable disease), death (n = 41), unknown (n = 63).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The 72% diagnostic discrepancy rate highlights substantial diagnostic complexity in pediatric CNS tumors, likely reflecting limited access to advanced pathology services. Variable time-to-diagnosis patterns suggest differential referral pathways across tumor types. High rates of missing outcome data (33.9%) limit survival interpretation. Findings underscore urgent need for multidisciplinary diagnostic pathways and strengthened national tumor registries in Armenia, and highlight the importance of strengthening partnerships with European countries to accelerate capacity building and improve clinical outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: EP10.37 Pediatric nervous system tumors in Armenia : diagnostic discrepancies and time to diagnosis in an institutional cohort

items.abstract: <jats:p>Multimodal affective computing requires extracting and integrating complementary acoustic and visual features with linguistic information, yet adaptively combining these heterogeneous representations before language generation remains challenging. We present EmoChain, a generative framework for sentiment analysis, fixed-label and open-vocabulary emotion recognition, and emotion reasoning. Pretrained encoders extract acoustic, static visual, and multiframe visual features. Their raw outputs are fed directly into the Token-Level Gated Multimodal Fusion (TGMF) module, while separate modality projectors map the original modality features into the language model’s embedding space. A fusion projector maps the fused representation into the same space. TGMF employs three source-specific experts and one joint expert, whose outputs are combined through input-dependent dense soft routing on a shared token grid. Fusion tokens and original modality tokens are jointly provided to the language model, which is adapted using two-stage instruction tuning for affective prediction and explanation generation. Across nine public affective benchmarks, EmoChain achieves an Avg.-9 score of 75.28 after Stage I, compared with 74.77 for AffectGPT, an improvement of 0.51 points (0.68%), and ranks first on three benchmarks among the selected baselines. Removing TGMF decreases performance on MOSEI and MELD by 0.46 and 0.41 points, respectively. On the EMER emotion reasoning dataset, EmoChain obtains Clue Overlap and Label Overlap scores of 6.74 and 7.85 after Stage II, indicating agreement with reference annotations. These results support token-level expert fusion as a component of multimodal affective understanding and generation. The language backbone has approximately 7 billion parameters, while the expert networks, router, and fusion projector contain about 7.74 million parameters.</jats:p>
title: EmoChain: Token-Level Gated Multimodal Fusion for Emotion Understanding and Reasoning

items.abstract: <jats:p>Early literacy is essential to the academic development of Key Stage 1 learners, particularly in acquiring word recognition, decoding, reading fluency, vocabulary, and reading comprehension skills. This study examined the literacy performance patterns of Key Stage 1 learners across CRLA Diagnostic and First-Term Assessments in selected public elementary schools in Consolacion, Cebu, as a basis for developing an instructional improvement plan. The study employed a descriptive-comparative research design involving 45 Key Stage 1 learners and six teacher-respondents from Danglag Elementary School, Paaralan ng Sentral ng Consolacion, and Tayud Elementary School. Data were obtained from existing CRLA Diagnostic and First-Term Assessment records and an adapted teacher questionnaire. Frequency, percentage, mean, weighted mean, and appropriate statistical tests were identified for analyzing learners’ literacy performance and teachers’ observations of persistent reading difficulties. The provisional  results indicated improvements in learners’ reading performance between the two assessment periods. Average reading speed increased from 18.40 to 25.60 words per minute. Improvements were also reflected in reading level, fluency, comprehension, and reading profile distributions. Teacher assessments identified persistent difficulties in word recognition and decoding (WM = 3.57), reading fluency (WM = 3.43), vocabulary and language understanding (WM = 3.43), and reading comprehension (WM = 3.43), all interpreted as Always Observed.  The findings highlight the importance of sustained, differentiated, and assessment-based literacy interventions. Accordingly, a proposed Early Literacy Enhancement and Reading Performance Improvement Plan was developed, focusing on decoding, fluency, vocabulary, comprehension, individualized reading support, teacher development, and home-school collaboration.</jats:p>
title: Literacy Performance Patterns of Key Stage 1 Learners Across CRLA Diagnostic and First-term Assessments: Basis for Instructional Improvement

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The application of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) in pediatric neurosurgery is on the rise, especially in the field of neuroimaging. However, the literature on the application of AI/ML in pediatric neurosurgery is fragmented. In pediatric neurosurgery, there are challenges in the application of AI/ML, especially in terms of sample size, developmental considerations, and safety.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In order to systematically review the applications of AI in pediatric neurosurgery across the following domains: (1) diagnosis and image-based classification, (2) surgical planning and patient selection, and (3) prediction of treatment response and clinical outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A systematic literature search was performed on electronic databases like MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore from database inception to August 31, 2025, and was updated prior to manuscript submission. Human studies published in English language and conducted on children with neurosurgical conditions and age ≤ 18 years were included. The included studies should involve AI/ML and deep learning techniques for diagnosis, surgical planning, and outcome prediction in hydrocephalus, brain tumors, epilepsy surgery, traumatic brain injury, and neonatal brain injuries. Total 20 studies were included in this systematic review. The bias was evaluated with tools like QUADAS 2, PROBAST, and Cochrane RoB 2. GRADE was used to grade the evidence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among the 20 studies, 8 related to hydrocephalus, 6 to brain tumors, 2 to epilepsy surgery, and 4 to traumatic or hemorrhagic brain injury. Twelve studies evaluated diagnosis and segmentation, and eight focused on outcome prediction. Deep learning models demonstrated high performance in ventricular segmentation and tumor classification (Dice 0.85–0.95; accuracy 84–95%). In addition, prognostic models demonstrated moderate discrimination (AUC 0.70–0.90), though they frequently lacked external validation. One randomized study demonstrated that NLP-based alerts improved timely referral for epilepsy surgery compared with usual care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AI techniques show significant promise in pediatric neurosurgery, particularly for ventricular volumetry, tumor imaging, and surgical decision-making. Most published works currently rely on retrospective study designs, emphasizing a critical need for multicenter validation, calibration reporting, and prospective clinical trials before widespread implementation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                    <jats:title>Clinical trial number</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Not applicable.</jats:p>
